## Cycle-6 verdicts — the G-13 / G-12 screen applied, and the five frontier families

These are the **current-state** verdicts, in the same style and with the same standing as the
Cycle-5 verdicts block: they supersede any earlier text on the same questions for current-state
purposes and leave the cycle-by-cycle gap text in place at the end of this file.

### Cycle-6 verdict on G-13 (publication timing) and G-12 (sign or existence) — applied to every active candidate

The Cycle-5 closure left two general questions standing (G-13: is the state published **before** the
decision? G-12: can a published state change the **sign** or **existence** of an effect, or only its
measurement quality?). Cycle 6 applied both as **screening conditions to every active candidate**,
and the results are recorded candidate-by-candidate in `idea_register.md`. The ledger's own entries
supply the institutional facts the screen turned on. The summary:

| Candidate | G-13 (state published before the decision) | G-12 (conditioning changes sign or existence) | Cycle-6 outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| IDEA-001 RECON-FLOW | **Pass** — the announcement is published before the effective close | **Pass on the existence limb only** — the side asymmetry (additions yield a harvestable spread, deletions do not); the flow-scaling limb conditions *size* only | Retained, re-scored, novelty stays 2/5 |
| IDEA-003 VRP-STATE | **Pass** — the gate is computed from live exchange-quoted option surfaces | **Pass** — the gate flips the *sign* of the premium's harvestability | Retained, unchanged |
| IDEA-004 SLOWCAP-COND | **Pass, conditionally** — the 13F-based crowd state is published on EDGAR within 45 days of each quarter end, so a quarterly-anchored rule is decision-time feasible; the binding constraint is proxy *validity* (G-04), not timing | **Pass** — a non-monotone conditioning implies a sign flip | Retained, re-scored |
| IDEA-005 ROLLCONCESS | **Pass** — COT is published before the roll window | **Fail** — the closest published test of its own state variable is null (S-099) and the family's post-2012 aggregate result is null (S-033); no located work supports the joint state | **Parked (P-009)** |
| IDEA-008 SECURITY-LEND | **Fail** — the named state (lending fee / borrow availability) is not publicly disseminated until **29 March 2029** at the earliest (S-126); the short-interest fallback is twice-monthly with a ~7–8 business-day publication lag (S-127) | **Pass in principle** (the event exists only when the constraint binds) — moot once G-13 fails | **Parked (P-010)** |
| IDEA-009 PERP-FUND | **Pass** — the venue publishes the funding rate for each period with zero lag | **Pass** — the level of the funding rate determines the *sign* of the position | Retained, unchanged |
| IDEA-010 CREDIT-ETF | **Partial** — the flow leg (shares outstanding) is published daily; the differentiating state (AP balance-sheet stress) is commercial | **Pass on the existence limb**, but the joint state is unpublished | Retained, re-scored down to 65.0 |
| IDEA-011 ACCTCLOCK | **Pass** — adoption calendars are regulator-published years ahead | **Pass** — the drift's existence depends on the information-quality state | Retained, re-scored |

### The five frontier families — screen verdicts (one search round each; all verdicts registered)

The Cycle-5 handoff named five mechanism families that had not been screened. Each was screened in
Cycle 6 against the published literature, one search round each, and **every verdict is registered
here including the negative ones**, as the handoff required.

- **Family 1 — statutory, date-bound obligations outside the EU ETS (the IDEA-013 template in a
  different market). VERDICT: MECHANISM FAMILY UNCLAIMED IN THIS FORM; ONE NEW CANDIDATE WRITTEN
  UP (IDEA-014).** The template — a price-insensitive, date-bound purchase obligation whose
  concession is paid by the obligated party — is published for the EU ETS (S-101: surrender-month
  returns "averaging more than 10% in Aprils"), so that version is a baseline. The **US Renewable
  Fuel Standard** is the same template with a different regulator, a different obligor population
  and, decisively, **a state that is published before the decision**: the obligation's size is
  codified in advance (S-128, S-130), the deadline is a published, derived quantity (S-129), and
  the deadline has already been moved once by published rule (S-131) — a fact that is itself a
  warning to any rule built on it. The RIN price is a studied, peer-reviewed object (S-134, S-135),
  it has a *published* price series (S-132) and a *tradeable* futures venue (S-136). No located
  work presents a **state-conditioned compliance-deadline concession** in this market. The
  controlling negative is cost and liquidity: the RIN market is documented as roughly one-tenth as
  liquid as comparable commodity futures, with transaction costs peaking at five times theirs, and
  as pricing near-expiry vintages *above* longer-lived ones (S-133). **This is a bounded negative:
  one search round was run, and the residual is precisely specified in G-15.**
- **Family 2 — sovereign issuance calendars (US Treasury quarterly refunding). VERDICT: PUBLISHED —
  BASELINE.** The quarterly refunding announcement is an issuer-run, published, recurring event
  (S-143), and its price consequences are already the subject of published work: a paper
  decomposing "debt supply shocks using Treasury auction announcements" (S-142) and a paper on
  "pre-refunding announcement gains" in Treasuries (S-144). The announcement-window question is
  therefore *not* a discovery, and the announcement is a **news** event whose surprise component
  requires expectations that are not published, so the residual is not a state-conditioned
  concession at all. No candidate.
- **Family 3 — fast-payment rails (FedNow, UK RTP, EU TIPS). VERDICT: PUBLISHED MECHANISM, NO
  CANDIDATE STRUCTURE — BASELINE.** The mechanism is published and documented: instant payments
  raise banks' liquidity demand because they remove the ability to delay and net payment flows
  (S-140), and 24/7 settlement is modelled as inducing a precautionary demand for central bank
  balances with upward pressure on the overnight rate (S-141). But the family's decision-time
  object is a **rail's adoption curve**, not a dated obligation: there is no date-bound,
  price-insensitive flow to capture, and the effect is a *level* shift in reserve demand that is
  repriced as it is learned rather than conceded. No candidate.
- **Family 4 — sovereign bond index inclusion and exclusion. VERDICT: PUBLISHED, PEER REVIEWED —
  BASELINE.** Inclusion-driven flows into local-currency sovereign debt indices are a published
  causal object: sovereign yields fall and the currency appreciates (S-137), rebalancing flows move
  prices, deepen the market and appreciate the currency with placebo tests around the event
  (S-138), and the scale and the correlated-yield consequences are documented institutionally
  (S-139). The equity-reconstitution analogue is IDEA-001's own territory. No candidate.
- **Family 5 — physical-delivery calendars in commodity futures. VERDICT: PUBLISHED MECHANICS —
  BASELINE.** The inventory-and-convenience-yield channel that makes a delivery calendar a price
  determinant is already registered in this ledger (S-038, S-039), the roll mechanics that generate
  the delivery-month pattern are peer reviewed (S-145 alongside S-032, S-033, S-034, S-036), and
  the *published* state the family would need — exchange warehouse stocks and delivery calendars —
  is the same published-inventory channel already in the baseline set. No candidate.

### New gaps opened in Cycle 6

- **G-14 (new) — a public borrow-cost / securities-lending-rate series.** Opened in Cycle 6 by the
  IDEA-008 parking. The binding constraint on IDEA-008 is not that no lender reports loan rates —
  it is that **no institution publishes them on a public schedule before 29 March 2029** (S-126).
  Until then, the candidate cannot be specified on public data, and re-specifying it around a
  different state (short interest, short volume, dealer-balance-sheet proxies) would be exactly
  the substitution the register's own rules forbid, because those measures do not measure borrow
  cost. **Unblocking condition, dated:** on or after 29 March 2029, re-read the Rule 10c-1a
  dissemination data (the RNSA's public reporting of Rule 10c-1a information, including loan-rate
  terms) and test whether a public, dated, security-level borrow-cost series exists with a
  publication date that precedes a decision date; only then re-open IDEA-008. Also note that the
  related aggregate short-position regime (Rule 13f-2 / Form SHO) has its own dated start —
  "until January 2, 2028" (S-126) — and is a *different* measure (positions, not borrow cost).
- **G-15 (new) — the RIN compliance-deadline price pattern.** Opened in Cycle 6 by the IDEA-014
  write-up. The question is precisely: **does the published weekly volume-weighted-average RIN
  price series (S-132) show a systematic difference between the pre-deadline and post-deadline
  windows, and is the sign of that difference predicted by the published net obligated position
  (published RVO minus published RIN generation)?** Three things are needed and none is available
  in this repository: (i) the price series itself, by RIN type, around the statutory deadlines
  (S-129), including the two *moved* deadlines in 2026 (S-131); (ii) the net obligated position
  state, which requires EPA's published generation data reconciled against the codified standards
  (S-128, S-130) and the small-refinery exemptions; (iii) a cost estimate for the venue, against
  the published market-quality evidence (S-133). **The sign is not asserted anywhere in IDEA-014** —
  it is the candidate's first empirical test, and it is why the candidate is scored at 60.0 and not
  higher.

  **Cycle 7 (bounded search verdict):** A bounded literature/search round (peer-reviewed RIN literature
  S-134, S-135; market-quality S-133; EPA regulatory texts S-128–S-131; EPA price/generation pages
  S-132) found **no published work that identifies a price pattern around the RFS compliance-reporting
  deadline conditioned on the published net obligated position, or that states the sign of such an
  effect.** EPA acknowledges the market may need time to react to compliance/SRE decisions (S-131) but
  provides no sign/magnitude. The deadline is known to move (S-131). The cost floor is material
  (S-133). **G-15 is therefore closed as a bounded negative on the published-literature side: the
  conditioning variable is unclaimed in the literature, so IDEA-014 is not a re-description of a
  published result; it remains a candidate.** Its sign is still unasserted and remains the candidate's
  first empirical test. Score unchanged at 60.0.
  (S-133). This is a **bounded negative** — novelty/sign remains untested; the search converted
  "unsearched" to "searched once and not found". The candidate stays at **60.0** (rank 7) pending
  data reconstruction/cost estimation; no validation specification written.
- **G-16 (new) — a public, validated proxy for dealer balance-sheet stress in credit.** Opened in
  Cycle 6 by the IDEA-010 re-score. IDEA-010's *differentiating* state is AP balance-sheet stress,
  which is commercial; the published substitutes (the Federal Reserve's standing repo facility
  take-up, TRACE dealer-position and interdealer-spread measures) are *different constructs* and
  have not been validated against any dealer-balance-sheet measure. The register does not permit
  re-specifying around an unvalidated proxy, so IDEA-010 is retained **only** with the condition
  that this validation is performed before any specification is written.

---

## Cycle 8 — primary gaps (bounded-negative closures, 2026-10-20)

- **G-16 — closed as bounded negative (literature side).** Web research confirms no freely available, decision-time public proxy for dealer balance-sheet stress in credit: dealer balance-sheet data remain proprietary/non-public, and published substitutes (standing repo facility take-up; TRACE dealer-position and interdealer-spread measures) are different constructs that have not been validated against any dealer-balance-sheet measure. IDEA-010's precondition therefore remains unmet; IDEA-010 stays retained only on the condition that a validated proxy is later found, and no validation specification is written. (Consistent with the prior handoff's stated finding; the search provider rate-limited during this cycle, so this is a bounded negative, not an exhaustive search.)
- **G-04 — IDEA-004 crowd-depth proxy validity: closed as bounded negative (literature side).** A bounded search confirms no freely available, decision-time public crowd-depth series exists for U.S. equities. The 13F-based crowding measures (S-026, and subsequent commercial implementations) are published with the 45-day filing lag and are stale for intraday/multi-day   decision timing in the sense required; borrow depth and true exit capacity remain broker-gated/proprietary and are not published. The publication cadence is feasible on a quarterly-anchored rule (filing cadence), so the binding constraint is proxy *validity*, not timeliness. IDEA-004 (rank 2) therefore remains constrained by this unclosable data gap (parked in effect on this precondition); no new public proxy was identified.

## Cycle 13 additions (S-146 … S-174) — the index-reconstitution corpus, the single-name variance-premium literature, the crowding proxies, and six frontier screens

Cycle 13's centre of gravity is the published 2024–2026 literature on index reconstitution. Four
entries (S-146, S-147, S-148, S-151) together determine the fate of the register's rank-1 candidate,
IDEA-001. The remainder close or bound the open gaps and record the frontier screens.

### S-146 — Greenwood, R. and Sammon, M. (2025)
"The Disappearing Index Effect." *The Journal of Finance* 80(2): 657–698.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.13410 · working-paper version: NBER Working Paper No. 30748
(December 2022), DOI https://doi.org/10.3386/w30748
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (peer-reviewed), with a published working-paper version.
- **Supports:** the S&P 500 *index effect* has collapsed. The abnormal return associated with an
  addition has fallen from an average of 7.4% in the 1990s to **less than 1% over the past decade**;
  deletions, which had large negative abnormal returns in the 1980s–1990s, average **0.1% between
  2010 and 2020**. The working-paper version of the same study reports the same collapse on a slightly
  different vintage of numbers (3.4% in the 1980s, 7.6% in the 1990s, **0.8%** over the past decade;
  deletions **−0.6%** for 2010–2020) — the *magnitudes are version-dependent, the collapse is not*.
  The working paper also states that "there is no apparent relationship between net purchases
  [by index trackers] and the index inclusion effect, for either additions or deletions", and reports
  an average inclusion effect in 2020 of **−3 basis points**.
- **Caveats:** the paper's "index effect" is the cumulative market-adjusted return from the last
  trading day before the announcement to the first trading day after implementation, decomposed into
  an announcement return and an implementation return — i.e. the same window IDEA-001 leg 1 trades.
  The working-paper text was read through the HBS-hosted PDF via the search index; the published
  abstract was read on the Wiley landing page via the search index; the NBER abstract was fetched
  directly.
- **Verification:** NBER working-paper page fetched directly (title, authors, abstract, December 2022
  issue date, DOI, and the "Published Versions" line pointing to JF 80(2) 657–698); Wiley and HBS
  landing pages read via the search index; DOI and journal metadata verified through the Crossref
  REST API.

### S-147 — Pegoraro, L., Sammon, M. and Shim, J. (2026)
"Optimal Index-Linked Rebalancing with Anticipatory Trading." Working paper, May 2026 draft
(SSRN 6772502).
URL: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6772502
- **Type:** Primary theory + prior empirical result (author-reported), **working paper — not
  peer-reviewed**.
- **Supports:** the mechanism that explains S-146. Speculators act as *anticipatory liquidity
  providers* around reconstitution: they pre-position before the effective date, which "shifts price
  pressure away from the reconstitution date"; "apparent front-running reflects competitive liquidity
  provision and benefits index investors"; trading costs decline as speculator competition rises;
  short interest **rises on implementation dates and falls afterwards** as speculators cover; the
  authors estimate that avoidable rebalancing costs borne by index-linked investors are small.
- **Caveats:** working paper; the principal application is the S&P 500; the specific empirical
  magnitudes quoted for implementation-day effects were read through the author's summary page and a
  2026 arXiv preprint that cites them, not from the paper's own tables.
- **Verification:** author/institution pages and the SSRN record read via the search index; SSRN
  direct fetch returned HTTP 403. **— Cycle-97 re-fetch attempt: NEGATIVE, recorded as an honest failed
  route, NOT an upgrade.** `https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6772502` was tried on
  21 October 2026 and returned **HTTP 403, 5,578 bytes (text/html)** — the SSRN bot block. The
  anticipatory-liquidity-provision mechanism, the "shifts price pressure away from the reconstitution
  date" claim, the short-interest-rises-on-implementation-dates finding and the small-avoidable-costs
  estimate therefore remain author-reported and index-rendered, **not line-verified**. This entry is
  unchanged in substance and is not re-scored.
- **Verification (Cycle 104):** Crossref posted-content REST `https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2139/ssrn.6772502` fetched directly (HTTP 200, 16,637 bytes; JSON). Deposited abstract confirms speculators act as liquidity providers at index reconstitution, trading costs decline with competition, pre-positioning shifts price pressure away from the reconstitution date, apparent front-running reflects competitive liquidity provision and benefits index investors, and avoidable rebalancing costs borne by index-linked investors are small relative to general price impact estimates. **Upgrade:** claims now line-verified at abstract level (not just author-summary/index-rendered). Annotation written into entry in Cycle 104.

### S-148 — Chinco, A. and Sammon, M. (2024)
"The passive ownership share is double what you think it is." *Journal of Financial Economics* 157:
103860.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2024.103860
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports:** (i) the passive ownership share of U.S. equities was **33.3% in 2021**, roughly double
  the 16% figure implied by index-fund ownership alone; (ii) a **construction method** for
  benchmark-specific tracked assets: for each index, the AUM tracking it is inferred from
  reconstitution-day closing volume, for the Russell 1000, Russell 2000, S&P 500, S&P MidCap 400 and
  Nasdaq 100, over 2000–2021; (iii) passive rebalancing "gets executed at the closing price on
  reconstitution day". This is the published answer to the register's G-02/G-07 question (how one
  might estimate the size of index-linked assets for a *specific* benchmark) and part of the answer
  to G-03.
- **Caveats:** the published estimates are annual point estimates for five indices through 2021, not
  a downloadable daily series; the underlying input is per-security closing-auction volume, whose
  long history is commercial; the paper is about the *size* of passive assets, not about price
  effects of reconstitution.

  meta-refresh to `/retrieve/articleSelectSinglePerm?Redirect=...&key=50ffba6...`, i.e. the Elsevier

### S-149 — State Street Global Advisors (2026)
"Closing time: How passive investing is reshaping equity market microstructure." SSGA Investment
Management Insights, 23 January 2026.
URL: https://www.ssga.com/au/en_gb/institutional/insights/how-passive-investing-reshaping-microstructure
- **Type:** Institutional research / marketing communication from the index manager itself
  (**interested party**).
- **Supports:** the effective-close convention directly, in the index manager's own words: "Index
  funds and ETFs are structurally incentivized to execute trades at the closing auction because
  official net asset values (NAVs) are calculated using closing prices, and any deviation can result
  in tracking error. Consequently, Market-on-Close (MOC) orders have become the dominant mechanism
  for end-of-day execution." Also: the US closing auction was **15.39% of daily volume in December
  2025** versus 8.40% in January 2018; developed-Europe 34.82%; Asia ex-Japan 16.78%.
- **Caveats:** an interested party describing its own practice; not an independent measurement of
  where passive funds actually trade; no rule text, no audit.
- **Verification:** page fetched directly (full text read, including the quoted sentence and the
  volume-allocation table).

### S-150 — Goyal, A., Jegadeesh, N. and Wu, Y. (2026)
"Price Impact in Closing Auctions, Opening Auctions, and Continuous Markets: A Benchmark for Cost of

DOI: https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022109026102592
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (peer-reviewed).

### S-151 — Sammon, M. and Shim, J. (2026)
"Who Clears the Market When Passive Investors Trade?" *The Review of Financial Studies* 39(10):
3330–3377.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhag032
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports:** the counterparty to a passive fund's demand is **the issuing firm itself** (firms are
  the primary sellers who clear index-fund buying), and most demand-side institutions trade *in the
  same direction* as index funds — i.e. passive demand is not offset by an opposing arbitrageur who
  would pay away the concession. This is the structural argument that the price concession at
  reconstitution is not naturally competed away, and it is the strongest published evidence *for*
  IDEA-001's persistence thesis.
- **Caveats:** it is evidence about who the counterparty is, not about the size of any price
  concession in the modern sample; the two papers must be read together with S-146 and S-147.
- **Verification (Cycle 104):** Crossref REST `https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/rfs/hhag032` fetched directly (HTTP 200, 29,377 bytes; JSON). Deposited abstract confirms firms are the primary sellers who clear the market for index fund buying (nearly one-for-one), most demand-side institutions trade in the same direction as index funds rather than accommodating passive demand, firms causally respond to exogenous passive demand with prices as coordinating mechanism, and they satisfy passive demand mostly through nonprimary market issuance (e.g. employee stock-based compensation). **Upgrade:** claims now line-verified at abstract level. Annotation written into entry in Cycle 104.

("Index Rebalancing and Stock Market Composition: Do Index Funds Incur Adverse Selection Costs?")
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (peer-reviewed), with a sign-flipped working-paper version.

ScienceDirect paywalled. **Honest negative** — entry remains index-rendered. Annotation written into entry in Cycle 105.

"The Price of Correlation Risk: Evidence from Equity Options." *The Journal of Finance* 64(3):
1377–1406.

### S-154 — Carr, P. and Wu, L. (2009)
"Variance Risk Premia." *The Review of Financial Studies* 22(3): 1311–1341.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhn038
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports (as a bounded negative for IDEA-003's single-name version):** variance risk premia on
  individual stocks are frequently **statistically indistinguishable from zero**; the negative premium is a
  large-index phenomenon (the S&P 100 carries a strongly negative, strongly significant premium), and
  the individual-stock premium that does exist is explained by exposure to a **common market variance
  risk factor** (a significant "variance beta" slope) rather than by single-name variance
  risk. **Cycle-107 correction:** the third limb as previously recorded ("individual-stock returns do
  not load on a variance risk premium factor") was **contradicted by the paper's own factor analysis
  and has been struck**; the second limb's wording "frequently zero or positive" has been corrected to
  "frequently statistically indistinguishable from zero". See the Cycle-107 verification bullet below
  for the verbatim evidence. **Cycle-109 re-base (the *published* body is now obtained, and the entry's
  figures are re-based on it):** the working paper's magnitudes are **retired** and replaced by the

    estimate* on one factor does flip positive, but that is S-153's individual variance risk factor at

    papers are consistent once read together.) The entry's Supports line is therefore **corrected in
    place** to read: individual-stock variance risk premia are **frequently statistically
    indistinguishable from zero**, while the negative premium is a large-index phenomenon.
  - **Limb 3 — CONTRADICTED, and struck in place.** The entry's third limb reads "individual-stock

    each single stock, but only prices the variance risk in the stock market portfolio. Based on this
    hypothesis, the average variance risk premium on each stock is not proportional to the total
    variation of the return variance, but **proportional to the covariation of the return variance with
    the market portfolio return variance**." It then estimates "LRPj = 0.0201 + 0.2675 β²V,j + e" and
    reports: "**The slope estimate is statistically significant and positive at 95 confidence level** …
    the market charges premium not on the total variance risk for each stock, but on its **covariance
    with a common variance risk factor**." Individual stocks therefore **do** load significantly and
    positively on a market variance risk factor. The third limb is **struck**, and the entry's corrected
    Supports line reads: individual-stock variance risk premia are frequently statistically

    individual-stock premium that does exist is explained by exposure to a **common market variance

  pypdf and read. The paper's own words confirm the construct verbatim: "**We demonstrate that the

### S-177 — Dew-Becker, I. and Giglio, S. (2025)
"The Decline of the Variance Risk Premium: Evidence from Traded and Synthetic Options." Chicago Fed Working Paper No. 2025-17, September 2025.

- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), working paper — not peer-reviewed.
- **Supports (for IDEA-003):** equity index options historically displayed sharply negative returns and CAPM alphas, but over the past ~15 years option alphas have become indistinguishable from zero; synthetic options never had negative alpha over the last 100 years, indicating equity investors never required high compensation for market downturns. An intermediary-based model explains both patterns, including the recent decline in the variance risk premium. Consistent with IDEA-003's state-gate framing: the unconditional harvest has weakened, so the gate on *when* to harvest is the load-bearing claim.
- **Caveats:** working paper; documents the decline in traded-option alphas but does not itself specify or test a gate; the aggregate VRP as a published object is unaffected (only harvestability is questioned).

## Cycle 14 (continued) gap verdicts

- **G-18 — BOUNDED NEGATIVE (no validated substitute; V-002 stays frozen).** G-18 asks whether a return-correlation crowding measure (comomentum, S-157: Lou & Polk 2021, RFS 35(6): 3272–3302) is a valid substitute for a holdings-based crowding measure (S-026: Brown, Howard & Lundblad 2021, RFS 35(7): 3231–3271, built from 13F-style hedge fund holdings with up-to-a-quarter reporting lag). S-157 shows comomentum is *correlated with* existing arbitrage-activity proxies, including institutional ownership of the winner decile (13F-based) and Chen–Da–Huang (2019) net arbitrage trading (abnormal hedge fund holdings minus abnormal short interest), and that comomentum forecasts momentum returns, volatility and skewness. But S-157 never tests whether comomentum is a valid *substitute* for the holdings-based measure, and no head-to-head validation of correlation-based vs holdings-based crowding was located in a bounded search across thirteen cycles. The closest comparison is a factor-crowding study (Dell, "Crowding and Factor Returns", SSRN 3803954) which finds its direct position-based crowding measure remains significant while the Lou–Polk correlation-based proxy adds little incremental predictive power once position-based crowding is included — i.e. the holdings-based measure subsumes rather than is replaced by the correlation-based proxy. Conclusion: comomentum is decision-time and free (S-157) but is **not a validated substitute** for S-026's holdings-based crowding. IDEA-004 must not be re-specified around an unvalidated proxy (register method). **V-002 (IDEA-004) remains frozen pending G-18 closure.** If a direct validation/comparison paper is located in a future cycle, G-18 can be reopened; otherwise it stands as a bounded negative.

### S-180 — Konstantinidi, E. and Skiadopoulos, G. (2016)
"How does the market variance risk premium vary over time? Evidence from S&P 500 variance swap
investment returns." *Journal of Banking & Finance* 62: 62–75.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbankfin.2015.10.006 · working-paper version: SSRN 2502822
(https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.2502822, 2014).
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), peer-reviewed.
- **Supports (for IDEA-003):** the variance risk premium's time variation is predictable from
  decision-time state variables, and **volatility-trading strategies that condition on those states
  outperform both buy-and-hold and the naive short-volatility strategy even after transaction
  costs**; the best-performing specification conditions on trading activity; and broker-dealers
  command a larger premium when trading conditions (their funding) deteriorate, extending the
  broker-dealer funding result of Adrian and Shin. For the register this is **prior art for the
  state-conditioned harvest**: "gate the variance-risk-premium harvest on a decision-time state" is
  a published *strategy family*, not an unclaimed idea. IDEA-003's residual is therefore narrowed to
  (i) the *state* — an option-surface-implied imminent-crash signal rather than trading activity —
  and (ii) the *sign* claim (the premium's harvestability, not merely its size, flips).
- **Caveats:** the paper measures the premium from **variance-swap quotes**, not from listed
  options, and the conditioning variable is trading activity rather than crash risk; it predates the
  modern option market structure (0DTE and retail flow, S-169) and therefore predates S-177's
  finding that traded-option alphas have decayed to approximately zero; it does not test a
  crash-state gate.
- **Verification:** **Crossref API fetched directly** — title, both authors (Eirini Konstantinidi,
  George Skiadopoulos), journal (*Journal of Banking & Finance*), volume 62, pages 62–75, issue date
  2016-01, DOI 10.1016/j.jbankfin.2015.10.006, Elsevier BV, ISSN 0378-4266, and the Elsevier PII
  S0378426615002836 all confirmed in the response. The working-paper identifier (SSRN 2502822,
  DOI 10.2139/ssrn.2502822) was returned by the same Crossref query in a separate row and is
  recorded on that basis. The quoted findings come from search-index excerpts of the published
  abstract and article text (including the working-paper version); the Crossref reference list also
  shows the paper citing Adrian and Shin's "Liquidity and leverage" (*Journal of Financial

### S-181 — Ahmed, S. (2026)
"The Variance Risk Premium Across Markets and Regimes: A Downside, Crash-Conditional Risk Premium,
Not Harvestable Carry." SSRN working paper 7046559, dated 3 June 2026.
URL: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7046559
- **Type:** Preprint (author-reported), **not peer reviewed**.
- **Supports (for IDEA-003 — both as prior art and as a convention warning):** the paper characterises
  the variance risk premium as "a downside, crash-conditional risk premium, compensation for a
  systematic tail rather than harvestable carry"; states that the premium "is crash-conditional only
  in an entry-timing sense (selling volatility into a jump loses)"; states that "the regime-average
  premium stays positive through every crisis and widens in high-stress and high-credit-spread
  states, when fear over-prices the volatility that subsequently mean-reverts"; and concludes that
  the premium is not harvestable carry because "even voltargeted and overlaid it retains an
  irreducible left tail". In register terms: **(a) the *interpretation* the candidate is built on —
  the premium as compensation for a tail, and the harvest's entry timing as the binding risk — is
  now published in the candidate's own vocabulary; (b) the published *sign* in crash-adjacent states
  is the opposite of the candidate's naive reading, because the paper measures the premium ex post;
  and (c) the residual left tail is documented against the harvest.**
- **Caveats:** a single-author preprint with no refereeing and author-reported magnitudes (an
  annualised Sharpe above six in a calm year; a cross-sectional information coefficient up to 0.84);
  **its premium is defined as option-implied minus *subsequently realized* volatility**, an
  ex-post convention, whereas IDEA-003's gate claim is about the *expected* premium (model-free
  implied minus the physical conditional expectation of variance) — the two conventions can move in
  opposite directions in the same state, which is precisely why the candidate's specification must
  now name its convention; the underlying datasets are the author's own assembled files, not
  independently reproduced here.
  **Cycle 105 provenance:** Crossref REST API `api.crossref.org/works/10.2139/ssrn.7046559`
  (posted-content record) returned HTTP 200 with a deposited abstract (abstract present: yes)
  confirming the VRP as downside/crash-conditional risk premium, not harvestable carry. Upgrade
  recorded in place.
- **Verification:** read via the search index (SSRN abstract-page render); the SSRN identifier
  7046559, the date 3 June 2026 and the abstract wording come from that render. The SSRN page
  itself was not fetched directly in this cycle, so the entry is **index-rendered, not
  independently verified**.

  available before the trades it describes.

Cycle 32's sources fall into four blocks: (i) the two entries minted in Cycle 31 but never written
into this ledger (S-188, S-189 — the ledger repair); (ii) the expected-premium corpus that closes
**G-19** for IDEA-003 (S-190 … S-193); (iii) the dealer-balance-sheet and ETF-arbitrage corpus that
closes **G-16** for IDEA-010 (S-194 … S-200); (iv) the EPA rule corpus that closes **G-20** for

### S-188 — Forbes, W.P. and Giannopoulos, G. (2015) — *repaired Cycle-31 entry*
"Post-Earnings Announcement Drift in Greece." *Review of Pacific Basin Financial Markets and Policies*
18(3): 1550019.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1142/S0219091515500198
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports (for IDEA-011, as a partial prior-art hit):** in the Greek market, 2000–2006 earnings
  announcements (announcement years 2001–2007), "PEAD [is] alive and well, and of growing importance
  in our Greek sample", and the authors attribute it to IFRS adoption: "It may be the adoption of
  international financial reporting standards (IFRS) has served to reduce earnings predictability in
  Greece and thus enhance PEAD in the Athens stock exchange (ASE) market." This is a published case in
  which **IFRS adoption *increases* rather than shrinks** post-adoption drift — directionally the
  candidate's effect, and the opposite of the candidate's stated hypothesis.
- **Caveats:** the result is market-specific (Greece: a small market with a code-law accounting
  regime, thin pre-IFRS disclosure and high individual-investor participation) and the mechanism the
  paper offers is a *reduction in the intensity of accounting conservatism and increased earnings
  volatility* under fair-value accounting — a disclosure-environment shock, not necessarily the
  candidate's comparability clock. It is a single-market study; it does not test a trading rule.
- **Verification:** OpenAlex API fetched directly (DOI, journal, volume, issue, article number, both
  authors, publication year 2015); the abstract and the quoted sentence were read via the search
  index rendering of the publisher page (10.1142/S0219091515500198); a longer author-revision
  discussion of the mechanism was read via the search-index rendering of the authors' ResearchGate
  copy of the revised manuscript.

### S-189 — Brochet, F., Jagolinzer, A.D. and Riedl, E.J. (2012) — *repaired Cycle-31 entry*
"Mandatory IFRS Adoption and Financial Statement Comparability." *Contemporary Accounting Research*
30(4): 1373–1400.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1111/1911-3846.12002 · working-paper version: Harvard Business School
Working Paper 11-109.
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports (for IDEA-011, as a partial prior-art hit):** UK firms, whose domestic standards were
  already close to IFRS, are used to isolate the *comparability* channel from information quality.
  "Abnormal returns to insider purchases — used to proxy for private information — are reduced
  following IFRS adoption"; the working-paper version quantifies the insider-purchase abnormal return
  decline at **4.2%** in six-month windows and the analyst-recommendation-upgrade decline at **2.9%**,
  robust across sub-samples isolating the comparability effect. **Mandatory IFRS adoption reduces
  insiders' ability to exploit private information** — consistent with the candidate's own
  comparability channel.
- **Caveats:** the *direction* of the drift implied by reduced private-information advantage is the
  opposite of the candidate's hypothesis (a better public information set should *reduce* drift, and
  this paper is evidence for that); it is a UK-firm study, and it measures information asymmetry
  rather than post-adoption drift. It is a mechanism-consistency citation, not a replication of the
  candidate's claim.
- **Verification:** OpenAlex API fetched directly (DOI, journal, volume, issue, pages, three authors,
  2012); the abstract and the quantified 4.2%/2.9% figures were read via the search-index rendering
  of the HBS working-paper PDF (hbs.edu/ris/Publication Files/11-109).

### S-190 — Rombouts, J.V.K., Stentoft, L. and Violante, F. (2020)
"Dynamics of variance risk premia: A new model for disentangling the price of risk." *Journal of
Econometrics* 217(2): 312–334.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2019.12.006 (first published online December 2019; issue
dated 2020)
- **Type:** Primary theory plus estimation (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports (for G-19, decisively, and in two directions):**
  (i) *The expected-premium convention is stated explicitly.* The variance risk premium is defined as
  "the difference between the risk neutral and physical expectations of an asset's total return
  variation", i.e. Π_t = E^Q[Σ_{t,t+1}] − E^P[Σ_{t,t+1}] — exactly the register's IDEA-003
  convention.
  (ii) *The sign in distress states has been tested under that convention.* The paper's central
  methodological finding is that the "vast majority of the literature estimates the VRP period-by-period
  using ex-post realisations ignoring its latent nature and temporal dependence", and that "such
  practice leads to a VRP that is too volatile and **systematically becomes negative, rather than
  largely positive, in periods of market distress**." The paper's own latent decomposition then
  reports that the continuous component of the VRP "is characterised by level and variance shifts,
  strong persistence, **is systematically positive and is higher in periods of market turmoil**".
  (iii) The paper does not impose sign constraints on the jump component.
- **Caveats:** the latent premium is a *model-based* conditional expectation (realized-volatility
  processes plus regime switching), not a raw filtered conditional expectation; the estimate is
  conditional on the model; and the paper prices the *equity* variance risk premium, not a
  single-name or option-surface-implied quantity. It is a decomposition of a published premium, not
  a test of a gated trading rule.
- **Verification:** Crossref REST API fetched directly (DOI, title, three authors, journal, volume,
  issue, pages, publication date 2020-02) and OpenAlex API fetched directly (work record, journal
  *Journal of Econometrics* 217(2), pp. 312–334, online-first year 2019); the abstract and the quoted
  passages were read via the search-index rendering of the publisher and SSRN records.

### S-191 — Zhou, J. (2018)
"Variance Risk Premia, Asset Predictability Puzzles, and Macroeconomic Uncertainty." *Annual Review of
Financial Economics* 10: 481–497.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-financial-110217-022737 · earlier working-paper version: Federal
Reserve Bank of St. Louis FEDS 2010-014, "Variance Risk Premia, Asset Predictability Puzzles, and
Macroeconomic Uncertainty."
URL (working paper): https://www.stlouisfed.org/research/publications/wp/2010-014
- **Type:** Review article (peer-reviewed), with a verified working-paper version.
- **Supports (for G-19):** the expected-premium convention is defined in the review's own notation:
  "The variance risk premium is defined as the difference between the ex-ante risk neutral expectation
  of the future return variance and the objective or statistical expectation of the return variance
  over the [t, t+1] time interval, VRP_t ≡ E^Q_t(Var_{t,t+1}) − E^P_t(Var_{t,t+1})", and the review
  states the *measurement* problem explicitly: the risk-neutral expectation "is typically replaced by
  the CBOE implied variance or VIX²" and the physical expectation is replaced either by a discretised
  realisation or by a filtered/model-based conditional expectation. The review is the standard
  reference for the distinction between the two conventions that G-19 asked about.
- **Caveats:** a review, not a new empirical test of the sign in crash-imminent states; the review's
  empirical content is on the *predictability* of asset returns from the premium, not on a
  state-conditional sign. It does not test an option-surface-implied crash state.
- **Verification:** Crossref REST API fetched directly (DOI, title, author, journal, volume, pages,
  2018); the definition and the measurement-problem passage were read via the search-index rendering
  of the Federal Reserve working-paper PDF (federalreserve.gov FEDS 2010-014). The Annual Reviews
  publisher page returned HTTP 403 to a direct fetch, so the review's own text is index-rendered and
  the definition is quoted from the verified working-paper version.

### S-192 — Bekaert, G., Engstrom, B. and Ermolov, M. (2023)
"Variance Risk Premium in Equilibrium Models." *The Review of Finance* 27(6): 1977–2014.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1093/rof/rfad005 · working-paper version: NBER Working Paper No. 27108
(October 2020), DOI https://doi.org/10.3386/w27108
- **Type:** Primary theory (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports (for G-19, and the single most direct statement on the sign of the *expected* premium in
  bad states):** "The equity variance risk premium is the expected compensation earned for selling
  variance risk in equity markets. **The variance risk premium is positive and shows only moderate
  persistence. High variance risk premiums coincide with the left tail of the consumption growth
  distribution shifting down.**" The expected premium is therefore (a) positive and (b) *larger* in
  states where the consumption left tail is worse — i.e. in bad, crash-prone states the expected
  premium widens rather than collapses.
- **Caveats:** an equilibrium model of the *equity* variance risk premium; the "bad state" is a
  consumption-tail state, not an option-surface-implied imminent-crash state, so the identification is
  at the level of state co-movement rather than at the level of the candidate's specific gate. It
  makes no claim about a gated trading rule.
- **Verification:** Crossref REST API fetched directly (DOI, title, three authors, journal
  *Review of Finance*, volume 27, issue 6, pages 1977–2014, 2023) with the abstract retrieved in the
  same record; the NBER working-paper identification was confirmed in the search index.

### S-193 — Gruber, M., Tebaldi, E. and Trojani, A. (2021)
"The Price of the Smile and Variance Risk Premia." *Management Science* 67(7): 4056–4074.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2020.3689
- **Type:** Primary theory plus estimation (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports (for G-19, as the closest published sign-flip in a variance-premium quantity in bad
  states):** the published abstract states that "the more persistent volatility factor and the
  skewness factor support a downward sloping term structure of variance risk premia in normal times,
  whereas **the most transient volatility factor accounts for an upward sloping term structure in
  periods of distress**". The earlier working-paper version of the same paper states that the estimated
  variance risk premia are "highly time-varying and unambiguously negative" on the Carr–Wu sign
  convention (i.e. unambiguously *positive* compensation) across the sample, while "the variance term
  premium may change sign".
- **Caveats:** the sign-flip is in the **term** premium (the slope of the variance-premium term
  structure), not in the *level* of the expected premium; the working-paper text is index-rendered
  rather than read from a publisher PDF in this cycle. It is the closest published analogue of a
  "variance-premium quantity changes sign in distress", and it is recorded here so that the register
  does not overstate the novelty of that observation.
- **Verification:** Crossref REST API fetched directly (DOI, title, three authors, journal
  *Management Science*, volume 67, issue 7, pages 4056–4074, 2021-04-01) with the published abstract
  retrieved in the same record; the working-paper variant of the abstract was read via the search-index

### S-194 — Raddatz, C.E. (2025)
"Authorized participants' regulatory constraints and limits to ETF arbitrage during market turmoil:
Evidence from the dash-for-cash episode." *Journal of Banking & Finance* 179: 107499.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbankfin.2025.107499
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports (for G-16, and it is the decisive citation for that gap):** the paper builds a dataset
  linking each US corporate-bond ETF to its authorized participants "using U.S. SEC regulatory
  filings", connects the APs to their financial statements, and measures **APs' regulatory capital
  ratios** — a *disclosed, filing-based* state. The finding is that APs' regulatory capital ratios
  conditioned the ETF arbitrage relationship during the March 2020 dash-for-cash: ETFs linked to APs
  at the 25th percentile of regulatory capital ratios saw a **0.69 percentage-point decline in
  arbitrage intensity**, against **0.39 percentage points** for ETFs linked to 75th-percentile APs;
  and "other AP characteristics, such as equity-to-assets ratios, cash-to-assets ratios, total assets,
  or AP activity concentration, do not play a significant role."
- **Caveats:** the outcome variables are the *elasticity of ETF arbitrage intensity* and ETF premia,
  not the level of the ETF–NAV discount and not a trading return; the episode is a single
  market-stress window; the AP capital ratios are quarterly-filed and therefore lagged, and the
  ETF↔AP mapping requires a bespoke construction from filings. It identifies the state; it does not
  test the candidate's two-legged rule.
- **Verification:** OpenAlex API fetched directly (DOI, title, author, journal *Journal of Banking &
  Finance* 179, article 107499, 2025) and the abstract and quoted figures were read via the
  search-index rendering of the publisher's ScienceDirect record.
- **Cycle-76 note on a related earlier version (recorded, not relied on).** The published result has a
  **documented earlier working-paper version with a different state variable**: "Does the Diversity and
  Solvency of Authorized Participants Matter for Bond ETF Arbitrage? Evidence from the Dash for Cash
  Episode", Claudio E. Raddatz K., University of Chile Department of Economics Working Paper wp519
  (2021), listed in RePEc under `udc:wpaper:wp519`. Its abstract states that "high AP **leverage** played
  a significant role in weakening this arbitrage during the dash-for-cash episode", with "the strength of
  the arbitrage relationship linking price signals to primary market activity weakened by 77 percent in
  ETFs related to more leveraged APs versus 64 percent for ETFs linked to less leveraged APs", and it
  notes that "AP leverage constraints operated in parallel to constraints faced by lead-market makers
  in secondary ETF markets, which were more closely related to regulatory capital limits". **The
  working-paper PDF was not retrieved in Cycle 76** (the RePEc record was fetched directly, HTTP 200;
  the publisher's own download endpoint and the University of Chile publication page both failed — the
  latter returning HTTP 404), so the passage above is **index-rendered** and **is not relied on for any
  claim**; it is recorded because it bears on the register's assessment of the candidate's *state*: the
  published relation has now been stated twice with **two different state variables** (leverage in the
  2021 version, regulatory capital ratios in the 2025 published version), which is a fact about the
  *published* strength of the relation, not about the candidate's residual.

### S-195 — Pan, K. and Zeng, Y. (2017; working-paper versions to 2019) — *corrects the register's citation*
"ETF Arbitrage under Liquidity Mismatch." ESRB Working Paper No. 59 (December 2017); NBER/LTAP
conference version (June 2017); SSRN working-paper version (SSRN 2895478, posted 8 January 2017, last
revised 30 March 2019).
DOI: https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.2895478 · PDF: https://www.esrb.europa.eu/pub/pdf/wp/esrb.wp59.en.pdf
- **Type:** Primary theory plus empirical result (**working paper, not peer-reviewed**).
- **Supports (for IDEA-010, and it is the source of the register's own "Pan & Zeng 2019" reference):**
  the paper formalises the AP dual-role conflict — "APs are also bond dealers and they use their own
  balance sheet in both roles" — and shows that "bond market illiquidity limits ETF arbitrage" and that
  "large bond flow shocks to AP balance sheets also limit ETF arbitrage, leading to persistent relative
  mispricings". Empirically: "An increase of 1% in the ETF premium generates an increase in AP
  arbitrage by 50 basis points; however, as market volatility rises, holding fixed the ETF premium, AP
  arbitrage declines"; the sensitivity decline "is asymmetrically larger when the ETF premium is
  negative"; and when APs hold extreme bond inventory imbalances, creations and redemptions can move
  "in the opposite direction than what would be implied by the initial relative mispricing".
- **Caveats (material, and they bear on G-16):** the paper's datasets are **proprietary** — "novel
  AP-level data", a "proprietary version of TRACE" with FINRA dealer identifiers, "proprietary
  time-series data on the daily creation and redemption baskets" for each ETF, and proprietary AP lists
  from two ETF sponsors covering "on average 83% of the total passive corporate bond ETF assets under
  management". This is the empirical provenance of the register's belief that "AP-level data is
  commercial"; the *published evidence* is proprietary-based even though the *state construct* is
  publicly reconstructable (S-194). The paper is a working paper, and the register's Cycle-6 citation
  "Pan & Zeng 2019" should be read as this SSRN revision date.
- **Verification:** search-index render of the ESRB working-paper PDF and the SSRN record (both
  authors, title, abstract, keywords, dates, DOI) and of the authors' hosted PDFs (Harvard scholar
  repository, NBER conference repository); the substantive quotations above were read from those
  renderings. No publisher version was located, so the entry is recorded as a working paper.
  **— Partly superseded in Cycle 76: the ESRB PDF was fetched directly and text-extracted, so the December 2017
  version's own passages are now line-verified; see the Cycle-76 upgrade bullet below. The SSRN 2019 revision's
  wording remains index-rendered.**
- **Cycle-76 verification upgrade — the entry is now partly line-verified, and one quotation-provenance
  correction is recorded.** The **ESRB working-paper PDF itself was fetched directly (HTTP 200, 1,504,861
  bytes, 74 pages) and text-extracted on 20 October 2026**; the title page ("Working Paper Series No 59 /
  December 2017 · ETF arbitrage under liquidity mismatch · by Kevin Pan, Yao Zeng") is **line-verified**,
  and the following passages are now **line-verified from the December 2017 ESRB version**:
  (i) the abstract's core claim — "we identify a conﬂict between APs' dual roles as bond dealers and as
  ETF arbitrageurs. When this conﬂict is small, liquidity mismatch reduces the arbitrage capacity of

  arbitrage, leading to large relative mispricing"; (ii) the empirical magnitude and its conditioner —
  "An increase of 1% in the ETF premium generates an increase in AP arbitrage by 50 basis points; however,
  as market volatility rises, holding xed the ETF premium, AP arbitrage declines: a one standard
  deviation increase in market volatility generates a 10% decline in AP arbitrage. Moreover, the decrease
  in arbitrage sensitivity is asymmetrically larger when the ETF premium is negative"; (iii) the general
  conditioner list — "the sensitivity of ETF arbitrage by APs is declining in market volatility, bond
  market illiquidity and costs of trade"; (iv) the sign-reversal mechanism — "ETF arbitrage may go in the

  provenance of the proprietary data — "we obtain a proprietary version of TRACE, which is a dataset of
  all secondary market corporate bond transactions, with dealer identiers from FINRA" and the two ETF
  sponsors' AP lists "which constitute our data sample, represents on average 83% of the total passive
  corporate bond ETF assets under management".
  **Quotation-provenance correction (no claim, magnitude, verdict or identifier changes):** the three
  strings quoted in the "Supports" bullet above — "APs are also bond dealers and they use their own
  balance sheet in both roles", "bond market illiquidity limits ETF arbitrage" and "large bond flow

  exact 2019 wording is still index-rendered. **No register verdict rests on the wording of those three
  strings.**
- **Cycle-76 new consequence for IDEA-010 (a published competitor conditioner).** The line-verified
  passage in (iii) is a **published conditioner of the same ETF-arbitrage relation the candidate
  conditions on — market volatility, bond-market illiquidity and trading costs** — and it is *available

### S-196 — Shim, J. and Todorov, K. (2021)
"ETFs, illiquid assets, and fire sales." BIS Working Papers No. 975 (**November 2021**).
URL: https://www.bis.org/publications/working-paper-975-etfs-illiquid-assets-and-fire-sales ·
PDF: https://www.bis.org/publications/working-paper-975-etfs-illiquid-assets-and-fire-sales.pdf ·
preprint version: SSRN 3886881, DOI https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3886881
- **Type:** Primary theory (institutional working paper).
- **Supports (for IDEA-010, as a published rival explanation for the ETF–NAV discount):** the model has
  "an ETF discount arises because the AP acts as a buffer between the ETF and the bond market, allowing
  the ETF price to fall while avoiding selling bonds in quantities that would trigger a fire sale",
  and it documents that "bond ETF baskets contain a small fraction of holdings ('fractional baskets'),
  which contributes to persistent discrepancies between ETF price and NAV". A discount can therefore
  arise from *basket composition*, with no AP balance-sheet constraint involved.
- **Cycle-78 upgrade — the document's own wording, and what it settles.** The entry was **index-rendered**
  until Cycle 78; the BIS PDF was then fetched directly (HTTP 200, 1.7 MB, **54 pages**, text extracted with
  `pypdf`) and the quoted passages are **line-verified**. The document's own wording is: "the portfolio of
  bonds that are exchanged for new or existing ETF shares (called creation or redemption baskets) often
  represents a small fraction of ETF holdings – a fact that we call '**fractional baskets**'"; "**ETFs with
  fractional baskets exhibit persistent premiums and discounts**, which is related to the slow adjustment of
  NAV returns to ETF returns"; and "We develop a simple model to show that an ETF's authorized participants
  (APs) can act as a **buffer** between the ETF market and the underlying illiquid assets, and help mitigate
  fire sales." The index-rendered sentence quoted above is a **paraphrase of this content, not the paper's
  wording**; the substance is confirmed and the wording is now given from the document. **Date correction:**
  the working paper is dated **November 2021** (cover page and landing page; the manuscript's own first page
  reads 14 July 2021, and the SSRN preprint is 2021) — the entry's earlier "June 2022" was wrong. **This
  bears directly on the parking of IDEA-010 (P-014):** the paper publishes a **mechanical** account of the
  corporate-bond ETF's ETF–NAV discount — **persistent** premiums and discounts tied to basket composition —
  in the candidate's own universe, and no published work separates it from a **transient** reading (G-34).
- **Caveats:** a model paper; the fractional-basket mechanism is not shown to dominate the AP-capacity
  mechanism empirically in this entry; the SSRN version is a **different, still index-rendered** document
  from the BIS working paper read here, and the register quotes the BIS version.
- **Verification:** **line-verified in Cycle 78** — the current BIS landing page was fetched directly (HTTP
  200; its JS shell carries the PDF link `…/working-paper-975-etfs-illiquid-assets-and-fire-sales.pdf`; the
  legacy URL `https://www.bis.org/publ/work975.htm` now **301-redirects** to that landing page and
  `https://www.bis.org/publ/work975.pdf` returns a JavaScript challenge rather than the PDF), and the PDF
  was fetched directly (HTTP 200, 1.7 MB, 54 pages) with its text layer extracted by `pypdf`; the OpenAlex
  API record for the SSRN preprint (title, two authors, DOI 10.2139/ssrn.3886881, 2021) was fetched directly

### S-197 — Siriwardane, E.N., Sunderam, A. and Wallen, J. (2025)
"Segmented Arbitrage." *The Journal of Finance* 80(5): 2543–2590.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.13469 · working-paper version: NBER Working Paper No. 30561
- **Type:** Primary theory plus empirical result (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports (for IDEA-010, as a published rival explanation):** the paper documents that
  **arbitrage spreads are sensitive to idiosyncratic balance-sheet shocks** and that
  "balance sheets are segmented — intermediaries specialize in certain trades", so the *funding source*
  rather than the AP's bond-inventory capacity is a first-order determinant of an arbitrage spread.
  For IDEA-010 this is a rival explanation for any ETF–NAV gap conditioned on intermediary
  constraints, and it supplies the register's best published template for what a *funding-segmented*
  arbitrage spread looks like.
- **Cycle-78 upgrade — line-verified, and the scope is wider than the entry recorded.** The NBER
  working-paper PDF was fetched directly (HTTP 200, 1.3 MB, **60 pages**, text extracted with `pypdf`), and the
  quoted passages are now the document's own words: "First, **funding is segmented**—certain trades rely on
  specific funding sources, making their arbitrage spreads sensitive to localized funding shocks. Second,
  **balance sheets are segmented**—intermediaries specialize in certain trades, so arbitrage spreads are
  sensitive to **idiosyncratic balance sheet shocks**." The paper studies **29 arbitrage spreads across the
  equity, fixed-income and foreign-exchange markets**, with an **average pairwise correlation of 21 %** — so
  it is *not* confined to the secured-funding setting the entry described: it is the register's broadest
  published statement that **arbitrage spreads are a function of the intermediary's constraint**, which is
  exactly the family-level support (and the rival) that IDEA-010's mechanism sits in.
- **Caveats:** the paper studies arbitrage spreads in intermediated settings, not bond-ETF arbitrage directly;
  its proxies for funding conditions and its identification are specific to its own setting and are not a
  substitute for a decision-time dealer-stress state for IDEA-010; the working-paper version (October 2022)
  is the document read here, and the *Journal of Finance* version (2025) is a later publication of the same
  work whose wording has not been separately verified.
- **Verification:** **line-verified in Cycle 78** from the NBER working-paper PDF (HTTP 200, 1.3 MB, 60 pages,
  text extracted with `pypdf`); OpenAlex API fetched directly in an earlier cycle (DOI, title, three authors,
  journal *Journal of Finance* 80(5), pp. 2543–2590, 2025) and the NBER working-paper DOI (10.3386/w30561)
  confirmed in the same query; the abstract had previously been read only through the search-index rendering of
  the publisher and NBER records.

### S-198 — Hempel, K., Kim, J. and Wermers, M. (2022)
"Financial Intermediary Funding Constraints and Segmented Markets: Evidence from SMCCF ETF Purchases."
Office of Financial Research Working Paper 22-01 (February 2022).
URL: https://www.financialresearch.gov/working-papers/22-01
- **Type:** Primary empirical result (institutional working paper).
- **Supports (for G-16, and it is the register's best *public* candidate for the missing AP/dealer
  balance-sheet state):** the authors state that "while we do not have information on AP-level
  inventories, we can indirectly infer their corporate bond inventories from **public FR 2004
  disclosures on aggregate primary dealer activities**", and they use that inference to measure
  positive AP balance-sheet shocks (funding for the Federal Reserve's SMCCF bond-ETF purchases) and
  their spillovers to ETF prices and to the underlying bonds.
- **Cycle-78 upgrade — line-verified, and the paper publishes the candidate's *universe*, not only the
  state.** The OFR PDF was fetched directly (HTTP 200, 1.3 MB, **75 pages**, text extracted with `pypdf`) and
  the quoted passage is the document's own: "While we do not have information on AP-level inventories, we can
  indirectly infer their corporate bond inventories from **public FR 2004 disclosures on aggregate primary
  dealer activities**." The document also publishes the AP-balance-sheet account **in the corporate-bond ETF
  universe itself**: SMCCF ETF purchases "generated intraday spillover price effects on a relatively short
  horizon (within 15 minutes) to other corporate bond ETFs with overlapping holdings"; corporate bonds with
  more exposure to the APs of the purchased ETFs "experienced lower yield spreads (higher prices)"; and
  "ETFs with greater overlap with SMCCF-purchased ETFs experience higher net inflows the day after closing
  at a price premium to NAV". **This is material to the parking of IDEA-010 (P-014):** the mechanical,
  intermediation-driven reading of the candidate's outcome is published in the candidate's own universe, and
  the state that identifies it is a **one-off policy episode**, not a continuously published decision-time
  state — which is the substance of the G-34 verdict.
- **Caveats:** the FR 2004 inventory series is an *aggregate* measure across primary dealers, not an
  AP-level or ETF-level measure; the inference is indirect and the paper's own events (SMCCF
  purchases) are policy-specific, so the series is a candidate state, not a validated decision-time
  variable for IDEA-010's daily rule; the **landing page URL recorded in this entry has moved** (the old
  `/working-papers/22-01` path now returns HTTP 404) and the document is read at its current address.
- **Verification:** **line-verified in Cycle 78** — the OFR PDF was fetched directly (HTTP 200, 1.3 MB, 75
  pages, text extracted with `pypdf`) at
  `https://www.financialresearch.gov/working-papers/files/OFRwp-22-01_financial-intermediary-funding-constraints-and-segmented-markets.pdf`;
  the entry had previously been verified only from a search-index rendering of the OFR landing page and PDF
  (title, three authors, report number 22-01, February 2022, and the FR 2004 passage). The SSRN mirror
  (4031881) was also attempted from a third-party mirror and returned **HTTP 403**, so the OFR copy is the
  document relied on.

### S-199 — Comerton-Forde, M., Ford, J., Foucault, P. and Jurkatis, T. (2025)
"Investors as a liquidity backstop in corporate bond markets." Bank of England Staff Working Paper
No. 1126 (**May 2025**).
URL: https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/working-paper/2025/investors-as-a-liquidity-backstop-in-corporate-bond-markets
- **Type:** Primary empirical result (institutional working paper).
- **Supports (for IDEA-010, as a published baseline for the "concession paid to liquidity providers"
  structure):** the paper documents that dealers pay "relationship discounts" to investors for past
  liquidity provision — roughly two thirds of the observed dealer discount is attributed to liquidity
  services — and that dealers' balance-sheet constraints shape corporate-bond liquidity. This is
  published evidence that a *dealer balance-sheet constraint expressed as a concession to the
  counterparty who supplies liquidity* is a documented market structure, which is the register's
  closest published baseline for the type of edge IDEA-010 claims.
- **Cycle-78 upgrade — line-verified, with a date correction and two additional magnitudes.** The Bank of
  England PDF was fetched directly (HTTP 200, 2.0 MB, **62 pages**, text extracted with `pypdf`). The
  document's own abstract reads: "During the March 2020 Dash-for-Cash, in bonds where investors stopped
  providing liquidity, transaction costs rose by **38%**"; "Dealers offer discounts to investors for past
  liquidity services to maintain liquidity provider networks. These discounts represent **two thirds of
  relationship discounts**." **Date correction:** the paper is **Staff Working Paper No. 1126, May 2025**
  (published 16 May 2025), not April 2025 as the entry recorded. Two further magnitudes, useful to the
  register's cost-floor argument: a client with one percentage point higher share in liquidity provision
  "receives an additional 0.1 bps discount on all trades, including deal trades", and hedge funds "receive
  a discount twice as large as the next closest client type".
- **Caveats:** the concessions documented are to *client liquidity providers* in the dealer sector, not
  to the ETF arbitrage channel; the paper is a staff working paper, and the discount decomposition is
  estimated at the dealer-client relationship level.
- **Verification:** **line-verified in Cycle 78** — the Bank of England PDF was fetched directly (HTTP 200,
  2.0 MB, 62 pages, text extracted with `pypdf`) at
  `https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/-/media/boe/files/working-paper/2025/investors-as-a-liquidity-backstop-in-corporate-bond-markets.pdf`;
  the entry had previously been verified only from a search-index rendering of the landing page (report
  number 1126, four authors, and the quoted relationship-discount finding).

### S-200 — Eisfeldt, A.L., Herskovic, B. and Liu, S. (2024)
"Interdealer Price Dispersion and Intermediary Capacity." NBER Working Paper No. 32998 (September 2024).
DOI: https://doi.org/10.3386/w32998
- **Type:** Primary empirical result (working paper; the register's "Eisfeldt et al. 2024").
- **Supports (for G-16, with two constraints on IDEA-010's state):**
  (i) the paper's own proxy for intermediation capacity is **interdealer price dispersion** from TRACE,
  and it is explicitly a *proxy*: dispersion measures "the negative effects of interdealer frictions and
  risk misallocation within the dealer sector". It is validated against model-based **fair-value
  spreads** and a "fair-value basis", not against any disclosed dealer funding value adjustment.
  (ii) two facts bear directly on IDEA-010's feasibility: "given the infrequent trading of bonds,
  calculating interdealer price dispersion daily is not feasible. For our baseline results, we measure
  bond-level interdealer price dispersion using the standard deviation in all interdealer trades
  occurring each **month**" — so the published dispersion measure is **monthly**, not daily; and the paper
  finds that "equity-weighted averages of dealer-level financial soundness **fail** to capture effects
  from interdealer frictions", i.e. aggregate dealer-balance-sheet averages are documented to be
  *inferior* proxies for intermediation capacity than the dispersion measure.
- **Caveats:** a working paper; the fair-value validation depends on a structural model and on equity
  data; the monthly frequency of the published measure is the binding constraint for a rule with a
  1–10 session holding horizon. It is *not* a validation of any proxy against disclosed dealer FVAs,
  which remains an unperformed exercise (and, per S-155, is not a sensible target anyway).
- **Cycle-78 upgrade — line-verified.** The NBER working-paper PDF was fetched directly (HTTP 200, 1.6 MB,
  **129 pages**, text extracted with `pypdf`) and both quoted passages are the document's own: "Given the
  infrequent trading of bonds, calculating interdealer price dispersion daily is **not feasible**. For our
  baseline results, we measure bond-level interdealer price dispersion using the standard deviation in all
  interdealer trades occurring each **month**."; and "**Equity-weighted averages of dealer-level financial
  soundness fail to capture effects from interdealer frictions** on risk misallocation within the dealer
  sector" (the document itself prints "soundness" as "**soundess**", a typo; the entry's quoted word is the
  correct spelling, and the document's form is recorded here so that a future re-check matches it). The paper
  adds that it computes dispersion **weekly** as a robustness exercise, so the monthly frequency is a
  *baseline* choice rather than a hard limit — but it remains the **published** measure's frequency, and the
  register's 1–10 session rule stands against it.
- **Verification:** **line-verified in Cycle 78** — the NBER working-paper PDF was fetched directly (HTTP
  200, 1.6 MB, 129 pages, text extracted with `pypdf`) at
  `https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w32998/w32998.pdf`; the OpenAlex API record (DOI, title,
  three authors, NBER WP 32998, 2024) had been fetched directly in an earlier cycle, and the quoted passages
  had previously been read only through the search-index rendering of the NBER working-paper record.

### S-201 — U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (2026)
"Renewable Fuel Standard Program: Reallocation of Volumes and Other Modifications" (the "Set 2 Rule").
91 FR 16388 (April 1, 2026); Federal Register document 2026-06275.
URL: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/04/01/2026-06275/renewable-fuel-standard-program-reallocation-of-volumes-and-other-modifications
- **Type:** Primary regulator material (final rule).
- **Supports (for G-20):**
  (i) *The volume requirement is calibrated to the agency's own supply projection.* The rule's statutory
  factor analysis uses the "Analyzed Volumes" (the agency's projected supply) and states that "the
  total quantity of renewable fuel we project will be supplied to the U.S. to meet these volume
  requirements (shown in Table I.A.1-2) are very similar to the quantities we projected would be supplied
  to meet the proposed volume requirements" — i.e. the RVO is set so that the *projected* supply meets
  it, so the *projected* net obligated position is near zero by construction.
  (ii) *Where the projection falls short, the shortfall is institutionally absorbed, not expressed as a
  binding market obligation.* For 2025 cellulosic: "our estimate of the number of 2025 cellulosic RINs
  that will be produced is 1.21 billion gallons … equivalent to 1.21 billion RINs. This projected volume
  is 0.17 billion fewer RINs than the 1.38 billion RINs needed to comply with the original 2025
  cellulosic biofuel standard, a shortfall of approximately 13 percent. We therefore find that the
  shortfall … triggers the need for implementation of the cellulosic waiver authority for 2025."
  (iii) The rule's own projection of the **2025 exempted** fuel volume is **7.55 billion gallons**,
  derived by "projecting … a three-year average of the actual exempted fuel volumes from 2022 through
  2024" — a lagged average, not a forecast of the current year's exemption decisions.
  (iv) The 2026 and 2027 standards include small refinery exemption (SRE) reallocation volumes of
  **0.99 billion RINs (2026)** and **1.04 billion RINs (2027)**.
- **Caveats:** the rule's tables are published as images in the Federal Register text version, so the
  billion-RIN volumes in Table I.A.1-1 were read from the agency's own summary of the rule (S-203)
  rather than from the table images; the quotations above are from the raw text version, which was
  fetched directly from the Federal Register's document server.
- **Verification:** the raw text of the rule was fetched directly from the Federal Register document
  server (`/documents/full_text/text/2026/04/01/2026-06275.txt`), and the document metadata
  (title, citation, publication date, raw-text URL) was verified through the Federal Register API.

### S-204 — Mann, S.V. and Powers, E.A. (2006)
"Determinants of bond tender premiums and the percentage tendered." *Journal of Banking & Finance*
31(3): 547–566.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbankfin.2005.12.008 · earlier working-paper version: SSRN 475561
(7 December 2003), DOI https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.475561
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports (for this cycle's new-venue family screen):** the price-insensitive flow at a published
  debt-tender deadline is a **published, quantified** object: "For the average (median) tender offer,
  the tender price is 4.75 (3.40) percent greater than the pre-tender market price while the
  percentage of bonds tendered is 82.3 (94.6) percent"; "a one percent increase in tender premium
  increases the tendering rate by as much as 10%"; and tenders are easier to complete when bond
  ownership is concentrated.
- **Caveats:** the paper studies the *determinants* of the tender premium and the tendering rate, not
  the price path of the bond into and around the tender deadline; it is an announcement-and-outcome
  study of corporate bond tenders, not a deadline-cluster study.
- **Verification:** OpenAlex API fetched directly (published record: title, two authors, journal
  *Journal of Banking & Finance* 31(3), pp. 547–566, 2006, DOI) and the working-paper abstract and
  highlights read via the search-index rendering of the SSRN record (SSRN 475561).
