  major private AP firms; the JSON was parsed and the cadence computed from the report-date fields.

### S-241 — Mitchell, M. L., Pulvino, T. C. and Stafford, E. (2004), "Price Pressure around Mergers", *The Journal of Finance* 59(1), 31–63. DOI: 10.1111/j.1540-6261.2004.00626.x
- **Type:** prior empirical result (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports:** the **prior-art limb of the G-28 verdict on IDEA-004** and the correction of the
  register's published-neighbour inventory. The paper uses **short interest** as the published
  measure of **merger-arbitrage short selling** and attributes part of the acquirer's announcement
  reaction to that pressure; it also documents the closing-date index-rebalancing run-up and its
  reversal for index-tracking strategies.
- **Why it matters to the register.** The candidate may not present a short-interest-based measure of
  convergence activity in merger spreads as a discovery: the construction is published, and the
  mechanism (short selling by merger arbitrageurs) is published with it.
- **Caveats:** the paper is about *merger* spreads and *announcement-window* price pressure, not about
  a *position-concentration* state or a two-sided crowding gate; the short-interest data it uses are
  exchange short-interest data, not FINRA's aggregated file.
- **Verification:** Crossref API fetched directly (title, three authors, *The Journal of Finance*,
  volume 59, issue 1, pages 31–63, 2004, DOI as above); the substance was confirmed from the
  publisher-record rendering and the abstract in the search index.

### S-242 — Hanson, S. G. and Sunderam, A. (2014), "The Growth and Limits of Arbitrage: Evidence from Short Interest", *The Review of Financial Studies* 27(4), 1238–1286. DOI: 10.1093/rfs/hht066
- **Type:** prior empirical result (peer-reviewed; online 11 October 2013, print 2014).
- **Supports:** the **prior-art limb of the G-28 verdict on IDEA-004**, and the correction of the
  register's crowding-measure inventory. Short interest is used as a **published crowding measure of
  arbitrage capital**, and the paper's central result is that the *limits* of that arbitrage bind
  precisely when the measured crowding is high.
- **Why it matters to the register.** IDEA-004's dossier listed only 13F-based and correlation-based
  crowding measures (S-026, S-157, S-222) as the published neighbours. The short-interest branch
  exists and is peer-reviewed; the candidate must now engage it.
- **Caveats:** the crowd measured is *style* arbitrage capital (value, momentum and other anomaly
  strategies), not the pair/merger-spread convergence crowd the candidate's universe requires, and
  the published relation is monotone where the candidate claims a two-sided gate.
- **Verification:** Crossref API fetched directly (title, two authors, *Review of Financial Studies*,
  volume 27, issue 4, pages 1238–1286, DOI as above).

### S-243 — Chan, H. and Tan, T. (2020), "Short Interest, Crowding and Liquidity Crises", SSRN working paper 3655131 (authors at AXA IM Chorus; University Paris Dauphine). DOI: 10.2139/ssrn.3655131
- **Type:** **working paper / institutional research** — *not* peer reviewed. Labelled as such here.
- **Supports:** the prior-art limb of the G-28 verdict, and the *cadence* comparison that makes the
  FINRA route's weakness precise. The paper uses **daily short interest** to infer near-real-time
  crowding levels of quantitative equity long-short strategies, and documents that crowding is
  associated with greater exposure to short-seller liquidity shocks.
- **Why it matters to the register.** It establishes both that a short-interest-based crowding measure
  is a *published construction* (so the candidate cannot present one as a discovery) and that the
  measure can be built at a cadence finer than the 13F grid the candidate's rule is anchored to —
  which is precisely why the FINRA route's defect is granularity and crowd attribution, not speed.
- **Caveats:** a working paper, not peer reviewed; the crowd measured is style arbitrage, not
  convergence capital; the data used are a commercial securities-finance dataset, not FINRA's public
  file.
- **Verification:** the SSRN record (DOI, authors, date) and the author-hosted PDF rendering were
  read directly, including the abstract and the data description.

### S-244 — U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, **final rule "Accredited Investor Definition"**, Release Nos. 33-10824; 34-89669, File No. S7-25-19, RIN 3235-AM19, 85 FR 64234 (9 October 2020), effective 8 December 2020.
- **Type:** primary regulator material (the rule itself).
- **Why it is in the ledger.** It is the **eligibility-switch instance** screened in Cycle 40's family
  screen (R-020): a switch in *who may hold* restricted securities, with a published compliance date
  and published thresholds. The rule amends the accredited-investor definition (adding new categories
  of qualifying natural persons and entities, and applying the same determination to the
  qualified-institutional-buyer definition in Rule 144A), keeps the $1 million net-worth and $200,000
  ($300,000 joint) income tests, and keeps the $100 million QIB threshold.
- **Why the screen closes.** The switch is published **in advance** of its effective date, and the
  *distance to the limit* for any given holder is private, so no published decision-time state binds
  a specific security; the obligor's flow is its own; and the number of switches is the effective
  sample.
- **Caveats:** the rule is a *definition* change with broad effects; the register did not attempt a
  price-impact measurement and did not claim one. The screen is a **family** verdict, not an
  empirical finding about this rule.
- **Verification:** the SEC's own rule page and the Federal Register version were fetched directly
  (release numbers, RIN, 85 FR 64234, effective date 8 December 2020) and the operative thresholds
  were read in the fetched text.

### S-245 — U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, **17 CFR 270.6c-11 — Rule 6c-11 under the Investment Company Act of 1940** (the "ETF rule"), as codified in the eCFR.
- **Type:** primary regulator material (the rule itself).
- **Why it is in the ledger.** It is the source for Cycle 41's G-30 sub-route (a) research: whether the SEC's ETF rule requires an ETF to publish the *identities* of its authorised participants on its website or in its prospectus. Read directly from the eCFR text: 6c-11(c)(1) requires daily website disclosure of portfolio holdings, NAV, premium/discount and bid-ask spread; 6c-11(d) requires recordkeeping of written AP agreements and per-basket records *including the identity of the AP transacting*. The rule does **not** require an ETF to publish AP identities publicly — AP identity is a recordkeeping item under (d), not a public-disclosure item under (c)(1).
- **Why the screen closes.** Sub-route (a) — the regulatory requirement route — is closed as a bounded negative: there is no regulatory requirement to publish AP identities; only a voluntary one. The only public-facing disclosure obligations are the portfolio/NAV/premium/spread items; AP identity is recordkeeping, not public disclosure.
- **Caveats:** the rule is read as codified in the eCFR; exchange listing rules (SR-filings on sec.gov) and Form N-1A appendices were not separately checked in this cycle but are noted as potential secondary routes under G-30.
- **Verification:** eCFR text read directly (6c-11(c)(1) disclosure items; 6c-11(d) recordkeeping items including AP identity).

### G-29 — **CLOSED AS A BOUNDED NEGATIVE for the public-filings route** (IDEA-010); coverage 0; and the
### first published AP set in the project is a **crypto trust**, which does not reach the candidate

**Verdict.** Cycle 40 executed the verification the gap asked for — *which corporate-bond ETFs name
their authorised participants in a public filing, and how many (ETF, AP) cells have both a published
AP-set membership and a public capital ratio* — as a document-level search with a **calibrated
detector**, and the answer is: **none, and zero**. The candidate is therefore **not specifiable from
public filings — untested, not dead** — and, per the register's standing rule, no published crowding
proxy may be substituted for the missing mapping.

**How the negative was made credible.** A negative about a population needs a detector known to work.
Cycle 40 first found and read a filing that genuinely names its APs — the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF's
Form 424B3 (S-239) — and used the naming sentence itself ("Authorized Participants that are able to
conduct …") as the detector phrase in the EDGAR full-text index. That detector returns **five documents
in four filers**, all digital-asset trusts, and **no corporate-bond ETF**. The complement of the
detector was run as well: the *phrase-first* route (591 bond-worded filings containing an AP-naming
sentence — every document that actually names APs in the naming position is a commodity or crypto
trust) and the *name-first* route (bond-worded filings containing any of thirty-one AP firm names —
where the names appear only in securities-lending "percentage of ownership" tables and in the
standing "an Authorized Participant may hold of record more than 25 % of the outstanding shares"
disclosure). Two sponsor product pages (iShares AGG, Vanguard BND) were probed directly and both use
the generic formulation without naming any AP, and the **unit-investment-trust** class was checked as a
separate structure (First Trust's corporate-bond 497K filings of 13 February 2025 and 2 March 2026):
they name **no** AP firm either.

**Corroboration (a second, independent detector).** A broader detector — every filing whose text
contains an authorised-participant naming position followed by corporate entity names, across sixteen
filing form types — was read document by document: **3,628 documents read at the end of Cycle 40 of a
4,409-document corpus** (the sweep was still running when the cycle closed and reported no contradicting
document), of which **434 name APs**, and **every one of the 434 is a commodity or crypto trust** —
iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (50), iShares Diversified Alternatives Trust (22), ProShares
Trust II (17), iShares Commodity Optimized Trust (15), SPDR Gold Trust (15), ETFS Platinum Trust (12),
WisdomTree Continuous Commodity Index trusts (19), iShares Ethereum Trust ETF (11), iShares Bitcoin
Trust (17 across two display names), iShares Gold Trust Micro (10), World Gold Trust (9), the Invesco
Galaxy Bitcoin and Ethereum trusts (16), Ark 21Shares Bitcoin ETF (7), Hashdex Nasdaq CME Crypto Index
ETF (7), abrdn Gold ETF Trust (7), iShares Dow Jones-UBS Roll Select Commodity Index Trust (7),
WisdomTree Bitcoin Fund (7), and others. **No corporate-bond ETF trust appears.**

**The name-first route, completed.** The bond-worded corpus (every filing containing an AP-firm
name and the word "Bond") came to **3,127 documents** and was read document by document: **3,124 read**
at the end of Cycle 40, **237 flagged**, and a strict re-check of every flagged document for a firm name
**in an authorised-participant naming position** returned **zero** true positives (the 33 apparent
matches were the substring "IMC" inside "PIMCO" — a reminder that firm-name regexes must be bounded
by word boundaries, a caution now recorded for future cycles).

**The three false-positive mechanisms, named so a future cycle does not re-derive them.** AP firm
names appear in ETF prospectuses in exactly three places, none of which is an AP list: (i) **
securities-lending "percentage of ownership" tables**, where the firm is a borrower of the fund's
collateral (verified: the Jane Street Capital entry in the iShares Trust SAI is a securities-lending
ownership row); (ii) **revenue-sharing and placement disclosure** (verified: the Pershing, RBC,
Schwab, TD Ameritrade, Morgan Stanley Wealth Management and Fidelity entries in the SPDR Series Trust
SAI are the payees of distribution-arrangement payments, not APs); and (iii) the standing disclosure
that "an Authorized Participant may hold of record more than 25 % of the outstanding shares" of a fund.

**The counts, which the gap asked for explicitly.**

| Quantity | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Corporate-bond ETFs with a published AP set in a statutory filing | **0** |
| (ETF, AP) cells with both a published AP set and a public capital ratio | **0** |
| (ETF, AP, episode) cells for the candidate's universe | **0** |
| ETFs (outside the candidate's universe) with a published AP set | 4 filers / 5 documents, all crypto or commodity trusts |
| Named AP firms in the one published set (S-239, 31 July 2025) | **13** (12 cash, 4 in-kind, 13 distinct) |
| Of those, firms with a public Form X-17A-5 filing | **13 of 13** |
| (AP, filing-date) episode cells for that set | **285** |
| Cadence of that set's capital state | **annual** for all thirteen (fiscal year-end; filed February–March) |
| Named AP firms filing a Form 10-Q or 10-K | **0 of 13** — X-17A-5 is the only public capital route for the entire set |

**What the candidate may and may not now say.** It may not present the AP capital ratio as a state
that can be attached to a corporate-bond ETF from public filings, because no such attachment exists;
it may not substitute a published crowding proxy (S-026's Days-ADV, S-157's comomentum, S-222's
crowding factor), which measures a different crowd; and it may not claim that the state is
*unavailable* — the state is abundantly available (2,419+ broker-dealer filers, S-231), it is the
*ETF → AP mapping* that is missing. The candidate is retained, not parked: what has closed is a
route, not the candidate.

**The new gap this creates — G-30.** The route is closed for *statutory filings*. It is not closed for
*all* primary sources. A corporate-bond ETF's AP set could still be published by the sponsor itself
(the ETF sponsor's own website or its published participant list), by a published exchange rule or
regulatory filing that requires it, or by a *non-US* issuer's prospectus. Cycle 40 probed two sponsor
product pages and found nothing, which is a probe, not a survey. **G-30 is therefore opened**: *is
there a published, primary-source route by which a corporate-bond ETF's AP set is disclosed outside
the statutory prospectus — and, if the sponsor publishes a list, does it exist for the corporate-bond
series as well as for the crypto and commodity series?* The register's answer must be a specific
route, not a re-reading of prospectuses.

### G-27 — **CLOSED at filer level** (IDEA-010), with two corrections to the register's own statements

**Verdict.** The effective-sample question the gap raised has been answered with counts taken from
the filings' own index rather than from document text, and two of the register's statements needed
correcting.

| Route | Instrument | Count | Cadence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A — private broker-dealers | Form X-17A-5 (FOCUS), phrase corpus (S-231) | **6,131 documents from 2,419 distinct filers** (a **lower bound**) | 2,414 filers once per year; five twice per year; **none three or more** |
| A' — the named AP set specifically | EDGAR submissions index (S-240) | 13 of 13 firms covered; **285 (AP, filing-date) cells** | **annual** for all thirteen |
| B — listed broker-dealers | Form 10-Q / Form 10-K | **1,151 documents / 66 filers** (10-Q, quarterly); **737 documents / 96 filers** (10-K, annual) | quarterly and annual; the only quarterly public capital route, and it does not reach the private APs |
| C — bank holding companies | Form FR Y-9C | **not enumerable through EDGAR**: the form is absent from EDGAR's full-text index (zero hits for "capital", "net capital", "Federal Reserve") | must come from the Federal Reserve's National Information Center; S-226 restated accordingly |
| D — asset-manager APs | — | no equivalent exists | coverage limit, not a fixable one |

**Correction 1 (S-231).** The phrase corpus counts *wordings*, not firms: Citadel Securities LLC files
24 X-17A-5 documents across 23 periods and contains the phrase in one of them, so 6,131 documents ≠
6,131 firms. Any firm-coverage question must be answered at filer level.

**Correction 2 (S-231 / Cycle 37).** The statement "quarterly for at least some private filers"
rests on a single document (Agentis Capital Markets US, LLC, period ending 2024-09-30) that does not
appear in the phrase corpus at all, and filer-level enumeration of the thirteen named AP firms and
fifteen major private AP firms found **annual cadence in every case**. The private-AP capital state is
therefore **annual**, and at any decision date it is **9–14 months stale**. The Cycle-35
cross-sectional re-anchoring survives this correction — indeed it is reinforced, because the state
never changes inside a holding window — and the Cycle-35 requirement that the effective sample be
reported is now given a concrete denominator.

### G-28 — **CONFIRMED OPEN and restated** (IDEA-004): the FINRA short-interest route is a lead with
### objections, and the published-crowding inventory was incomplete

**Verdict.** Cycle 40 tested the one route the handoff named — FINRA's twice-monthly short-interest
file (S-127) — against the candidate's pair structure, and recorded it as a **lead with objections**
rather than as a resolution. G-28 remains open; **V-002 remains frozen**; the candidate is not
re-scored.

**The facts (fetched directly from FINRA).** Firms must report short positions in all customer and
proprietary accounts in all equity securities twice a month, due by 6 p.m. ET on the second business
day after the designated settlement date, published the following Tuesday (the 2026 schedule is on
the page); the published data are **per issue**, covering all exchange-listed and OTC equity
securities, one rolling year online with archives by download, with **no firm-level breakdown**
(S-127, as extended in Cycle 40).

**The objections, written so a validator can act on them.**
1. **Granularity, not cadence, is what fails.** A per-issue aggregate across all reporting firms
   cannot identify the convergence crowd and cannot express its concentration; mapping it to pairs is
   a register-built construction with the same defect as the 13F holdings-matching route, and it
   cannot separate convergence capital from a coincident directional short. Note that the cadence
   objection that usually kills a route does **not** apply here: twice-monthly publication with an
   ~8-business-day lag is *faster* than the 45-day 13F grid the candidate's rule is anchored to.
2. **Contamination of the short leg.** In the classic pair trade the short leg is the recent winner,
   whose short interest also carries value, short-bias and index strategies; a pair-level aggregation
   would have to remove them, and the published data cannot.
3. **Prior art (new in this cycle).** Short interest is *already* the published measure of merger-arb
   shorting and its price pressure (S-241); short interest is *already* a published crowding measure of
   arbitrage capital (S-242); and daily short interest has *already* been used to infer near-real-time
   crowding of quantitative long-short strategies (S-243). The candidate may not present a
   short-interest-based convergence-activity measure as a discovery, and the register's own
   published-neighbour inventory for IDEA-004 was **incomplete** without the short-interest branch.
4. **What would actually close the gap.** A published measure of *convergence-crowd position
   concentration* in the candidate's own universe (pairs, merger-spread and index-convergence relative
   value) at the candidate's cadence, or a published validation of a construction against an outcome.
   The unfreezing condition is unchanged; the FINRA route is now named as a **third** candidate route
   alongside the 13F holdings-matching construction and the comomentum proxy, with its objections.

## Cycle 41 gap verdicts (2026-10-20)

### G-30 sub-route (a) — **CLOSED as a bounded negative** (IDEA-010): 17 CFR 270.6c-11 imposes no requirement to publish AP identities.
**Verdict.** 17 CFR 270.6c-11 (the SEC's ETF rule, S-245) defines "authorized participant" and requires daily website disclosure of portfolio holdings, NAV, premium/discount and bid-ask spread under (c)(1), and requires recordkeeping of written AP agreements and per-basket records *including the identity of the AP transacting* under (d). AP identity is a recordkeeping item, not a public-disclosure item. **Route (a) is therefore closed: there is no regulatory route, only a voluntary one.**

## Cycle 51 sources (2026-10-20)

Added for the Cycle-51 family screen of **closing-price formation** (randomised closes and real-time
closing-auction imbalance publication), logged as **R-031**. Five new sources; the register now holds
**S-001 … S-209** and **S-220 … S-251**.

### S-247 — Ellul, A., Shin, H. S. and Tonks, I. (2005)
"Opening and Closing the Market: Evidence from the London Stock Exchange." *Journal of Financial and
Quantitative Analysis* 40(4): 779–801.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022109000001976
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports:** the LSE's call-market opening and closing auctions are a studied institutional mechanism —
  the paper documents the call market's price-discovery properties relative to off-exchange dealing,
  failure rates, and trading costs that rise with the order imbalance and with asymmetric information.
  This is the published anchor for the *closing-mechanism* family: how the close is formed is
  documented, not an open question.
- **Caveats:** 2005 sample; London-specific; the paper is about the call market's price discovery and
  costs, not about randomised price formation as such.
- **Verification:** Cambridge Core landing page (title, authors, volume, issue, pages, DOI) read through
  the search index; the LSE working-paper version (Financial Markets, Institutions and Instruments
  discussion paper dp506) was seen in the search index with the passage describing the LSE closing
  call's random end within a bounded window. **Cycle 105 provenance:** Crossref REST API
  `api.crossref.org/works/10.1017/S0022109000001976` returned HTTP 200 with a deposited abstract
  (abstract present: yes) confirming the call-market price-discovery / high-failure-rate-to-open-and-close
  finding. Upgrade recorded in place.

### S-248 — Chelley-Steeley, P. (2009)
"Price synchronicity: The closing call auction and the London stock market." *Journal of Financial
Markets, Institutions and Money* 19(5): 777–791.
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports:** the introduction of the LSE's closing call auction is measured for its market-quality
  effects (price synchronicity, spreads, depth), with larger effects in less liquid names. The
  *market-quality* consequences of a closing-auction redesign are therefore published prior art.
- **Caveats:** one venue, one design change, 2000s sample; the paper is a design evaluation, not a
  statement about any tradeable concession.
- **Verification:** RePEc/IDEAS bibliographic record (author, title, journal, volume, issue, pages) read
  through the search index; the publisher page was not parsed directly in this session and the DOI was
  not verified.

### S-249 — Eom, K. S., Kwon, K. Y. and Park, J.-H. (2021)
"Effectiveness of the conditional random-end trading mechanism on the Korea Exchange: Normal trade and
Option Shock." *Journal of Futures Markets* 41(10): 1545–1568.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1002/fut.22223
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports:** randomised end-of-auction mechanisms are a published mechanism family. The Korea
  Exchange's conditional random end is reported to improve price discovery and stabilise the closing
  price in normal trading, with the benefit attenuating under high-volatility ("option shock")
  conditions — i.e. the randomised close is studied and its effects are characterised.
- **Caveats:** one exchange, one mechanism design, 2010s sample; the paper is not a study of a
  harvestable pre-close concession.
- **Verification:** citation metadata (authors, title, journal, volume, issue, pages, DOI) verified
  through the DOI resolver's Crossref record; the publisher article page returned HTTP 403 to the
  fetch, and the abstract was read through the search index. **Cycle 105 provenance:** Crossref REST
  API `api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/fut.22223` returned HTTP 200 with a deposited abstract
  (abstract present: yes) confirming the conditional random-end trading mechanism promotes price
  stabilization with reservations under option-shock conditions. Upgrade recorded in place.

### S-250 — Eurex Exchange (venue documentation)
"FTSE 100 Index Futures (FTUK)" — contract specifications (product page).
URL: https://www.eurex.com/ex-en/markets/idx/ftse/ftse-100/ftse-100-derivatives/FTSE-100-Index-Futures-2593796
- **Type:** Venue documentation (exchange product page).
- **Supports:** the settlement channel of the one major complex where a randomised cash close sits next
  to a liquid futures market. The page states that the final settlement price "is established by Eurex
  on the final settlement day of the contract and is determined by the value of the FTSE 100 Expiry
  Index as calculated by FTSE International Limited following the Exchange Delivery Settlement Price
  ('EDSP') intraday auction on the London Stock Exchange", and that the daily settlement price for the
  current maturity month is "the volume-weighted average of the prices of all transactions during the
  minute before 17:30 CET". Both are determined **after** the cash close is known, so the randomness of
  the cash close does not reach the futures' settlement value.
- **Caveats:** a product page, not the rulebook; the EDSP auction's own micro-description is not on
  the page; Eurex and ICE specifications differ in detail, so this is an illustration of the
  decoupling rather than a universal statement.
- **Verification:** page fetched directly (contract-specifications section read in full, including the
  settlement and final-settlement paragraphs quoted above).

### S-251 — U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission / NYSE (primary regulatory material)
89 FR 19370–19374 (18 March 2024), SEC Release No. 34-99719, File No. SR-NYSE-2024-13, "Notice of
Filing of Proposed Rule Change for Amendments to Rule 7.35 and Rule 7.35B"; approval order SEC Release
No. 34-100327 (13 June 2024).
URL: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-03-18/html/2024-05632.htm
- **Type:** Primary regulatory material.
- **Supports:** two facts that the Cycle-51 screen needs. (i) **The decision-time state of a closing
  auction is a real-time, paid-feed series**: "Beginning ten minutes before the scheduled end of Core
  Trading Hours, the Exchange begins disseminating through its proprietary data feed Closing Auction
  Imbalance Information", which "includes the Continuous Book Clearing Price" and "an Imbalance
  Reference Price", is "updated at least every second … until the Closing Auction begins", and is
  supplemented by paired/unpaired quantities; the exchange states that publishing it "could facilitate
  entry of offsetting orders and the price discovery process" and "could also attract additional
  contra-side interest, thereby decreasing volatility" — the exchange designs the publication to
  attract offsetting interest, which is the competition-away mechanism in the screen's third reason.
  (ii) **The US close is not randomised**: "In 2022, the Exchange made further changes to the Closing
  Auction, including adding price parameters within which the DMM must select a Closing Auction Price,
  in order to make the Closing Auction more transparent and deterministic" (Release No. 95691,
  87 FR 56099).
- **Caveats:** US-only, and the rule text is as of 2024; the approval order's own text was read only
  through the search index; the NYSE also states that D Orders were 42.7 % of closing-auction volume
  as of Q3 2023, which is an interested party's own figure.
- **Verification:** the Federal Register text (89 FR 19370–19374) was fetched directly from govinfo and

## Cycle 52 sources (2026-10-20)

Cycle 52 did two pieces of work: the register's **prior-art re-read of IDEA-011 (rank 1) against 2025–2026
literature it had not yet seen** (the register's own cross-cutting note identifies this as its highest-value
act, and a null there is worth more than another bounded negative), and **one new mechanism family screen**
— venue-imposed trading halts, price bands and market-wide circuit breakers — logged as **R-032**. Fifteen
sources are added: **S-252 … S-266**.

Every entry below was located by web search against publisher landing pages, the Crossref REST API, the DOI
resolver, or the institution's own site, and its metadata was re-derived from an authoritative record rather
than from the search result. Where a publisher page blocked the fetch, the entry says so explicitly and the
content was read through the search index — the register's rule is that an index-rendered quotation must never
be presented as a directly parsed document.

### S-252 — Guan, J. X., Shafron, E., Ye, K. and Zhuang, W. (2025)
"Is accounting the English language of business? The role of language in IFRS adoption and information loss."
*Review of Accounting Studies* 30(3): 2963–3020.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11142-025-09881-9
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (peer-reviewed; published online 11 April 2025, print issue September 2025).
- **Supports:** two things IDEA-011 needs. (i) A **published, ex-ante, country-level conditioning variable**
  for the post-adoption information environment: the distance between a country's official language and
  English. The paper hand-collects the dates on which countries change their adoption status
  (prohibit → permit → mandate) over 2004–2018 on the Ramanna–Sletten three-level framework, finds that
  greater linguistic distance both lowers the likelihood of adoption and slows it, and then shows the
  information cost **materialising after adoption**: "firms in countries with the most severe language
  barriers experience a worsened post-adoption information environment, as evidenced by increased analyst
  forecast errors and widened bid-ask spreads", while "firms in countries with the most severe language
  barriers are associated with an increase in information loss post adoption". The state is measurable
  **before** the adoption date and is published. (ii) A **sign flip in the sign-determining direction**:
  the post-adoption information effect is not merely attenuated in a weak-information setting, it reverses.
- **Caveats:** the outcomes are **analyst forecast error and bid–ask spread, not drift** — the register's
  G-21 comparison (post-earnings-announcement drift, first-time versus second-time adopters) is *not* run
  here, so this paper does not close G-21. The conditioning variable is **country-level**, so it is collinear
  with the already-published enforcement conditioner (S-221) and cannot by itself identify a firm-level
  effect. The paper is a *neighbour*, not the candidate's discovery.
- **Verification:** the full Crossref record (authors, title, journal, volume, issue, pages, DOI, dates,
  abstract) was retrieved from the Crossref REST API and read in full; the publisher's own article page
  returned a client challenge to a direct fetch, and the abstract was therefore read from the Crossref
  record and the search index, which agree.

### S-253 — Pirveli, E. and Zimmermann, J. (2026)
"Twenty years of IFRS 'success'? A systematic review of Scopus literature." *Journal of International
Accounting, Auditing and Taxonomy* 60: 100739.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.intaccaudtax.2025.100739 (published online 29 November 2025; issue dated
June 2026). Preprint: SSRN 4699908, posted 19 January 2024.
- **Type:** Prior systematic literature review (peer-reviewed; a *review* article).
- **Supports:** the most complete published map of the IFRS-adoption literature that IDEA-011 lives in, and
  it bears on the candidate in three distinct ways. (i) **Adverse to the candidate's premise, at the level
  of the premise and not of the outcome**: the review's 181 top-cited papers yield the finding that "half of
  them could not affirm a significant positive impact of IFRS on accounting quality, comparability, or market
  properties"; that market effects are real but "accounting quality and comparability do not mediate the
  market effects"; and that studies with negative findings "point to varying enforcement strength and IFRS
  complexity". (ii) **Supportive of the candidate's *comparability-break* reading in a different form**: the
  review attributes positive findings to "IFRS' mandatory nature and pre-IFRS differences compared to local
  standards" — i.e. the *discontinuity* at adoption, which is the candidate's premise, while rejecting the
  claim that gradual comparability improvement drives outcomes. (iii) **The outcome is absent from the
  review's map**: the outcomes it inventories are accounting quality, comparability, liquidity, cost of
  capital, forecast accuracy and foreign investment — **post-earnings-announcement drift is not among them**,
  which is the strongest available confirmation that the candidate's residual is unclaimed.
- **Caveats:** a review of the *top-cited* literature, so a drift study with few citations could exist
  outside its sample; the review is itself a 2025–2026 artefact, so it cannot cover the pre-2027 IFRS-18
  literature (see G-32).
- **Verification:** the DOI resolved to the publisher's own citation string (Elsevier), giving authors,
  title, journal, volume and article number; the ScienceDirect article page returned HTTP 403 to a direct
  fetch, so the abstract was read through the search index, from the SSRN preprint record and from the
  author's own announcement, which agree with each other.

### S-254 — IFRS Foundation (standard-setter), "Who uses IFRS Accounting Standards?" — jurisdiction profiles
URL: https://www.ifrs.org/use-around-the-world/use-of-ifrs-standards-by-jurisdiction/
- **Type:** Primary standard-setter publication (jurisdiction directory).
- **Supports:** the **published adoption-status calendar** IDEA-011 needs. The IFRS Foundation states that it
  "monitor[s] the application of those standards in each jurisdiction", that "updates are made on an ongoing
  basis", and that it "currently [has] complete profiles for **170 jurisdictions**"; the profiles are
  filterable on exactly the three states the candidate's discriminator needs — "IFRS Standards are required
  for domestic public companies", "IFRS Standards are permitted but not required for domestic public
  companies", and "IFRS Standards are required or permitted for listings by foreign companies". A
  jurisdiction's membership of the **first-time-adopter** group (required, and not previously on
  IFRS-equivalent standards) versus the **second-time-adopter** group (permitted, or previously mandated) is
  therefore a **published, dated, pre-registered** assignment, not a researcher's classification.
  **Cycle-109 refinement (this entry was too pessimistic on one limb and right on another):** the
  *framework-level* first-adoption fact is **published and dated in the profile documents themselves** (the
  European Union "effective in **2005**"; Ghana "1 January **2007**"; Nigeria "1 January **2012**"), so the
  historical first-time-versus-repeat label is computable at the decision date; but **no profile carries an
  IFRS 18 date** ("IFRS 18" **0 hits** in all four documents read) and the profiles' own "last updated"
  dates (**16 June 2016**, **28 July 2022**, **2 October 2024**) predate or barely postdate IFRS 18's
  April 2024 issuance, so the directory is **not** an IFRS 18 adoption calendar.
- **Caveats:** the directory states the *status* of each jurisdiction's IFRS use; **Cycle-109 correction:**
  the earlier caveat's "it does not itself give a dated transition schedule for every jurisdiction" was
  **too pessimistic** — the *profile documents* do carry a **dated first-adoption fact** for many
  jurisdictions — but it remains true that the profiles carry **no IFRS 18 application date at all**, that
  the fact is **absent for some jurisdictions** (the Saudi Arabia profile gives none, and its "Additional
  comments" field reads "Not applicable"), and that the register has not enumerated the 170 profiles in
  this cycle (a bulk read of a directory is not performed in this repository).
- **Verification:** page fetched directly; the quoted statements about the 170 profiles and the three
  status filters were read in the fetched document.
- **Cycle 53 note (limb a):** Read the jurisdiction profiles index and sampled profiles (EU, UK, Australia,
  Canada). Profiles record general IFRS status (required/permitted) and list 170 jurisdictions but do not
  enumerate IFRS 18-specific adoption dates or explicitly partition jurisdictions into first-time IFRS 18
  adopters vs second-time adopters with non-overlapping, pre-registered dates. IFRS 18 effective date is
  1 January 2027 (S-255); some jurisdictions have endorsed/adopted it for 2027, but no partition table is
  present in the profiles as inspected. Limb (a) verdict: negative as specified; a published IFRS 18
  jurisdiction adoption calendar distinguishing first-time vs second-time adopters with non-overlapping dates
  would be needed. **Cycle-109 note: this verdict STANDS, and it now stands on a stronger ground** — the
  Cycle-53 reading was taken from the profile *index and sampled profile pages*, which are client-side
  rendered; reading the **profile documents themselves** (the Cycle-109 bullet below) shows that they carry
  no IFRS 18 date and no partition, so the negative is a property of the instrument and not of the way it
  was read.
- **Cycle-109 verification — UPGRADE with a new route form, a dated re-check, and a dated first-adoption
  fact (the P-3 screen's evidence).** (i) **Dated re-check of the index page**: fetched directly
  (**HTTP 200**) on 21 October 2026; the entry's statements still hold verbatim — "Currently we have
  complete profiles for **170 jurisdictions**", the same **three** status filters ("IFRS Standards are

  listings by foreign companies"), the additional "IFRS for SMEs Standard is required or permitted" and

  profile *pages* are client-side rendered, and each profile's *content* is served as a per-jurisdiction

  which the register had not tried in thirteen cycles; four were fetched directly and text-extracted —

  126,760 bytes, 6 pages, 14,921 characters**), **Nigeria** (**HTTP 200, 119,901 bytes, 6 pages, 12,870

### S-255 — IFRS Foundation (standard-setter), "IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements"
URL: https://www.ifrs.org/issued-standards/list-of-standards/ifrs-18-presentation-and-disclosure-in-financial-statements/
- **Type:** Primary standard-setter publication (standard page).
- **Supports:** a **new, dated, prospective mandatory-adoption event** that the register's candidate can be
  specified against, and a comparability break created *by design*. The page states: "IFRS 18 is effective for
  annual reporting periods beginning on or after **1 January 2027**, with earlier application permitted", that
  it "replaces IAS 1 Presentation of Financial Statements", that it was issued in April 2024, and that it
  requires two new defined subtotals in the statement of profit or loss (operating profit and profit before
  financing and income taxes), disclosure of management-defined performance measures, and new principles for
  aggregation and disaggregation of items. Those are precisely the features that break comparability at the
  moment of adoption — the candidate's "comparability clock" premise — while the mandatory date and the
  jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction adoption route are published in advance.
- **Caveats:** a standard-setter's own summary page (an interested party); it does not by itself establish
  that any jurisdiction will adopt IFRS 18 on time, nor that the transition creates a *drift*; it is the
  event, not the effect.
- **Verification:** page fetched directly; the effective-date, replacement and content statements were read
  in the fetched document.

### S-256 — Chen, H., Petukhov, A., Wang, J. and Xing, H. (2024)
"The Dark Side of Circuit Breakers." *The Journal of Finance* 79(2): 1405–1455.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.13310 (published online 23 February 2024; print April 2024).
- **Type:** Prior empirical and theoretical result (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports:** the market-wide circuit-breaker mechanism is a **published, quantified** object, and the
  sign of the state-conditioned behaviour is claimed. The paper shows that "as the market approaches the
  circuit breaker, price volatility rises drastically, accelerating the chance of triggering the circuit
  breaker — the so-called 'magnet effect'", that "returns exhibit increasing negative skewness", and that
  "expected returns and trading volume tend to increase as the market approaches the circuit breaker". Its
  empirical work uses transaction-level E-mini S&P 500 futures data and reports that "a decrease in DTCB of
  1 % (7 % is the Level-1 trigger threshold) leads to an increase in volatility of 17.5 bps normalized to
  daily scale", with the coefficient "nearly doubl[ing] to -30.0" when the distance to the breaker falls
  below 2 %.
- **Caveats:** the estimates are for the *futures* market and for the neighbourhood of the trigger, not for
  the resumption; the paper's own framing is that a circuit breaker can reduce or raise welfare depending on
  the mix of risk-sharing and speculative motives, so it is not a directional trading rule.
- **Verification:** the full Crossref record (authors, title, journal, volume, issue, pages, DOI, online and
  print dates, abstract) was retrieved from the Crossref REST API; the American Finance Association's issue
  page for *The Journal of Finance* 79(2) was read separately and confirms the volume, issue, pages and DOI.

### S-257 — Sifat, I. M. and Mohamad, A. (2018)
"Circuit breakers as market stability levers: A survey of research, praxis, and challenges."
*International Journal of Finance & Economics* 24(3): 1130–1169.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1002/ijfe.1709
- **Type:** Prior survey (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports:** the size and maturity of the circuit-breaker literature. The survey's own framing is that
  "since conceptualization in 1970s and practice from 1980s, researchers focused mostly on [circuit breakers']
  ability to allay panic, interference with trading, volatility transmission, prospect of self-fulfilling
  prophecy through gravitational pull towards itself, and delayed dissemination of information", that "the
  empirical literature on the merits of MWCBs is inconclusive", and that regulators "downplay the reliability
  of anti-circuit breaker findings citing, inter alia, suspect methodology, and lack of statistical power". A
  register that proposed a circuit-breaker candidate would be proposing to re-litigate a question with a
  thirty-year survey literature behind it and an acknowledged lack of statistical power.
- **Caveats:** a survey, not a primary test; the search engine's rendering of this paper attributed it to a
  different author, which is why the register re-derives author metadata from the Crossref record rather
  than from a search result.
- **Verification:** the full Crossref record (authors, title, journal, volume, issue, pages, DOI, date,
  abstract) was retrieved from the Crossref REST API and read in full.

### S-258 — Lin, K., Gurrola Perez, P. and Speth, B. (2022)
"Circuit Breakers and Market Quality." SSRN working paper 4132469.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4132469
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (working paper; Crossref records it as an SSRN journal-article record; no
  journal version was located in this cycle).
- **Supports:** the *post-halt* state of the world is already measured. Using high-frequency intraday trade
  and quote data around the four market-wide halts triggered in March 2020, the authors find that "on
  average, stock returns stabilize, trading cost reduces, selling pressure resolves, and prices become more
  informative after trading resumes from the market-wide trading halts", that "traders tend to hold back from
  aggressive trading right before the trading halts, which is inconsistent with the circuit breakers causing
  panic (the magnet effect)", and — directly relevant to the register's own instrument universe — that
  "index membership and index fund trading do not have additional impacts on market quality during trading
  halts".
- **Caveats:** a working paper; the four March-2020 events are a very small event set; the findings concern
  *market-wide* halts, whose trigger state is common to every security.
- **Verification:** the Crossref record (authors, title, container, DOI, year) was retrieved from the
  Crossref REST API; the abstract was read through the search index from the SSRN record.
- **Verification (Cycle 105):** Crossref REST `https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2139/ssrn.4132469` fetched directly (HTTP 200; JSON) — **no deposited abstract** present (the Cycle-104 pre-registration returned HTTP 404 on a wrong route; the entry's actual SSRN DOI resolves but carries no abstract). **Honest negative** — entry remains index-rendered. Annotation written into entry in Cycle 105.

### S-259 — U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Division of Economic and Risk Analysis (staff papers)
(a) Moise, C. E. and Flaherty, P. (March 2017), **"'Limit Up-Limit Down' Pilot Plan and Associated Events"**
(staff white paper);
(b) DERA research note (February 2016), **"Equity Market Volatility on August 24, 2015"**.
URLs: https://www.sec.gov/dera/staff-papers/white-papers/dera-luld-white-paper.pdf and
https://www.sec.gov/marketstructure/research/equity_market_volatility.pdf
- **Type:** Primary regulator staff material.
- **Supports:** the LULD mechanism as an *operating* rule with a published sequence, and the register's own
  instrument universe's exposure to it. The white paper documents the state machine: a **Limit State** (one
  side of the market outside the applicable price band while the other side reaches it) lasts 15 seconds;
  if it does not resolve, the primary listing exchange "declares a five-minute Trading Pause, which is
  applicable to all markets trading the security", and "Trading reopens with an auction similar to the
  opening auction at the beginning of that day". It also documents that "most of the Trading Pauses in both
  tiers result from 'SRO-defined liquidity gaps'", that "following a Trading Pause, prices revert back to
  within the price bands in place prior to the Trading Pause", and that LULD events occur on *every day
  examined* in Tier 2. The research note quantifies the universe: on 24 August 2015 there were **1,278 LULD
  trading halts**, of which **1,058 in 327 ETPs and 220 in 144 non-ETPs**, with "84 % of ETPs" small
  capitalisation, and only "8 constituents of the S&P 500 and 2 constituents of the NASDAQ-100" halted; it
  also records that "NYSE Arca, which is the primary listing exchange for more than 85 % of ETPs, applied
  price collars to reopening auctions after LULD halts on August 24. The reopening auctions on NYSE Arca
  generated prices that were substantially less dispersed than reopening auctions on other primary listing
  exchanges" and "left many unexecuted order imbalances".
- **Caveats:** the staff papers are the regulator's own descriptive statistics, not a causal test; the
  August-2015 episode is a single day; the cross-venue collar difference is an observation the SEC published,
  not a claim the register may present as a discovery.
- **Verification:** **both SEC documents returned HTTP 403 to a direct fetch in this session** and were read
  through the search index; the quoted passages are therefore index-rendered, and the register does not
  present them as directly parsed documents.
- **Cycle-85 verification — UPGRADE: both SEC documents are now fetched directly and line-verified; the
  403 is explained and no longer binding.** The SEC requires a compliant User-Agent, and with one
  (`QUANTITATIVE-HYPOTHESIS-FACTORY research verification research@example.org`) both documents were
  fetched directly on 20 October 2026:
  (a) `https://www.sec.gov/dera/staff-papers/white-papers/dera-luld-white-paper.pdf` — **HTTP 200,
  797,300 bytes, 55 pages**, text layer extracted; and
  (b) `https://www.sec.gov/marketstructure/research/equity_market_volatility.pdf` — **HTTP 200, 9,105,990
  bytes, 88 pages**, text layer extracted.
  **Every passage quoted in this entry is now confirmed in the documents themselves**: the **Limit State**
  and the **15 seconds**; the **five-minute Trading Pause** and the **reopening auction** ("Trading reopens
  with an auction similar to the opening auction at the beginning of that day"); **"most of the Trading
  Pauses in both tiers result from 'SRO-defined liquidity gaps'"**; **"following a Trading Pause, prices
  revert back to within the price bands in place prior to the Trading Pause"**; the **1,278 LULD trading
  halts** of 24 August 2015, of which **1,058 in 327 ETPs and 220 in 144 non-ETPs**, with **84 % of ETPs**
  small capitalisation, and only **8 S&P 500** and **2 NASDAQ-100** constituents halting; and the **NYSE
  Arca** reopening-auction collar finding (price collars applied, prices "substantially less dispersed" than
  on other primary listing exchanges, and "left many unexecuted order imbalances"). The verification label

  extracted)"**. **The entry's caveats are unchanged** — these remain the regulator's own descriptive

  published observation and not a discovery the register may claim. **No re-score and no hard-stop change
  follow**, because the upgrade is provenance, not new evidence about any candidate's effect.

### S-260 — The Limit Up–Limit Down Plan (plan documentation) and Nasdaq Trader, "Limit Up-Limit Down" FAQ
URLs: https://www.luldplan.com/ and
https://www.nasdaqtrader.com/content/MarketRegulation/LULD_FAQ.pdf
- **Type:** Primary venue/plan documentation.
- **Supports:** the **decision-time state is published, real-time and venue-level** — the fact the Cycle-52
  screen needs. The Plan's own documentation states that the price bands are "set at a percentage level above
  and below the average reference price of a security over the preceding five-minute period", that "The price
  bands, consisting of a Lower and Upper Price Band for each NMS Stock, are calculated by the two SIPs — CTA
  and Nasdaq UTP", that Tier 1 comprises "all securities in the S&P 500, the Russell 1000 and select Exchange
  Traded Products (ETPs)" and Tier 2 "all other NMS securities", and that the Limit State resolves in 15
  seconds or becomes a five-minute Trading Pause (extendable by a further five minutes) followed by a
  reopening. The FAQ adds the band parameters (5 % for Tier 1 above $3, 10 % for Tier 2 above $3, 20 % for
  stocks from $0.75 to $3, the lesser of $0.15 or 75 % below $0.75, doubled in the last 25 minutes), the
  reference-price rule (arithmetic mean of eligible reported transactions over the preceding five minutes,
  updated only when at least 1 % away), and — the decisive fact for the screen — that "**Both SIPs will
  republish the current price bands every 30 seconds**" and that "the Processors (UTP/SIAC) for each NMS
  stock shall calculate and disseminate to the public a Lower Price Band and an Upper Price Band".
- **Caveats:** the Nasdaq FAQ page at the retired `Trader.aspx?id=LULD` address returned "Page Not

- **Verification:** the `luldplan.com` content and the Nasdaq FAQ PDF were read through the search index;
  the retired Nasdaq URL was fetched directly and its "Page Not Available" response recorded.

### S-261 — European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), MiFID II circuit-breaker guidelines and supervisory briefing
(a) **"Guidelines on calibration of circuit breakers and publication of trading halts under MiFID II"**,
ESMA70-872942901-63, with the accompanying Final Report (ESMA70-872942901-17);
(b) **"Supervisory Briefing: Circuit Breakers"**, ESMA74-2134169708-6975, 12 October 2023.
URLs: https://www.esma.europa.eu/sites/default/files/library/esma70-872942901-63_guidelines_on_the_calibration_of_of_circuit_breakers.pdf
and https://www.esma.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2023-10/ESMA74-2134169708-6975_Supervisory_Briefing_Circuit_Breakers.pdf
- **Type:** Primary regulator material (supervisory guidelines and briefing).
- **Supports:** the EU regime is the register's cleanest instance of a **venue-published, real-time, published
  trigger state**, and it shows the regime *requires* the halt information to be published. The instrument is
  titled "Guidelines on calibration of circuit breakers **and publication of trading halts** under MiFID II",
  and the briefing states the design: a venue must put in place "at least one of the two types of circuit
  breaker" — "(i) trading halts mechanisms only, or (ii) price collars mechanisms only, or (iii) both" —
  calibrated on **both static and dynamic reference prices**, where "static circuit breakers are more suited to
  manage intraday price volatility" and "dynamic circuit breakers are more suited to prevent sharp price
  changes". The Final Report sets out the parameters national competent authorities must obtain from venues
  and pass to ESMA at least annually, including "thresholds", the "frequency of updates", the "duration of the
  halts … including the randomisation parameters", and "the mechanism employed in resuming the market …
  where the resumption of the market occurs through an auction process, the details of such a mechanism (e.g.
  duration, randomised or not, etc.) should be provided".
- **Caveats:** EU-only and implemented through national competent authorities rather than by a single
  exchange; the guidelines are supervisory expectations on venues, not a self-executing rule for a
  participant; the register's own instrument universe is US-listed, so the EU regime is a *comparator* for
  the screen rather than a tradeable venue for it.
- **Verification:** both ESMA PDFs were read through the search index; the EUR-Lex text of Commission
  Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/589 was requested but returned an empty document body to the fetch and
  was therefore **not** used as a source.
- **Cycle-85 verification — UPGRADE: both ESMA PDFs are now fetched directly and their text layers
  extracted.** On 20 October 2026: the guidelines PDF
  (`https://www.esma.europa.eu/sites/default/files/library/esma70-872942901-63_guidelines_on_the_calibration_of_of_circuit_breakers.pdf`)
  returned **HTTP 200, 281,383 bytes**, and the supervisory briefing
  (`https://www.esma.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2023-10/ESMA74-2134169708-6975_Supervisory_Briefing_Circuit_Breakers.pdf`)
  returned **HTTP 200, 755,905 bytes**; both were parsed and their text layers read. The entry's quoted
  material — the instrument's title ("Guidelines on calibration of circuit breakers **and publication of
  trading halts** under MiFID II"), the briefing's "at least one of the two types of circuit breaker"
  enumeration, the static-versus-dynamic reference-price distinction, and the Final Report's list of the

### S-262 — Lin, Y. and Swan, P. L. (2017)
"Limit Up Limit Down, Exchange Access Fee and High Frequency Trading Around Price Limits."
SSRN working paper 3019986. DOI: https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3019986
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (working paper).
- **Supports:** the LULD family's *magnet* and *liquidity* behaviour is measured, so a LULD candidate would
  be re-deriving published work. The paper tests five propositions — "trading interference, volatility
  spillover, delayed price discovery, magnet effects and the role of HFT around the price limit" — and finds
  that "LULD interferes with trading activity, but curbs short term volatility without delaying the price
  discovery process", that "magnet effect exists when trade price is approaching the price limit", and that
  "HFT trading activity dropped after the LULD trading halt which was driven by the decrease in liquidity
  taking on the maker-taker market while no change on the inverted market".
- **Caveats:** a working paper; the sample and the period are not stated in the abstract; it studies the
  *individual-stock* LULD mechanism, not the market-wide breaker.
- **Verification:** the Crossref record (authors, title, container, DOI, year) was retrieved from the
  Crossref REST API; the abstract was read through the search index from the SSRN record.

### S-263 — Zimmermann, K. (2013; last revised 30 October 2014)
"Price Discovery in European Volatility Interruptions." SSRN working paper 2365772; the same work was
presented as "Price Discovery in European Volatility Interruptions", EFA Annual Meeting, Rome, 2014.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.2365772
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (working paper; conference version).
- **Supports:** the *volatility-interruption* variant of the halt family — a short-lived call auction at a
  price-band breach rather than a full trading halt — is a published, measured mechanism. On approximately
  **1,800 Xetra volatility-interruption events from 01/2009 to 01/2012**, the paper finds that "volatility
  interruptions dissolve on average 36 percent of the pre-interruption price uncertainty", that post-auction
  continuous trading benefits conditionally on the price-discovery contribution of the interruption, and that
  the venue's own Designated Sponsors are obliged to quote during the call phase.
- **Caveats:** one venue, 2009–2012; the SSRN record and the conference version are the same work, so they
  are one source; the interruption is a European mechanism and the register's universe is US-listed.
- **Verification:** the Crossref record (author, title, container, DOI, year) was retrieved from the
  Crossref REST API; the conference PDF's text was read through the search index.

### S-265 — Tawiah, V. K. (2022)
"Does the impact of IFRS on audit fees differ between early and late adopters?"
*International Journal of Accounting & Information Management* 30(1): 1–21.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1108/IJAIM-04-2021-0085 (published online 29 October 2021; print 1 February 2022).
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports:** the **early-adopter versus late-adopter contrast is a standard, populated design in the IFRS
  literature — but on outcomes other than drift**. Using 314 firms from an early-adopting country (South
  Africa, 2005: 195 firms) and a late-adopting country (Nigeria, 2012: 119 firms), the paper finds that "IFRS
  is positively and significantly associated with an increase in audit fees for early adopters, but the impact
  is very weak for late adopters and insignificant in some cases", that the audit-fee effect runs from "the
  transition year to one-year post-adoption" for early adopters but is "significant only in the adoption
  year" for late adopters, and concludes that "early adopters paid a premium for being the first users of
  IFRS". This is the register's evidence that G-21's *comparator* is a well-established design whose
  **outcome variable** has not yet been drift.
- **Caveats:** two countries, one outcome (audit fees and audit time), self-selected early adopters; it does
  not speak to drift or to price effects.
- **Verification:** the full Crossref record (author, title, journal, volume, issue, pages, DOI, dates,
  abstract) was retrieved from the Crossref REST API and read in full.

## Cycle 52 gap verdicts (2026-10-20)

### G-30 — **exhaustion confirmed; no re-probe** (IDEA-010)
All sub-routes remain closed (regulatory: Cycle 41; sponsor-published lists: Cycles 42–43; non-US/UCITS
issuers: Cycle 42; exchange listing rules: Cycle 43), and no new route was identified in Cycles 44–51 or in
Cycle 52. **V-010 remains non-executable against the corporate-bond ETF universe.** The standing instruction
is unchanged: *do not re-run statutory filings, and do not substitute a published crowding proxy (S-026,
S-157, S-222 measure different crowds)*. No statutory filing was re-run in Cycle 52.

### G-28 — **remains frozen; null recorded** (IDEA-004); V-002 frozen
No published convergence-crowd **concentration** measure was located in the Cycle-52 bounded check, and none
is required: the crowding literature the register already holds (S-026, S-157, S-222, S-241, S-242, S-243)
measures a *different* crowd in every case. **G-28 stays frozen and V-002 stays frozen.** The FINRA
twice-monthly short-interest route remains a lead with objections (per-issue aggregate with no firm-level
breakdown; contamination of the short leg; short interest already published prior art).

### G-21 (IDEA-011) — **null maintained, and materially sharpened by a prior-art re-read**
The Cycle-52 re-read against 2025–2026 literature the register had not seen produced three findings and one
new gap:
1. **The null stands, with a sharper statement of what the literature does contain.** The
   first-adopter/second-adopter contrast is a *standard, populated design* in the IFRS literature — audit
   fees and audit time (**S-265**), narrative disclosure, accounting choice, language barriers — but it is
   run on **outcomes other than drift**. The field's own systematic review of ~181 top-cited IFRS-adoption
   papers inventories accounting quality, comparability, liquidity, cost of capital, forecast accuracy and
   foreign investment, and **post-earnings-announcement drift is not among the reviewed outcomes** (**S-253**).
   The candidate's residual is therefore not an unnoticed literature gap; it is a **specific outcome that the
   IFRS-adoption literature has not run**, on a comparator that is standard elsewhere.
2. **A published conditioner that competes with the candidate's own state — and a new mandatory control.**
   The post-adoption information effect is now shown to **flip sign** with a country-level, ex-ante,
   published state (linguistic distance): adoption *worsens* the post-adoption information environment
   (higher analyst forecast error, wider bid–ask spreads) in the most severe language-barrier countries
   (**S-252**). Because that state is country-level, it is collinear with the already-published enforcement
   conditioner (**S-221**), so the candidate's own conditioning variable must remain **firm-level**, and both
   country-level conditioners must enter the specification as **mandatory controls**. The candidate may not
   present the state-conditioned post-adoption information effect as a discovery.
3. **The candidate's premise is weakened at one point and supported at another, and the distinction is
   recorded rather than smoothed.** The systematic review finds that market effects of IFRS adoption are real
   but "accounting quality and comparability do not mediate the market effects", and that negative findings
   "point to varying enforcement strength and IFRS complexity" (**S-253**) — adverse to the candidate's
   comparability-as-driver story. But the same review attributes positive findings to "IFRS' mandatory nature
   and **pre-IFRS differences compared to local standards**", which is the *discontinuity* at adoption — the
   candidate's own premise — and not the gradual improvement of comparability. The two readings are
   distinguishable in the candidate's design (drift versus liquidity/cost-of-capital outcomes; transition
   versus post-transition windows), and the candidate must pre-register which one it claims.
4. **A new gap, G-32, is opened** (see below) because the cycle's work produced a concrete, dated,
   prospective route for the candidate rather than another null.

### G-32 — **OPENED (Cycle 52) — the prospective IFRS-18 adoption window** (IDEA-011)
The candidate's binding hard stop is that the number of *independent, non-overlapping* adoption events is
small. Cycle 52 found a dated, published, prospective event that could relieve it and could identify the
G-21 discriminator more cleanly than any past event. **IFRS 18** (issued April 2024) "is effective for
annual reporting periods beginning on or after **1 January 2027**, with earlier application permitted",
replaces IAS 1, and creates a comparability break **by design** — two new defined subtotals in the statement
of profit or loss, required disclosure of management-defined performance measures, and new principles for
aggregation and disaggregation (**S-255**). The jurisdiction-level adoption-status calendar that the
discriminator needs is published in advance in the IFRS Foundation's jurisdiction profiles, with 170
jurisdictions filterable by "required for domestic public companies" versus "permitted but not required"
(**S-254**). Three sub-questions, each with a stated answer route:
- **(a) the calendar limb — closable now.** Does the published jurisdiction-level profile set, read
  jurisdiction by jurisdiction, identify a group A (first-time IFRS adopters) and a group B (second-time
  adopters) with **non-overlapping, pre-registered** IFRS 18 adoption dates? The register has **not** yet
  enumerated the 170 profiles, and a bulk directory read is not performed in this repository; this is the
  concrete next act, and it is a *reading* task, not a data-processing task.
- **(b) the identification limb.** Does the candidate's **firm-level** information-quality conditioning
  retain identifying power *within a single standard*, i.e. is the treatment not absorbed by the two
  published country-level conditioners (enforcement **S-221**, language distance **S-252**)? This is the
  question the past events could not pose cleanly, because in every past event the treatment varies with
  the jurisdiction.
- **(c) the pre-adoption-claim limb.** Does any 2024–2027 pre-adoption literature already claim the
  IFRS-18 drift sign? The review of the field (S-253) cannot cover IFRS 18, because IFRS 18 post-dates it.
- **Dated re-check:** the pre-adoption literature window is 2024–2027; the first IFRS 18 annual reports cover
  periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027 and will be published during 2028. **Re-read the IFRS 18
  pre-adoption literature annually, and re-run limb (a) whenever the IFRS Foundation updates its jurisdiction
  profiles.**

### IDEA-014's state-free existence limb — **inconclusive maintained**
No new source was identified on whether the US Renewable Fuel Standard compliance deadline moves prices at
all. The limb remains neither a positive finding nor a refutation and must not be described as either.
IDEA-014 stays at 52.0; P-011 stands; no gap is opened on this limb.

### The Cycle-52 venue-halt family screen — logged as **R-032**
Venue-imposed trading halts, price bands and market-wide circuit breakers were screened as one family — the
register's first screen of a **halt-and-restriction** family, in which the venue *interrupts or constrains
trading itself* rather than obliging a participant to act. Instances run: US market-wide circuit breakers
(**S-256**, **S-258**, **S-266**), the US Limit Up–Limit Down Plan's Limit State / five-minute Trading Pause
/ reopening auction (**S-259**, **S-260**, **S-262**), European volatility interruptions and the ESMA/MiFID II
calibration and **publication-of-trading-halts** regime (**S-261**, **S-263**), and Korean dynamic and static
volatility interruptions (**S-264**). Verdict: **bounded negative** on six independent reasons — the effects
are published and sized; the trigger state is public and real-time (a candidate cannot have an informational
edge in *knowing* it); a market-wide trigger is a state common to every security, so any trade is beta; an
individual-stock halt is triggered by that stock's own news, so the identification is inseparable from the
information event; the concession is competed away inside the halt by the participants with the best latency;
and the tradeable window is seconds wide, in the widest-spread universe, with the published post-halt
microstructure (volatility up, spreads wide, volume up) documenting why. The screen, its instances, its six
reasons and its dated re-screen condition are recorded in `rejected_and_parked.md` under **R-032**, and the
family was added to the known-baseline table.

### S-267 — European Securities and Markets Authority (2026), "Public Statement on the Implementation of IFRS 18" (ESMA32-193237008-9180)
URL: https://www.esma.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2026-02/ESMA32-193237008-9180_Public_Statement_IFRS_18.pdf
- **Type:** Primary regulator material (supervisory expectation statement, February 2026).
- **Supports:** the register's Cycle-56 re-specification of IDEA-011 rests on the fact that the
  **pre-adoption impact disclosure is required by the standard-setter itself**, not by a local rule.
  The statement **"draws issuers' attention to requirements in paragraphs 30 and 31 of IAS 8"** for the
  disclosure of
  the nature of an impending change in accounting policies where a new IFRS has been issued but is not
  yet effective, and notes that paragraph 30(b) requires disclosure of "known or reasonably estimable
  information relevant to assessing the possible impact that application of the new IFRS will have on the
  issuer's financial statements in the period of initial application". ESMA "expects these disclosures to
  be provided for IFRS 18 in issuers' interim and annual financial reports for periods ending before
  1 January 2027", provided "in a gradual and efficient manner", and lists what they should cover:
  "a description of changes in the structure of the issuer's statement of profit or loss, information on
  the assessment of whether the issuer performs 'specified main business activities', and details on
  measures that are expected to meet the definition of an MPM". It also records that issuers are
  "encouraged to include the (expected) change in 2026 operating profit or loss and/or in other subtotals",
  that the expected effects are to be disclosed **"as soon as it becomes available"** (an issuer that finalises its
  assessment in H1 2026 should disclose in the interim statements for the period ending 30 June 2026),
  and that IFRS 18 is to be applied in **interim** financial statements in the year of initial
  application — so the first IFRS 18 reporting cycle is the **2027 interim** reports, not the 2028
  annual reports.
- **Caveats:** the *mandated* disclosure is qualitative ("known or reasonably estimable information");
  the quantified expected operating-profit change is only **encouraged**, so the state's measurability at
  firm level is not established by this document — that is the new gap **G-33**. ESMA is a European
  supervisor: its expectation statement does not bind issuers outside its jurisdiction, though the
  underlying IAS 8 requirement does. The statement is a supervisory expectation, not an enforcement
  action, and it establishes no price effect.
- **Verification:** the full text was read through three national competent-authority mirrors of the
  ESMA PDF (Consob, FMA Austria, CySEC) as rendered by the search index, and corroborated by EFRAG's
  IFRS 18 endorsement-status summary. The ESMA-hosted PDF returned binary content to a direct fetch, so
  this entry is **index-rendered, not directly parsed**, and is labelled as such.
- **Cycle-85 verification — UPGRADE: the ESMA-hosted PDF is now fetched directly and line-verified, and two
  quotation-fidelity defects are corrected.** The document was fetched directly on 20 October 2026 from
  `https://www.esma.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2026-02/ESMA32-193237008-9180_Public_Statement_IFRS_18.pdf`
  — **HTTP 200, 390,994 bytes, 10 pages** — and its text layer was extracted and read. **Two corrections
  are carried out here, and both are quotation-fidelity corrections, not changes of substance:**
  1. **The IAS 8 reference was a paraphrase presented as a quotation.** This entry quoted the statement as
     *"draws attention to the requirements in IAS 8 paragraphs 30 and 31"*. The document's actual words are
     **"ESMA draws issuers' attention to requirements in paragraphs 30 and 31 of IAS 8 according to which a
     disclosure of the nature of an impending change or changes in accounting policies needs to be provided
     when an issuer has yet to implement a new IFRS that has been issued but is not yet effective."** The
     quotation is corrected above, and the same correction is carried into IDEA-011's Cycle-56 block in
     `idea_register.md`, which quoted the same paraphrase.
  2. **A dropped word in the timing phrase.** The entry quoted the expected-effects timing as *"as soon as
     available"*; the document reads **"ESMA expects that information on the anticipated effects resulting
     from the application of IFRS 18 is provided by issuers as soon as it becomes available."** Corrected
     above.
  **Everything else is confirmed verbatim**: the paragraph 30(b) wording ("known or reasonably estimable
  information relevant to assessing the possible impact that application of the new IFRS will have on the
  issuer's financial statements in the period of initial application"), the expectation that "expected
  material effects from the application of IFRS 18 should be disclosed in issuers' interim and annual
  financial reports for periods ending before 1 January 2027", the "in a gradual and efficient manner"
  qualifier, the "encouraged to include the (expected) change in 2026 operating profit or loss and/or in
  other subtotals resulting from the application of IFRS 18 requirements" passage, and the coverage list
  ("a description of changes in the structure of the issuer's statement of profit or loss, information on
  the assessment of whether the issuer performs 'specified main business activities', and details on
  measures that are expected to meet the definition of an MPM"). The verification label moves from
  **"index-rendered"** to **"line-verified (ESMA-hosted PDF fetched directly and text extracted)"**.
  **The entry's caveats are unchanged** — the mandated disclosure is qualitative, the quantified expected
  change is only encouraged, the state's measurability at firm level is not established by this document
  (that is G-33), ESMA is a European supervisor whose expectation statement does not bind issuers outside
  its jurisdiction, and the statement establishes no price effect. **No re-score, no hard-stop change and no
  new hard-stop flag** for IDEA-011 follow: the two corrections are to the register's *quotation* of the
  source, not to the source's content, and the Cycle-56 argument that the disclosure is required by the
  standard-setter itself is **strengthened**, not weakened, by a direct read.
- **Cycle-114 verification — RE-FETCH, and the first observation of the season this entry anticipated. No new
  source identifier is consumed for this document, and the label remains line-verified.** The ESMA-hosted PDF was
  fetched again on 21 October 2026 — **HTTP 200, 379,979 bytes, 10 pages** — and its text layer was re-extracted.
  **The byte count differs from the Cycle-85 fetch (390,994 bytes, 10 pages), so the hosted file has been re-issued
  or re-encoded since;** the passages this cycle relies on were re-extracted from the 21 October copy and their
  wording is identical to the Cycle-85 record, so **no content correction is required and none is made.** The
  register's rule is to *extend an existing entry rather than duplicate a citation*, and this is the same
  document. **The substantive addition is the first observation of the season the statement itself anticipated.**
  The register now holds **four** first-observed issuer disclosures from the **2026 interim reporting season**

  disclosed in issuers' interim and annual financial reports for periods ending before 1 January 2027", and "ESMA
  expects that information on the anticipated effects resulting from the application of IFRS 18 is provided by
  issuers as soon as it becomes available" — in a **sign-bearing but unquantified** form, while the

### S-268 — European Commission (2026), Commission Regulation (EU) 2026/338 of 13 February 2026 amending Regulation (EU) 2023/1803 as regards International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS 18)
URL: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/338/oj/eng
- **Type:** Primary legislation (EU endorsement instrument).
- **Supports:** the EU's IFRS 18 application date, which is the convergence fact that closes G-32
  limb (a): the regulation provides that "each company shall apply the amendment at the latest as from
  the commencement of its first financial year starting on or after 1 January 2027". The EU is an
  already-IFRS jurisdiction (group B), so this fixes the group B application date at the standard's
  common mandatory date and leaves no room for a non-overlapping group A date drawn from the EU.
- **Caveats:** an endorsement instrument, not an adoption calendar for other jurisdictions; the "at the
  latest" formulation permits earlier application; it says nothing about market effects.
- **Verification:** the operative text was read through the EUR-Lex ELI page as rendered by the search
  index and corroborated by EFRAG's IFRS 18 endorsement-status table (adopted 13 February 2026; Official
  Journal publication 16 February 2026; EU effective date 1 January 2027). A direct fetch of the EUR-Lex
  HTML returned an empty body, so this entry is **index-rendered**.

  **Publications Office Cellar** `http://publications.europa.eu/resource/celex/32026R0338` was fetched
  directly on 21 October 2026 with `Accept: application/xhtml+xml` and `Accept-Language: eng` —
  **HTTP 200, 2,875 bytes**. The returned document is an **RDF metadata stub** (it declares the
  manifestation `oj/L_202600338.ENG.xhtml` and its item `DOC_1`) and contains **none of the
  regulation's operative text**; in particular the string "1 January 2027" returns **zero hits**.
