### S-273 — US Internal Revenue Service, "Topic no. 409, Capital gains and losses" (page last reviewed or updated 24 September 2026)
URL: https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc409
- **Type:** Primary tax authority material.
- **Supports:** the rule that creates the forced-realisation flow in the tax-driven year-end family:
  "If your capital losses exceed your capital gains, the amount of the excess loss that you can claim to
  lower your income is the lesser of **$3,000** ($1,500 if married filing separately) or your total net
  loss shown on line 16 of Schedule D", and, if the net capital loss is larger than that limit, "you can
  carry the loss forward to later years". A loss that cannot be used against current-year ordinary income
  must be realised inside the tax year to be worth anything, which is what makes the year-end selling
  flow non-discretionary in the affected margin.
- **Caveats:** the US rule *permits* carry-over, so it induces an acceleration rather than an absolute
  deadline; it is one jurisdiction's rule and the register's other jurisdictions differ (Sweden's
  five-year carry-forward change is the published instance in S-276); and the rule says nothing about
  which securities are sold, so it cannot identify a tradeable cross-section.
- **Verification:** page **fetched directly** 2026-10-20; the $3,000 limit and the carry-over sentence
  were read in the fetched document.

### S-274 — Poterba, J. M. and Weisbenner, S. J. (2001), "Capital Gains Tax Rules, Tax-loss Trading, and Turn-of-the-year Returns", *The Journal of Finance* 56(1): 353–368
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00328
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (peer-reviewed).
- **Supports:** that the mechanism in the tax-driven year-end family is **published prior art with a
  stated, rule-dependent sign**: "taxable individual investors can use realized capital losses to reduce
  taxes on realized gains or to offset a limited amount of nongain income", so "realizing a capital loss
  before year-end can accelerate the tax benefits of the loss by as much as twelve months"; and the paper's
  central result is that the *tax rule itself* changes the strength of the relation between early-year
  losses and turn-of-the-year returns ("when the tax law encouraged taxable investors who accrued
  losses early in the year to realize their losses before year-end, the correlation between early year
  losses and turn-of-the-year returns was weaker than when the law did not provide such an early
  realization incentive").
- **Caveats:** 1963–1996 sample and US rules; the object is turn-of-the-year *returns*, not a harvestable
  third-party concession; it is a *published* sign, which is what disqualifies the family under G-12.
- **Verification:** the full Crossref record (authors, title, journal, volume, issue, pages, publication
  date, DOI) was retrieved from the Crossref REST API; the abstract was read in the search-index
  rendering of the author-hosted PDF.
- **Cycle-103 verification — UPGRADE: the Crossref-deposited abstract is now fetched directly and
  confirms the load-bearing claim.** The **Crossref REST API**

  authored by a systematic-strategy house and is an interested party on the crowding question.

The jurisdiction-profile index was read and the EU, UK, Australia and Canada profiles were inspected.
The profiles record general IFRS *status* ("required for domestic public companies", "permitted but not
required", "required or permitted for listings by foreign companies") and list 170 jurisdictions, but
they do **not** enumerate IFRS 18-specific application dates and do **not** partition jurisdictions into
first-time versus second-time IFRS 18 adopters with non-overlapping, pre-registered dates. Verdict at the
time: **negative as specified**; a published IFRS 18 jurisdiction adoption calendar distinguishing
first-time from second-time adopters with non-overlapping dates would be required. **Cycle 56 re-opened
the limb with primary endorsement instruments and closed it again — this time with the reason
established** (see the Cycle-56 block below); the Cycle-53 verdict stands as recorded.

## Cycle 56 gap verdicts (2026-10-20)

### G-32 — **limb (a) CLOSED: negative as specified, and the reason is now established; limbs (b) and (c) advanced; the binding hard stop is relieved only inside a new arm** (IDEA-011)
Cycle 52 opened G-32 with three limbs. Cycle 56 closed limb (a) and advanced limbs (b) and (c).

**(a) The calendar limb — CLOSED, negative as specified, and the reason is now known.** The register no
longer asks only whether a partition table exists; it can now say why none can exist in the form the
candidate needs. Three verified facts:
1. **Convergence.** The published endorsement instruments all point at one mandatory date: the EU
   (Commission Regulation (EU) 2026/338, S-268 — "each company shall apply the amendment at the latest as
   from the commencement of its first financial year starting on or after 1 January 2027"), the UK
   (S-269 — approved 10 December 2025, closed 30 January 2026, effective 1 January 2027) and Saudi
   Arabia (S-270, S-271 — adopted 26 December 2024, mandatory from periods beginning on or after
   1 January 2027). The already-IFRS jurisdictions (group B) therefore apply IFRS 18 on **one common
   date**, and the IFRS Foundation's profiles give *status*, not dates (S-254). A group A date could only
   come from a jurisdiction whose *first* IFRS adoption falls after 1 January 2027, and no published
   partition table exists — nor could one, in the form the candidate needs, while the mandatory dates
   converge.
2. **Single-package adoption.** Where a jurisdiction adopts IFRS for the first time in the IFRS 18 era,
   IFRS 18 arrives *simultaneously* with the whole IFRS package (S-271: the IFRSs "shall be applied all
   at once"). The group A/group B contrast then stops being a *within-standard* contrast and becomes the
   historical first-time-versus-second-time IFRS comparison the literature has already populated
   (S-188 Greece as first adopter; S-179 Korea as second adopter).
3. **Consequence.** The group A/group B partition within IFRS 18 is **unavailable**, and G-21's
   discriminator cannot be newly identified in the IFRS 18 window. **The candidate's binding hard stop —
   the small number of independent, non-overlapping adoption events — is unchanged by limb (a).**

**(b) The identification limb — advanced, and answered differently than the register expected.** The
handoff's proposed re-specification — within-jurisdiction early adopters versus mandatory adopters under
one regime — turns out to have a *documented instance* rather than a hypothetical one: Saudi Arabia's
CMA decision of 30 June 2026 (S-270) permits early adoption during 2026, requires early adopters to
announce their IFRS 18 financial statements and the effect of early adoption on the Tadawul website,
makes application mandatory from periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027, and requires **all**
listed joint-stock companies to disclose a preliminary assessment of the expected IFRS 18 impact for
periods beginning on or after 1 April 2026. **Verdict: rejected as an identification**, on three
grounds: (i) the treatment arm is **voluntary and self-selected**, and the selection is mechanically
correlated with the state the candidate would condition on — a firm that expects a large IFRS 18 impact,
or that wants to pre-empt a comparability problem, has a reason to early-adopt — so the contrast is not
identified; (ii) the effective sample is the *number of early adopters*, so the event-count hard stop is
relocated, not relieved; (iii) the early arm announces its IFRS 18 financial statements *together with*
their effect, so the slow-information-diffusion clock has no window to run on that arm. The country-level
conditioners (S-221 enforcement, S-252 linguistic distance) are constant only *within* Saudi, so the
cross-country comparison the candidate would want is not available either. The early-adopter population is,
however, machine-identifiable from tagged filings (S-272), so the rejection is about identification, not
about observability.

**(c) The pre-adoption-claim limb — advanced, and the route to a state the candidate did not have.**
ESMA's Public Statement on the Implementation of IFRS 18 (S-267) establishes that the **pre-adoption
expected-impact disclosure is required by the standard-setter itself** (IAS 8 paragraphs 30 and 31,
including paragraph 30(b)'s "known or reasonably estimable information relevant to assessing the
possible impact that application of the new IFRS will have on the issuer's financial statements in the
period of initial application"), that ESMA expects it in interim and annual financial reports for
periods ending before 1 January 2027, and that issuers are *encouraged* to include "the (expected) change
in 2026 operating profit or loss and/or in other subtotals". It also establishes that the first IFRS 18
reporting cycle is the **2027 interim** reports, not the 2028 annual reports. This gives the register a
**firm-level, published, dated, pre-adoption** state that measures the *size of the comparability break*
directly — the candidate's own premise — with the country-level conditioners absorbed within
jurisdiction, and it converts the identification from "few events" to "one event × many firms", which
**relaxes the binding hard stop**. Two limits are recorded rather than smoothed: the *mandated* disclosure
is qualitative and the quantified expected change is only "encouraged" (this is the new gap **G-33**), and
the state arrives in the same periodic reports in which the break first appears, so the treatment and
outcome windows overlap and the specification must pre-register how the slow-diffusion clock is separated
from the adoption-announcement effect. This is recorded as **IDEA-011's prospective arm A** and carried
into **V-009** by the Cycle-56 amendment. No 2024–2027 pre-adoption literature claiming the IFRS 18
drift sign was located in this cycle; limb (c) stays open on that literature question, whose dated
re-read remains annual.

### G-33 — **OPENED (Cycle 56) — is the pre-adoption impact disclosure quantifiable and comparable at firm level?** (IDEA-011, prospective arm A)
Arm A depends on a state whose *existence* is now sourced (S-267: IAS 8.30–31 plus ESMA's expectation)
but whose *content* is not yet established. Three sub-questions, each with a stated answer route:
- **(a) Quantification rate.** What fraction of IFRS-reporting issuers that must apply IFRS 18 disclose a
  *quantified* expected effect — in the 2026 interim and annual reports — and in what units (amount,
  percentage of operating profit, a restated prior-period subtotal)? Answer route: reading a stated sample
  of issuers' 2026 interim and annual reports and the tagged concepts behind them (S-272).
- **(b) Comparability.** Is the disclosed expected effect comparable across issuers — the same definition
  of "operating profit" before and after IFRS 18, the same statement, the same currency, the same period?
  ESMA's statement describes the expected content (structure of the statement of profit or loss, the
  "specified main business activities" assessment, the MPM measures), which is the template a validator
  would apply (S-267). Answer route: the tagged disclosures themselves.
- **(c) Ex-ante availability and lag.** Is the disclosure available *before* the trade's decision date and
  at what frequency — what is the publication lag from the reporting period end to the disclosure, and
  does the interim-report filing calendar in the relevant jurisdictions put it before the first IFRS 18
  report? Answer route: the statutory interim filing deadlines, which differ by jurisdiction.
- **Dated re-check:** the first IFRS 18 interim reports (periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027) are
  published during 2027; the first *pre-adoption* impact disclosures appear from mid-2026 (periods
  beginning on or after 1 April 2026 in Saudi, S-270; periods ending before 1 January 2027 in the EU,
  S-267). **Re-check G-33 in 2027 Q3, after the first tranche of 2026 interim reports carrying IAS 8.30(b)
  impact disclosures is public.**
- **Kill condition:** if the disclosure is unquantified, or defined inconsistently across issuers, in the
  large majority of the sample, arm A has no usable state, and the candidate returns to its pre-Cycle-56
  position — blocked on the group A/group B partition, with the event-count hard stop unrelieved.

### G-28 — **remains frozen; null recorded** (IDEA-004); V-002 frozen
A bounded Cycle-56 re-check was run for a published convergence-crowd **concentration** measure. What was
located does not meet the register's bar: the nearest published measure of convergence-crowd crowding is
the pairwise-comovement "CoMetric" (S-280), whose *series* is the author's proprietary computation over
non-public data, and which measures comovement rather than capital concentration; the surrounding
literature the register already holds measures a different crowd in every case (S-026, S-157, S-222,
S-241, S-242, S-243); and the practitioner crowding diagnostics that surfaced are proprietary models,
vendor spread-compression rankings and commentary, not published, reproducible series. **G-28 stays frozen
and V-002 stays frozen.** The FINRA twice-monthly short-interest route remains a lead with objections
(per-issue aggregate with no firm-level breakdown; contamination of the short leg; short interest already
published prior art).

### G-30 — **exhausted confirmed, no re-probe** (IDEA-010)
All routes outside the statutory prospectus remain exhausted (not found), as re-confirmed across Cycles
41–56: regulatory route closed in Cycle 41 (17 CFR 270.6c-11 imposes no public disclosure requirement for

### IDEA-014's state-free existence limb — **inconclusive maintained**
No new source was identified on whether the US Renewable Fuel Standard compliance deadline moves prices at
all. The limb remains neither a positive finding nor a refutation and must not be described as either.
IDEA-014 stays at 52.0; P-011 stands; no gap is opened on this limb.

### The Cycle-56 tax-driven year-end flow family screen — logged as **R-035**
Year-end capital-loss harvesting under loss carry-forward rules, and the paired institutional
window-dressing flow, were screened as one family — the register's first screen of a **tax-incentive
flow** family, in which no participant is *obliged* to act and the flow's existence and strength are set
by a tax rule rather than by an obligation, a switch or a venue rule. Verdict: **bounded negative** on
five independent reasons — the mechanism is published prior art with a rule-dependent sign and with a
published null in at least one jurisdiction (S-274, S-275, S-278); the sign-determining state (which
investors realise which losses) is private tax-lot data, so any cross-sectional condition would be a
construction rather than a published series; the constrained flow is the seller's own tax obligation, so
there is no third-party concession to harvest; the buyer side is published prior art as well (S-277); and
the rule-dated natural experiment the family would need has already been run in the literature
(S-276, S-279, S-274). The screen, its instances, its five reasons and its dated re-screen condition are
recorded in `rejected_and_parked.md` under **R-035**, and the family was added to the known-baseline
table.

estándares contables".** Six-month period ended 30 June 2026.
URL (Spanish original, the CNMV filing and the authoritative text): https://www.repsol.com/content/dam/repsol-corporate/es/accionistas-e-inversores/cnmv/2026/oir23072026-estados-financieros-resumidos-consolidados-primer-semestre-2026.pdf

**Verbatim (English PDF, PDF line-wrapping joined, wording unchanged):** "With regard to the future
application of IFRS 18 "Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements", although this standard will
not have an impact on the Group's income, cash flows or financial position, it will introduce new
presentation criteria (mainly with respect to the income statement and statement of cash flows and, to a
lesser extent, the balance sheet) as well as new disclosure requirements and criteria for aggregating and
disaggregating information in the financial statements and in the notes. The main impacts identified
correspond primarily to the three categories for presenting income and expenses (operating, investing and
financing) and the subsequent new subtotals (" operating income" and " income before financing and taxes
"); the criteria for presenting certain items, both in the income statement (most notably the presentation
of exchange differences within each category based on the nature of the item giving rise to such
differences) and in the statement of cash flows (most notably dividends received from investees within
investing cash flows); and the fact that "operating income" is considered to be the new starting point for
preparing the statement of cash flows. As of the date of authorization for issue of these Financial

**S-287 — Lu, X., et al. (2023). "Night minus day: The informational role of overnight trading." Journal of
Financial Economics.** DOI: 10.1016/j.jfineco.2023.03.002. Metadata-verified via Crossref REST API.
Documents the cross-session price formation channel: overnight news impounds into prices at the next open,
and the stale-price window between close and open is a real, documented phenomenon.
**Verification:** metadata-verified via Crossref; abstract and title confirmed; full text not fetched.
**Supports:** R-036 screen — cross-session price formation is published prior art with a sign driven by
overnight information, not an unclaimed concession.

stale prices and non-synchronous trading across sessions. Documents that prices observed at different
sessions are non-synchronous and that the close-to-open window contains information impounded at the next
open.
**Verification:** metadata-verified; title and authors confirmed via Crossref. **Supports:** R-036 screen —
stale-price window between sessions is a documented microstructure fact, not an unclaimed edge.

**S-289 — Challet, D., & Gourianov, A. (2018). Opening auctions.** hal-01702726. Documents opening-auction
price discovery and how overnight imbalances are absorbed at the next open.
**Verification:** metadata-verified via HAL open archive; DOI/hal identifier confirmed. **Supports:** R-036
screen — opening auctions absorb overnight imbalance, leaving no persistent stale-price concession.

## Cycle 58 sources (S-291 … S-309)

All entries below were located by the Cycle-58 searches and **verified by the cycle itself**. Where the
verification method was the Crossref REST API, the DOI, title, authors, container title, year, volume,
issue and pages were all read from the API response. Where the method was a direct document fetch, the
quoted passage was read in the document itself. **No identifier, title, author or DOI in this block was
supplied by a search agent without being re-read by the cycle** — the register's standing rule, given that
identifiers supplied by a research agent have previously been found wrong.

**Second verification pass, later in Cycle 58.** Every entry in this block was then re-derived
**independently** against Crossref and, for the four primary documents, against a fresh download of the
document with its text layer extracted and searched. That pass found **eight defects**, all now corrected
in place below and itemised in the **"Cycle 58 second-pass corrections"** block at the end of this file:
two wrong volume/issue records (S-288, S-289), a truncated title (S-292), a wrong online date (S-291), an
unconfirmed issue number (S-295), a **paraphrase presented as a quotation** (S-299), a typographic
alteration inside a quotation (S-303) and another paraphrase presented as a quotation (S-304). **No
verdict, no gap closure and no score changed as a result** — but the evidentiary record of the cycle's
one rejection (R-038) and one family screen (R-037) was made exact.

### S-291 — Chen, Y., Da, D. and Huang, D. (2019)
"Arbitrage Trading: The Long and the Short of It." *The Review of Financial Studies* 32(4): 1608–1646.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhy097
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported; first published online 29 August 2018, print issue
  April 2019).
- **Supports (for G-04 / G-28):** a **published, position-based measure of arbitrage activity at the
  security level** — abnormal hedge-fund holdings (AHF), abnormal short interest (ASR) and their net
  combination (AHFSR) — that separates hedging and negative-hedging demand from the arbitrage activity
  it accompanies.
- **Caveats:** the measure is **security-level and single-sided**; the crowding it detects is anomaly- and
  stock-level, not a paired, netted convergence crowd, and it inherits 13F's reporting lag.
- **Verification:** Crossref REST API (DOI, title, all three authors, container title, volume, issue,
  pages, issued date 2018-08-29 and print date 2019-04-01).
- **Second-pass correction (Cycle 58):** the first version of this entry recorded the online date as
  "28 November 2018". The Crossref record gives **29 August 2018** as both the issued and the
  published-online date (and the print issue date is 1 April 2019). The correction is a date only; the
  entry's substance is unaffected.
- **Why it is new to the ledger:** the Cycle-35 G-18 gap-verdict reasoning already *cited* "Chen–Da–
  Huang (2019) net arbitrage trading" as an external claim, but **no S-identifier existed for it**. The
  claim was therefore sitting in the register without a ledger entry, in breach of the rule that every
  external claim points to a source entry. This entry closes that defect.

### S-292 — Coval, J. and Stafford, E. (2007)
"Asset fire sales (and purchases) in equity markets." *Journal of Financial Economics* 86(2): 479–512.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2006.09.007
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported).
- **Supports (for G-01 / IDEA-002):** the published, peer-reviewed form of the **funding-state → flow
  price impact → reversal** relation, on the *seller's* side: hedge funds facing large redemptions sell
  their common holdings, the resulting price pressure is measurable, and the subsequent reversal is also
  measurable; investors trading against the constrained sellers earn significant returns for supplying
  liquidity.
- **Caveats:** the conditioning state is the **seller's redemption pressure**, not the *intermediary's*
  funding cost; the setting is US mutual funds in 1998–2004; and the effect is a temporary price-pressure
  phenomenon rather than a persistent slope asymmetry.
- **Verification:** Crossref REST API (DOI, title, both authors, container title, volume, issue, pages,
  year); abstract read from the publisher/index rendering.
- **Second-pass correction (Cycle 58):** the first version of this entry recorded the title as
  "Asset fire sales." The published title is **"Asset fire sales (and purchases) in equity markets"**
  (Crossref title field, and the ScienceDirect record for the same DOI). The truncated title would have
  made the entry unmatchable against the publisher's own listing; the substantive claim is unaffected.
- **Cycle-103 verification — NEGATIVE, recorded as an honest failed route, NOT an upgrade.** The
  **Crossref REST API** `https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.jfineco.2006.09.007` was fetched
  directly on 21 October 2026 — **HTTP 200, 11,283 bytes** — and confirms the work's **identity**
  (title "Asset fire sales (and purchases) in equity markets", authors Coval and Stafford,
  *Journal of Financial Economics* **86**(2): 479–512, DOI `10.1016/j.jfineco.2006.09.007`) but holds
  **no abstract**. **The route is therefore exhausted: the deposited record is bibliographic only.**
  The entry's quoted abstract passages therefore remain index-rendered and are NOT line-verified.
  This entry is unchanged in substance and is not re-scored.

### S-293 — Huang, S., Hu, R., Song, Y. and Xiang, H. (2026)
"Same Dollar, Different Impact: Investor Flows are Not Equally Price-Moving." SSRN working paper 6266398
(doi:10.2139/ssrn.6266398).
- **Type:** Working paper (preprint; a journal version was located at the Journal of Financial Planning's
  site but its pagination and editorial status were **not** independently verified, so it is registered
  here as a preprint).
- **Supports (for G-01 / IDEA-002):** published evidence that **flow price impact is heterogeneous in the
  investor's funding state** — the same dollar of flow moves the price more for one investor type than for
  another — and that the heterogeneity is a function of the seller's redemption/redemption-pressure state.
- **Caveats:** the state is the *seller's* funding state, so it supports the *mechanism* of a
  funding-state-conditioned flow-impact relation while leaving IDEA-002's *intermediary*-side
  conditioning untouched; it is a preprint; and the direction of the published relation is that the
  *funding-constrained* flow is the more price-moving one.
- **Verification:** Crossref REST API (DOI, title, all four authors, container title "Journal of
  Financial Planning", year, type "posted-content"); abstract read from the journal's own page and from
  the preprint's abstract.

### S-294 — Neel, M. (2017)
"Accounting Comparability and Economic Outcomes of Mandatory IFRS Adoption." *Contemporary Accounting

- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported).

  23 June 2016 and in print 1 March 2017. The entry as written is confirmed; only the phrase "all four
  authors" in the verification line was wrong — the paper is **single-authored** — and it is corrected
  here. The entry's substance is unaffected.

### S-300 — Fang, W. (2026)
"China's Autocallable Cycle: Dealer Hedging Flows, Market Impact, and Lessons for Japan's Structured-Note
Market." SSRN working paper 7346463 (doi:10.2139/ssrn.7346463), written 24 August 2026, posted
28 August 2026.
- **Type:** Working paper (preprint; not peer-reviewed; author's declaration of a prior industry role).
- **Supports (for the R-037 screen):** the **most direct prior-art hit on the screened family**. The paper
  claims that Chinese autocallable ("snowball") notes "generated predictable, state-dependent dealer
  hedging flows around their knock-in and knock-out barriers", reconstructs the January 2024 knock-in
  episode from the hedging side, finds that "the economically relevant quantity is the hedge released
  across the barrier region rather than a pointwise delta at the contractual barrier", reports
  event-window regressions showing basis widening and activity increases in the CSI 500/1000 futures

  **outstanding notional × barrier concentration × maturity concentration × local dealer gamma**.

  identification"; the flow magnitudes are **hypothetical** ("hypothetical one-way flows of RMB 5–10bn per
  100 index points"), and the paper's own transferability analysis states that **"only one of the four
  variables is currently measurable from public disclosure"** for the Japanese market it proposes to
  extend the framework to.
- **Verification:** direct fetch of the preprint's abstract page (title, author, dates, abstract,
  DOI, declaration); the paper's full text was **not** read, so nothing is asserted beyond its abstract.

### S-305 — Barclay, M. and Hendershott, T. (2003)
"Price discovery and trading after hours." *The Review of Financial Studies* 16(4): 1041–1073.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhg030
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported).
- **Supports (for the R-036 screen, replacing the unverifiable S-290):** the canonical peer-reviewed
  treatment of after-hours trading: after-hours **price discovery is concentrated in a small subset of
  stocks**, and for those stocks the after-hours transaction price **leads the next open**. This supports
  both of the limbs the R-036 screen rested on S-290 for — that after-hours price formation is a
  documented channel, and that the after-hours session is **thin and concentrated**, so the round-trip cost
  of trading in it is high.

  year).

### S-306 — Auh, J. K. and Cho, W. (2023)
"Liquidation Cascade and Anticipatory Trading: Evidence from the Structured Equity Product Market."
*The Review of Asset Pricing Studies* 13(1): 53–98 (first published online 4 April 2022).
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1093/rapstu/raac010
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported; peer-reviewed). An earlier working-paper version of the
  same project is posted on SSRN under abstract id **3719988**; the working-paper version is recorded in
  secondary listings under the title "Liquidation Cascade and Hedging Front-Running: Evidence from the
  Structured Equity Product Market". **Second-pass caveat (Cycle 58):** SSRN's abstract page returned an
  automated-access block (HTTP 403) in this cycle, so the working-paper **title** could not be confirmed
  from the source itself; what *was* confirmed is that the record at abstract id 3719988 carries the same
  abstract's opening sentence ("We show that structured equity derivatives can cause significant price
  pressure of the underlying stock upon an event of dramatic payoff change") and the same project. The
  published article is the citation the screen relies on, and it is verified.
- **Supports (for the R-037 screen):** the **decisive prior art on the screened family**. From the
  publisher-deposited abstract: "We show that structured equity derivatives can cause significant price
  pressure of the underlying stock upon an event of dramatic payoff change. Moreover, one event causes
  another: the event cascade amplifies the magnitude of the impact. We find that a single event accounts
  for a −6.4 % return on the event day, and it increases the probability of a subsequent event by 21.3 %.
  Given the negative price impact, traders try to liquidate ahead of each other, exacerbating the degree
  of price pressure. Our results uncover the chain-reaction and (mis)coordination mechanism in complex
  derivatives markets that can provoke substantial price shocks."
- **Caveats:** the setting is the **Korean retail equity-linked securities (ELS)** market, 2006–2017, and
  the events are knock-in events on single stocks; it is not a US or EU retail structured-note study, and
  it does not condition on a *published* barrier level as a decision-time variable; and the −6.4 % event
  figure is an unconditional event-day mean, not a tradeable excess return.
- **Verification:** Crossref REST API, including the **publisher-deposited abstract** (DOI, title, both
  authors with affiliations, container title, volume, issue, pages, online date). The publisher's full
  text was **not** read (the article page refused automated access), so nothing is asserted beyond the
  deposited abstract and the metadata.

"Knock-In and Stocks Market Effect Due to ELS Issuance and Hedging." *Journal of Derivatives and

### S-308 — Broadie, M., Glasserman, P. and Kou, S. G. (1997)
"A Continuity Correction for Discrete Barrier Options." *Mathematical Finance* 7(4): 325–349.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9965.00035
- **Type:** Prior method paper (peer-reviewed; the canonical barrier-option reference).
- **Supports (for the R-037 screen):** the published basis for the **barrier shift** that the industry
  applies to smooth the very discontinuity the screen proposed to trade — the correction
  exp(±βσ√Δt) with β ≈ 0.5826 for discretely monitored barriers, and the documented deterioration of
  barrier and delta approximations as the underlying nears the barrier. The discontinuity is therefore a
  known, quantified, *corrected-for* modelling artefact rather than an unmodelled market fact.
- **Caveats:** it concerns option pricing and delta approximation for discretely monitored barriers, not
  the hedging of issued retail notes and not any price effect in the underlying.
- **Verification:** Crossref REST API (DOI, title, all three authors, container title, volume, issue,
  pages, year).
- **Why it is new to the ledger:** it was located in the Cycle-58 second-pass sweep of the R-037 family
  and is the **published claim that the screened family has already been turned into a tradeable
  strategy** — the last piece of the screen's "not an unclaimed mechanism" case, and the only source the
  register holds on the *volatility-surface* expression of dealer hedging of retail structured products.

### S-309 — Barthe, E. (2024)
"Do Retail Structured Products Distort Equity Volatilities?" SSRN working paper 5049552
(doi:10.2139/ssrn.5049552), written 4 December 2024, posted 16 December 2024.
- **Type:** Working paper (preprint; **not peer-reviewed**; no journal version was located).
- **Supports (for the R-037 screen):** the published, *strategy-level* claim on the screened family.
  From the publisher-deposited abstract: "I investigate how the hedging activity of structured products
  affects equity volatilities … When a new retail structured product is issued (autocallable, barrier
  reverse convertible, reverse convertible etc.), it creates a net supply of gamma. The rehedging activity
  of banks compresses the realised volatility of those underlyings. The volumes are large enough to have
  a significant impact on the volatility surfaces of the most popular underlyings. That phenomenon gives
  birth to profitable trading strategies in dispersion format."
- **Why it matters for the screen.** (i) It states the family-level effect with the **sign the register's
  screen was testing** — dealer rehedging of retail structured products *compresses* realised volatility
  and shifts the volatility surface, which is a **damping** concession (the same sign as S-298), not a
  directional price concession in the underlying. (ii) It says the effect has **already been converted into
  a strategy** — "profitable trading strategies in dispersion format" — so the family is not merely
  published, it is *claimed as tradeable*, which is the register's "known baseline" test in its sharpest
  form. (iii) It therefore removes the last plausible residual for a candidate in the family: the
  direction (damping), the mechanism (gamma supply and bank rehedging), the venue (retail structured
  products), the instrument (single-name and index underlyings) and the trade expression (dispersion) are
  all claimed in the literature.
- **Caveats:** it is a **preprint**, the abstract was read from the Crossref/SSRN deposited abstract and
  the **full text was not read**, so nothing is asserted here beyond the abstract; the "profitable trading
  strategies" claim is the **author's own claim** and is not an independently reproduced result; and the
  paper's own framing is about *volatility* effects and dispersion trades rather than about the
  underlying's price path through a barrier, so it is a **near-neighbour** of the R-037 screen rather than
  a direct hit on it.
- **Verification:** Crossref REST API (DOI, title, author, type "posted-content", year 2024, and the
  publisher-deposited abstract). The SSRN landing page itself refused automated access in this cycle, so
  the abstract was read from the Crossref deposit rather than from the SSRN page; the write/posted dates
  were read from the SSRN search-index record and are recorded as such.

## Cycle 66 sources (2026-10-20)

Cycle 66 ran the register's **prior-art re-read of IDEA-009** — the one active candidate whose published-neighbour
inventory was still the thinnest (S-158 and S-159 only) and which had not been re-read against literature it had
not yet seen since Cycle 13 — and screened **state-kind template (I)**. Thirteen new source entries are minted
below: **S-310 … S-322**. **Five were fetched directly and text-extracted** (S-315, S-316, S-319, S-320 and the
venue documentation S-321); the remainder are verified by **Crossref metadata**, with **index-rendered** abstracts
in the SSRN and repository cases (S-310, S-311, S-312, S-317, S-318) because those landing pages refused automated
access (HTTP 403), **index-confirmed** wording in S-314 (the NBER PDF was fetched directly and its text layer was
present in the returned stream, but the quoted statistics also appear in the index-rendered highlights and are
recorded at that weaker status), a **publisher-deposited abstract** in S-313, and a **bibliographic record only** in
S-322 because its abstract was not retrievable. **No wording in this block is presented as a directly parsed
document unless the entry says so.**

### S-310 — Shek, H. (2026)
"Conditional Arbitrage Capacity: Evidence from Crypto Perpetual Funding Rates." SSRN working paper 7520320
(posted 26 September 2026). DOI: https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7520320
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), SSRN preprint; single author; **not peer-reviewed**.
- **Supports (for IDEA-009):** a **direct published test of the candidate's own prediction 1**, on 274
  funding-rate extreme events across BTC, ETH and SOL from 2021 to 2026: events on **up days revert by +1.88 %

### S-311 — Shek, H. (2026)
"Limits to Coordination: Funding Drag in Crypto Perpetual Funding Rates." SSRN working paper 7529458
(posted 29 September 2026). DOI: https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7529458
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), SSRN preprint; single author; **not peer-reviewed**.
- **Supports (for IDEA-009):** the **speed of parity restoration after a funding-rate extreme is dominated by
  realised volatility**. Across 1,696 events on 18 Binance perpetual contracts, high-volatility events take a
  median of 27.0 hours to correct against 3.0 hours for low-volatility events (log-rank χ² = 147.25,
  p < 0.0001); a one-standard-deviation rise in realised volatility lowers the hazard of correction by about
  41 % (HR = 0.5935); a placebo on volatility-matched non-event hours finds only extreme events are slow to
  correct (27.0 h against 10.0 h); a recursive-partitioning tree puts the strongest heterogeneity at the ratio
  vol24/vol168, with correction time spanning 11.53 to 122.62 hours; and the effect is present both before and
  after the FTX collapse (HR 0.570 versus 0.702).
- **Why it matters for IDEA-009:** the candidate's frozen exit rule (V-008: hold 1–3 funding periods) is **not**
  the published structure of the correction. A fixed 8–24 hour horizon is, on this evidence, a rule that works
  in low-volatility episodes and misses in high-volatility ones — so the exit must be specified conditionally, or
  the test must pre-register that a fixed-horizon null is not a kill.
- **Caveats:** single-author preprint, author-reported, not reproduced here; the entry is index-rendered, so the
  hazard-ratio and survival-timing definitions are not verifiable from this record.
- **Verification:** Crossref REST API (DOI, title, author, year 2026, type "posted-content") — **the
  DOI is now independently Crossref-confirmed** (Cycle-67; first attempt returned HTTP 429, retry

### S-313 — Zhivkov, P., Todorov, V. and Georgiev, S. (2026)
"Temporal Dynamics of Market Microstructure in Cryptocurrency Perpetual Futures: Econometric Evidence from
Centralized and Decentralized Exchanges." *International Journal of Financial Studies* 14(5): 103 (MDPI;
ISSN 2227-7072), published 23 April 2026 (received 11 March 2026, revised 10 April 2026, accepted 15 April
2026). DOI: https://doi.org/10.3390/ijfs14050103
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), **peer-reviewed journal article** (MDPI, open access,
  CC-BY).
- **Supports (for IDEA-009):** an econometric study of 9.1 million hourly funding-rate observations across 26
  exchanges and 812 symbols (14 November 2025 to 13 January 2026) in 53 overlapping seven-day rolling windows,
  using GARCH(1,1), Bai–Perron structural-break detection, CUSUM stability testing and Granger causality in
  bivariate VAR frameworks. It reports that the two-tiered market structure documented in a static snapshot
  (centralised venues tightly integrated, decentralised venues fragmented) **persists qualitatively but varies
  substantially in magnitude, with the integration gap ranging from −0.041 to 0.222**; that **structural-break
  tests detect no discrete regime shifts, the market evolving through gradual drift**; that **near-integrated
  (IGARCH) volatility behaviour appears in only 24.5 % of windows**, concentrated in specific periods; that
  **mid-tier exchanges lead the largest venue (Binance) more frequently than the reverse**, challenging a
  size-based price-discovery hierarchy; and that **intraday spread patterns are statistically significant and
  linked to funding-rate settlement mechanics, with spreads peaking approximately two hours after standard
  settlement times**.
- **Why it matters for IDEA-009:** the spread-timing result is a **cost-model fact** for any rule that trades
  around a funding settlement — the candidate's cost floor is worst shortly after the settlement it is keyed
  to — and the "gradual drift, no discrete regime shifts" result is a caution against regime-switching state
  constructions built on discrete regime labels.
- **Caveats:** a two-month window is short for a market-structure claim; the findings are author-reported; the
  companion static study the authors extend (Zhivkov 2026, *Mathematics* 14(2), DOI 10.3390/math14020346) was
  not read.
- **Verification:** Crossref REST API verified — DOI 10.3390/ijfs14050103, title, all three authors and their
  affiliations, container *International Journal of Financial Studies*, volume 14, issue 5, article 103,
  published-online 23 April 2026, and the **full abstract as deposited by the publisher**, which is the source
  of every finding quoted above. The publisher's own page and PDF endpoint returned **HTTP 403** to a direct
  fetch, so the article body was not read; the abstract is Crossref-deposited rather than index-rendered.
  *Cycle-66 correction (made before the cycle closed): an earlier draft of this entry attributed the article

  **HTTP 404** on a direct Crossref lookup — the 404 was the signal that the journal attribution was wrong.

### S-315 — Kim, J. and Park, H. (2025)
"Designing funding rates for perpetual futures in cryptocurrency markets." arXiv:2506.08573
(submitted 10 June 2025; q-fin.MF; q-fin.PR).
arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08573
- **Type:** Prior theoretical result (author-reported), arXiv preprint; **not peer-reviewed**.
- **Supports (for IDEA-009):** a mathematical-finance treatment of the funding mechanism. It reports that funding
  mechanisms can be **designed** so that the perpetual price stays aligned with its target value; that **replicating
  portfolios** exist for perpetual futures; and — the point that bears directly on the candidate's state — that
  **path-dependent funding rates are the practical case, because in most exchanges the funding fee is the average
  of values over the past 8 hours rather than the current spot price**, so the realised funding rate is inherently
  path-dependent. Existence and uniqueness results are obtained with path-dependent infinite-horizon BSDEs.
- **Why it matters for IDEA-009:** the candidate's state variable is the *realised* funding rate, which is
  therefore a **moving average of the premium index over the preceding window**, not an instantaneous measure of
  the crowd. That is a measurement property of the state that the candidate's dossier does not currently record.
- **Caveats:** preprint; the paper is about pricing and design, not about the return predictability of the
  funding level.
- **Verification:** **arXiv abstract page fetched directly and read** — title, both authors, submission date
  (10 June 2025), subject classes, DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2506.08573 and the full abstract were confirmed from the
  arXiv record. The body text was read only through the arXiv HTML rendering surfaced by the search index.

"Crypto Perpetuals Funding." Case study for *Machine Learning for Trading* (3rd edition).
URL: https://www.ml4trading.io/case-studies/crypto-funding-arbitrage/
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), **book case study with public notebooks — not peer-reviewed**.
- **Supports (for IDEA-009):** an author-reported, cost-aware, walk-forward test of funding-rate mean-reversion
  across 19 Binance perpetual contracts on an 8-hour cadence (rebalances at 00:00/08:00/16:00 UTC), with 44
  features, HAC-adjusted information coefficients, Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery correction, a two-tier
  maker/taker cost model and **two** cross-validation folds (2-year training, 1-year validation). Its stated
  synthesis is, in the author's words, "**the book's clearest negative result. Validation Sharpe +0.80 collapses
  to -1.17 in holdout (-247% decay). The 2024-2025 crypto bull run reversed the cross-sectional funding
  patterns. Verdict: Reframe -- viable only with explicit regime detection.**" The case study also records that
  the funding rate is used as a **feature, not a label** ("the question is whether extremes predict subsequent
  price moves"); that linear models produce negative information coefficients, i.e. the signal is genuinely
  non-linear; that positive Sharpe coexists with negative CAGR under 8-hour rebalancing; that the universe is
  "the smallest cross-section in the book" with "intentionally limited statistical power"; and that the study is
  an ML feature study rather than a test of a pre-specified trading rule.
- **Why it matters for IDEA-009:** this is the **nearest published out-of-sample failure** of the funding-rate
  mean-reversion premise, and it identifies **regime dependence** as the reason — which is the same condition the
  published conditional result (S-310) makes structural.
- **Caveats:** not peer-reviewed; the author's own results; a different construction (cross-sectional ML, 44
  features, two folds) from the candidate's dated single-asset decile rule, so it is **near-neighbour evidence,
  not a test of the candidate's specification**.
- **Verification:** the case-study page was **fetched directly and text-extracted** — the quoted verdict line, the
  universe and cadence, the fold structure and the cost-model description were all read from the returned page.

### S-320 — Das, A. (2023)
"Testing the Theory: Is the Perpetual Swap funding rate predictive?" Brave New Coin, 1 March 2023.
URL: https://bravenewcoin.com/insights/testing-theory-is-perpetual-swap-funding-rate-predictive
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), **industry research outlet — not peer-reviewed**.
- **Supports (for IDEA-009):** a published test of BitMEX's 2017 hypothesis that more extreme funding-rate values
  predict the next funding-period return, on BitMEX funding data from 2 November 2022 to 22 February 2023. The
  article records that funding was generally within ±0.05 %, that it fell to −0.2 % in November 2022 with
  z-scores up to 8 standard deviations, and that the regression of log(price at T1 / price at T0) on the funding
  rate published at T0 gives **slope −0.668, R² = 0.00109, F = 0.388 on 357 degrees of freedom**, with the
  index-price variant giving **R² = 0.0168**. Its stated conclusion is that "it does not appear that there is a
  strong relationship between funding rate and price", but that "in the most extreme cases when funding payments
  are set to be high, there are market reversals"; it also records that mean reversion "did occur but not
  immediately after a high negative funding rate rounds", and that the bearishness of the FTX collapse dominated
  the funding signal.
- **Why it matters for IDEA-009:** this is the **closest published test of the candidate's own prediction 1**,
  and it is a near-null for the general form while reporting reversals **only at the extremes** — which is
  simultaneously the strongest published support for the candidate's decile-extreme design and the strongest
  published evidence against its unconditional version.
- **Caveats:** not peer-reviewed; a short, crisis-dominated sample (three months, one venue); the author states
  that the underlying spreadsheets are available on request; the reported R² and slope are the author's.
- **Verification:** the article was **fetched directly and text-extracted** — the date, author, sample window,
  the regression table (slope, intercept, standard errors, R², F, degrees of freedom) and the conclusions were all
  read from the returned page.

### S-321 — dYdX (venue rulebook, undated page; read 20 October 2026)
"Funding" documentation. URL: https://docs.dydx.xyz/concepts/trading/funding
- **Type:** **Primary venue documentation** (the venue publishes its own funding rule).
- **Supports (for IDEA-009 and for the R-046 screen):** the venue's published funding specification. The premium
  component is computed from the impact bid and impact ask prices against the index price, with the impact
  notional set as 500 USDC divided by the initial-margin fraction; the premium is a time-weighted average of 60
  one-minute premiums over the preceding hour; the funding rate is the premium component divided by eight plus a
  fixed interest-rate component; funding is charged **hourly** on the platform. The document also publishes the
  **cap**: "The 8-hour rate cap is calculated by 600% * (Initial Margin - Maintenance Margin)", with the tier table
  (large-cap 5 %/3 %, mid-cap 10 %/5 %, long-tail 20 %/10 %), so the BTC-USD eight-hour rate is capped at
  600 % × (5 % − 3 %) = 12 %. And it publishes that **governance can adjust the funding parameters** — the
  funding-rate clamp factor, the premium-vote clamp factor, the minimum number of votes per premium sample, the
  epoch/funding interval and sampling interval, and the liquidity tier (impact notional).
- **Why it matters:** this is the register's cleanest *venue-published* instance of the **clamp/cap as a
  published function parameter of a continuously published state**, and it shows that the parameter is
  **governance-adjustable** — i.e. the state is not stable across regimes without a re-specification.
- **Caveats:** an undated documentation page (read on 20 October 2026); it is one venue's specification and the
  register does not generalise from it to other venues; the documentation is descriptive of the rule, not evidence
  of any price effect.
- **Verification:** the page was **fetched directly and text-extracted** — the funding formula, the cap formula and
  tier table, the hourly settlement and the governance-adjustable parameter list were all read from the returned
  page.

### S-322 — Rajendran, S. and Singaravelu, D. (2026)
"Order-flow toxicity in cryptocurrency perpetual futures: Order flow signals, price-impact persistence, and the
limits of volatility-based metrics." *International Review of Economics & Finance* 112: 105876
(DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.iref.2026.105876; published online 30 September 2026; December 2026
issue). SSRN version: posted 19 March 2026, last revised 5 October 2026, 30 pages; earlier working
title "Predicting Adverse Selection in High-Frequency Cryptocurrency Markets Using Gradient Boosting".
Replication code: Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21617203.
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), **peer-reviewed journal article**.
- **Cycle-67 upgrade — the abstract is now retrieved.** The publisher's page returned HTTP 403 to a
  direct fetch in Cycle 66, and the entry was recorded at title level only. In Cycle 67 the DOI was
  followed through the ScienceDirect record and the **full abstract was read directly** (the
  SSRN record and the journal's own highlights page render the same text). The findings below are
  therefore **line-verified**, not index-rendered.
- **Supports (for IDEA-009, cost side):** a severity-weighted **gradient-boosted detector of
  order-flow toxicity** trained on BTC/USDT and ETH/USDT on Bybit on **~31.08 million
  second-level observations per asset (~62.16 million combined)**, with a strict walk-forward
  protocol and predictors constructed **exclusively from information available through the prior
  second**. Two anchor results: (i) at the primary 1 % gate the **no-volatility** specification
  generates an illustrative avoided-loss estimate that is **statistically distinguishable from
  zero and replicates closely across two assets differing ~35-fold in price level**; (ii)
  **tail-risk concentration and economic value diverge systematically** — the simple return-,
  flow- and volatility-based learned benchmarks achieve **higher tail-risk efficiency**, so
  "efficiency alone is an unreliable indicator of informational specificity". The authors use
  **order-flow toxicity rather than confirmed informed trading** and interpret their TailScore as
  a practically relevant adverse-selection **risk-ranking signal, not a direct measure of private
  information or a realised trading strategy**.
- **Why it matters for IDEA-009:** this is the nearest published cost-side quantification for the
  family the candidate sits in. A funding-rate reversal rule is short volatility and long
  adverse-selection risk; the paper's headline — that the signals which *rank* toxicity are not
  the same signals which *avoid* its cost, and that excluding contemporaneous volatility still
  leaves a detectable toxicity signal — is the published statement of the cost floor V-008 must
  beat. It also supplies, for the first time in this register, a **published, walk-forward,
  out-of-sample cost benchmark at second-level frequency in this venue class**.
- **Caveats:** the paper's outcome is a *toxicity ranking*, not a trading return; its "illustrative
  avoided-loss" is an estimate, not a realised P&L; the universe is two assets on one venue; and
  the published replication archive (Zenodo) contains the processed labelled datasets and model
  artefacts but **not** the raw Bybit order-book data, so the raw-input side is not reproducible
  from the archive alone.
- **Verification:** the DOI was followed to the ScienceDirect record and the **abstract was read
  directly** in Cycle 67 (title, both authors, journal, volume, article number, publication date,
  highlights and abstract all confirmed from the returned record). The SSRN record and the
  journal's own highlights page render the same abstract. *Cycle-66 debt closed: the entry
  previously recorded only a bibliographic record and stated that the abstract was not retrieved.*

## Cycle 58 state-integrity repairs

Cycle 58 verified the Cycle-57 source block entry by entry, because that block supports **G-33's
kill condition**, which is the closure of the register's rank-1 candidate's only live arm, and because
**R-036's five reasons cite it**. The verification found eight defects. **No verdict changed**; the
evidentiary base of R-036 was repaired and G-33's record was made exact.

### Repair 1 — S-287's title and author initial were wrong
The entry recorded: "Lu, X., et al. (2023). 'Night minus day: The informational role of overnight
trading.' *Journal of Financial Economics*." The DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2023.03.002 resolves to **Lu, Z.,
Malliaris, S. and Qin, Z. (2023), "Heterogeneous liquidity providers and night-minus-day return
predictability", *Journal of Financial Economics* 148(3): 175–200**. The **title was wrong**, the **author
initial was wrong** ("X." for "Z."), and the venue and year were right. The paper's content *is* on point
for the R-036 screen (it is about night-minus-day return predictability), so the screen's first reason
stands on a corrected citation.

## Cycle 58 gap verdicts

**G-01 — CLOSED AS A NEGATIVE (IDEA-002, FUNDSTATE). The candidate is rejected (R-038).**
The question the register set was whether a public, defensible funding-state proxy can be constructed that
demonstrably predicts disclosed dealer funding value adjustments over a multi-year sample. It cannot,
and — more importantly — the question cannot be answered in a way that bears on the candidate, for three
independent reasons.
1. **The proposed validation is tautological for the candidate's own claim.** A dealer's funding value
   adjustment is *computed from its own funding curve* (S-010, S-155); a funding-cost proxy that
   "predicts" it is therefore an accounting identity, not evidence that the proxy measures the thing
   IDEA-002 actually conditions on — **dealer-specific balance-sheet capacity**. S-297 records the same
   point from the other side: whether FVA is a cost or a benefit of intermediation is itself an open
   debate, so the target is not even unambiguously signed.
2. **The target is thin, non-comparable and not multi-year.** Dealer FVAs are disclosed as annual,
   point-in-time amounts, by a handful of disclosing dealers, at materially different levels of
   materiality and under differing definitions; no continuous public series exists (S-155's caveat, which
   this cycle re-confirmed rather than contradicted); and the published tabulation is a short window
   rather than a multi-year series. A validation sample over "a multi-year sample" is not constructible
   from published dealer disclosure.
3. **The state the candidate needs is dealer-specific, while every public ingredient is market-wide.**
   The public ingredients are market funding-cost series; the closest *dealer-specific* public measures
   are the Federal Reserve's quarterly Senior Credit Officer Opinion Survey (qualitative net percentages)
   and the NY Fed's daily SOFR statistics (S-155). A market-wide composite cannot measure a single
   dealer's balance-sheet capacity, and with a market-wide state the conditioning changes only the
   *size* of an effect — failing G-12's sign-and-existence limb — while the relation it would condition is
   published (S-009) and its nearest published empirical form is a *seller-side* funding-state → flow
   impact → reversal result (S-292, S-293).
   The register's own files also record the closest published prior art for the *sign* of a
   funding-state-conditioned flow effect, and it is the **seller's** funding state (S-292, S-293), not
   the intermediary's.
   **Therefore IDEA-002 is rejected rather than re-specified** — which is exactly what its own dossier
   (prediction 4: "must be dropped rather than re-specified") and its own parking entry (P-004: "If not,
   this candidate should be rejected rather than re-specified") prescribed. Score withdrawn. No `V-`
   specification was ever issued for IDEA-002, so none is withdrawn.

**G-04 — CLOSED IN THE CANDIDATE'S FAVOUR on the proxy-validity limb; G-28 CONFIRMED OPEN AND FROZEN
(IDEA-004, SLOWCAP-COND).**
- **G-04's validity limb is satisfied.** The question was whether the crowding proxy the candidate would
  use is valid against a published outcome. It is: each crowding construct the register holds has been
  validated against a published outcome — the holdings-based Days-ADV crowding construct against
  crash/tail risk (S-026, S-222), the correlation-based comomentum construct against arbitrage activity
  and returns (S-157) — so the register never needed the comomentum-versus-holdings validation it had
  originally required. **G-04 is closed on that limb.**
- **What remains is the identity limb, and it is registered as G-28 (frozen).** The candidate's state
  must be a position-concentration measure of **the convergence crowd in the candidate's own universe**,
  and no published measure of that crowd was located. **This cycle reached a structural, not merely a
  search-based, reason for the null**, which is the new content: every published crowding, arbitrage-
  activity and concentration construct the register now holds is **security-level and single-sided** —
  abnormal hedge-fund holdings and abnormal short interest (S-291), short-interest-implied arbitrage
  capital (S-242), ownership dispersion (S-296), the holdings-based Days-ADV crowding measure (S-026,
  S-222), and correlation-implied comomentum (S-157) — because each is built from *disclosed aggregate
  positions* in securities. **A convergence crowd is defined by a pair of positions**: long one leg, short
  the other. A single-sided, security-level measure cannot represent it, because the same disclosed long
  holding may be a convergence leg or a directional bet, and the short leg is either invisible or
  contaminated by unrelated shorting. So the absence is a property of the available position-disclosure
  sources, not of the register's searching — which is a stronger and more durable null than "nothing
  was found".
- **Consequence.** IDEA-004 stays at **69.0, rank 2**; **V-002 stays frozen**; the candidate may not
  substitute any published crowding proxy, because each measures a different crowd (the standing
  prohibition from Cycles 35, 37, 40, 52 and 56).

**G-21 — CONFIRMED NULL AND SHARPENED (IDEA-011, ACCTCLOCK).**
- **The null holds and is now stated in a stronger form.** No published study compares first-time with
  second-time adopters of the same standard on any market outcome, including post-earnings-announcement
  drift. Three cycles have now established this (Cycles 37, 52 and 58).
- **The discriminator is not merely unrun — it is unused by the field's largest comparability study.**
  S-294 is a large peer-reviewed study whose design is a **first-time-adopter** design *by construction*
  (mandatory IFRS adoption is, for the adopting jurisdictions, adoption of IFRS for the first time), and
  its outcomes include **analyst forecast accuracy and forecast agreement** — but **not**
  post-earnings-announcement drift. The nearest published *outcome* family to the candidate's
  information-environment claim is likewise a first-time-adopter study (S-295). A study that ran the
  first-time-versus-second-time contrast on drift would therefore be a genuine contribution rather than a
  replication, which raises rather than lowers the candidate's novelty — and lowers its evidence
  dimension, because the field's own evidence base does not contain the comparison.
- **The direction of the published evidence does not resolve the candidate's premise.** S-294 concerns the
  *level* of information quality after comparability improves (more accurate forecasts, better agreement);
  IDEA-011's claim concerns a *transition* window between the adoption announcement and the first full
  reporting cycle. The two are not the same object, so S-294 neither supports nor refutes the candidate's
  directional drift claim — but it does impose a requirement: **the candidate must pre-register that its
  claim is a transition-window effect**, because the published steady-state evidence runs the other way.
- **G-32 limb (c) is not re-read this cycle** (it is annual and the next re-read is due in 2027) and
  limb (a)'s re-open condition is unchanged. **No score change (69.0, rank 1).**
   - **Two new facts about the candidate's mechanism scope**, read from the G-33 documents themselves:
   (i) **IFRS 18 changes no recognition, no measurement and no reported amount — but it changes
   presentation across three statements, not one.** Standard Life's interim report states that "IFRS 18 does
   not change the recognition or measurement of assets, liabilities, income or expenses" (S-285), and
   Repsol's states that the standard "will not have an impact on the Group's income, cash flows or financial
   position" (S-281). **This is the part that bounds the candidate's mechanism**: the comparability break
   the candidate's clock is about is *substantive-neutral* — it does not create an economic difference, it
   creates a presentation difference. **But it is not confined to the statement of profit or loss.**
   Repsol's own words: the standard "will introduce new presentation criteria (mainly with respect to the
   income statement **and statement of cash flows and, to a lesser extent, the balance sheet**)"; the affected
   items are "the three categories for presenting income and expenses (operating, investing and financing) and
   the subsequent new subtotals (" operating income" and " income before financing and taxes ")"; the
   criteria for presenting certain items apply "both in the income statement (most notably the presentation of
   exchange differences within each category based on the nature of the item giving rise to such differences)
   and in the statement of cash flows (most notably dividends received from investees within investing cash
   flows)"; and "operating income" becomes "the new starting point for preparing the statement of cash
   flows". The Tadawul index rendering says the same of the cash-flow reconciliation's starting point and
   adds that goodwill must be presented as a separate line (S-286, index-rendered). **Corrected scope
   statement:** the break runs over (a) the statement of profit or loss's new categories, subtotals and
   reclassification criteria; (b) the **statement of cash flows**, whose starting point becomes operating
   income and whose investing/operating split changes; (c) the **balance sheet**, to a lesser extent, in the
   presentation of goodwill as a separate line; (d) the aggregation, disaggregation and management-
   performance-measure disclosures; and (e) **nothing that changes recognition, measurement or any reported
   amount**. This *sharpens* the candidate's rule and is recorded as a narrowing **in the candidate's
   favour** — the break is a presentation break, not an economic one — but under the Cycle-35/52 precedent
   it does not move a score, because it bounds the mechanism rather than supporting the directional drift
   claim. **A first version of this entry stated that the break ran "over nothing else — no cash-flow, no
   balance-sheet, no measurement change"; the first two limbs were wrong and are corrected here.** The
   measurement limb was right.
   (ii) **The EU endorsement date is corroborated by an independent primary issuer document**: Airbus
   SE's H1 2026 financial statements state that "IFRS 18 has been endorsed by the EU on 13 February 2026"
   (S-283), matching S-268. G-32 limb (a)'s closure therefore now rests on two independent primary
   confirmations rather than one.

**R-037 — CONTRACTUAL BARRIER HEDGING FAMILY SCREEN, BOUNDED NEGATIVE.**
Screened as one family, against the literature, before any conclusion: the published knock-out / barrier
level in the term sheet or Key Information Document of an autocallable, barrier reverse auto or knock-out
structured note, and the *discontinuity in the issuer's or dealer's hedging* when the underlying trades
through it. The full five-reason rationale, the known-baseline row and the dated re-screen condition are
in `rejected_and_parked.md` under **R-037**. No dossier was created; no `IDEA-` identifier was consumed;
no score changed; no validation specification was added. **No new gap is opened**, because the screen's
reasons are **independent of any data availability** — the mechanism, its sign and its anticipation are
already published (S-306, S-307, S-299), the discontinuity is removed by standard practice (S-308, S-299,
S-304), and the magnitude is unmeasurable and, where estimated, small and conditional (S-300, S-301,
S-302) — so a better state would not revive the family.
**Note on how this block was written.** The first pass at this verdict rested on S-298, S-300 and S-304 and
argued that "the published state does not determine the sign". A broader literature sweep then located
**S-306**, a peer-reviewed study of the *same* mechanism in the Korean retail ELS market with a quantified
event-day effect (−6.4 %) and an explicit finding of **anticipatory trading**, and with it **S-307** and
**S-308**. The screen's first reason therefore became *stronger* — the mechanism and the sign are
published prior art with magnitudes, not merely asserted — while the "state does not determine the sign"
sub-argument was **withdrawn**: the published *payoff structure* does fix the direction of the hedge
adjustment at a given barrier (a down-and-in knock-out requires the issuer to sell the underlying on
breach; an up-and-out call barrier requires it to buy), so what survives is not a sign ambiguity but the
stronger objections that the effect is *anticipated* (S-306), *engineered away* (S-308, S-299, S-304) and
*unmeasurable* (S-300, S-301, S-302). The verdict is unchanged; its basis is corrected.

## Cycle 58 second-pass corrections

The Cycle-58 block above was **verified a second time, independently**, before the handoff was
written: every DOI-bearing entry was re-derived against the Crossref REST API, and the four primary
documents (S-301, S-302, S-303, S-304) were downloaded again and their **text layers extracted and
searched**, because a reading that cannot be re-checked by extraction is a reading that the next agent
cannot audit. **Eight defects were found and corrected in place in that pass; a further six were found
when Repair 8's document retrieval was completed (items 9–14 below). No verdict, no gap closure and no
score changed.**

1. **S-288 — wrong volume, issue and pages.** The Cycle-58 repair itself gave *Studies in Economics and
   Finance* "30(1): 7–31"; the Crossref record gives **31(4): 354–370**. Corrected in the entry *and* in
   the repair that claimed to have fixed it.
2. **S-289 — wrong volume, issue and pages.** The repair gave *Market Microstructure and Liquidity*
   "5(1)"; the Crossref record gives **4(01n02): 1950001**, issued March 2018, online 18 August 2019.
   Corrected in both places.
3. **S-291 — wrong online date.** "28 November 2018" → **29 August 2018** (Crossref issued and
   published-online dates; print issue April 2019).
4. **S-292 — truncated title.** "Asset fire sales." → **"Asset fire sales (and purchases) in equity
   markets."** The truncated form would have been unmatchable against the publisher's own listing.
5. **S-294 — wrong authorship in the verification line.** The entry's verification line said "all four
   authors"; the paper is **single-authored** (Neel, Michael). The record itself was correct.
6. **S-295 — unconfirmed issue.** The Crossref record carries **no issue number** for
   *International Review of Financial Analysis* 21, 56–63; the issue is recorded as unverified rather
   than verified.
7. **S-299 — a paraphrase presented as a quotation.** The entry quoted "the delta of an autocallable
   product can vary rapidly near the barriers, making delta hedging costly to implement" as the source's
   words. The publisher-deposited abstract says the product's delta "can become too large near the
   barriers" and that the authors "apply payoff modification and barrier shifting techniques". The
   quotation was replaced with the source's wording in **three** places — the ledger entry, the R-037
   entry in `rejected_and_parked.md`, and the known-baseline table row — because the register's rule is
   that an index-rendered or reworded passage may not be presented as a directly parsed one.
8. **S-303 and S-304 — two further wording defects.** S-303's barrier sentence was rendered "60 % of the
   Initial Reference Value"; the document reads **"60% of the Initial Reference Value"**, and the
   determination period ("7 September 2028") is now recorded as well. S-304's "brokers' hedging activities
   may have exacerbated market selling pressure" was a reworded quotation; the document reads **"whether
   brokerage houses' hedging activities may have exacerbated market selling pressure"**.

**What the second pass confirmed, verbatim, from the primary documents.** S-301: "around 60 different
products"; "the volume issued, the minimum return, the offer date, strike date and expiry date"; Chart
V.10's France-2017 shares (capped calls 4 %, auto-callables 29 %, protected trackers 43 %, uncapped calls
13 %, other 11 %); "have declined sharply" (Germany); "appears to have witnessed a collapse in sales
volumes overall" (Italy). S-302: "any other relevant features such as a strike, barrier or guarantee",
in the autocallables section last updated 14 November 2022. S-303: "Barrier Level: The Barrier Level is
equal to 60% of the Initial Reference Value of the relevant Underlying"; "The Issuer may enter into hedging
arrangements with market counterparties in connection with the issue of the Securities in order to hedge
its exposure". S-304: "You buy the futures as you approach the barriers, but then the problem is once you
hit the knock-in, the barrier disappears, and your delta reverts back"; "moving the knock-in level model
basis lower to reduce the amount of futures they have to buy to hedge"; and Cboe's dissent from the BIS
conclusion, in this issue's "Q&A: Cboe VIX" section.

**One source added.** **S-309** (Barthe 2024) was located during the second pass and registered: it is
the published, strategy-level claim on the R-037 family — dealer rehedging of retail structured products
compresses realised volatility and "gives birth to profitable trading strategies in dispersion format" —
and therefore strengthens the screen's verdict rather than altering it.

**Repair 8 completed — the six G-33 interim reports were retrieved, read and recorded.** The Cycle-57
block had left Repair 8 as an open promise: the five disclosure phrases in the gap-verdict were
paraphrases presented as quotations, the six ledger entries carried no URLs, and the documents themselves
had not been independently read. All six were then retrieved (five directly; one not at all) and the
ledger was corrected in place. **Six further defects were found and corrected; no verdict, no gap closure
and no score changed.**

9. **S-281 … S-286 — the disclosure language was paraphrase, and the phrases were mis-assigned.** Each
   entry now carries the issuer's verbatim wording, the document's URL, and the verification method
   actually used. "will examine the impact" is **Euronext Securities Athens**'s wording, not Airbus's;
   "the assessment remains ongoing" is **Standard Life**'s, not Haleon's; Airbus's actual wording is "The
   Company is currently analysing the potential impacts of this new standard"; Haleon's is "the Group
   continues to assess the impact of IFRS 18, with initial system and process changes underway"; Repsol's is
   "the Group is still assessing the impacts arising from the application of this standard".
10. **S-281 … S-286 — the disclosures were mis-characterised as IAS 8 paragraph 30–31 impact
    disclosures.** They are *standards issued but not yet effective* and *recent accounting developments*
    notes. The string "IAS 8" occurs **zero** times in the extracted text of all five fetched documents and
    does not appear in the Tadawul index rendering. This confirms rather than undermines the register's
    hypothesis.
11. **S-286 — a false verification line.** The entry read "issuer/exchange document fetched directly". The
    Saudi Tadawul document was **never fetched**: every route returned HTTP 403 (Akamai), a 522, a 504, an
    empty reader-proxy body or a 404, and the Wayback availability API returned no snapshots. The entry is
    now marked **NOT VERIFIED**, the text is labelled index-rendered, and the corpus is restated as **5 of 6
    line-verified, 6 of 6 index-confirmed**, with the cross-jurisdiction comparability of the sample
    expressly not established.
12. **The comparability break was under-scoped in four places.** The Cycle-58 gap verdict, the IDEA-011
    dossier, the shortlist row and the V-009 amendment all stated that the break runs over the profit or
    loss statement "and over nothing else — no cash-flow, no balance-sheet, no measurement change". The
    **first two limbs were wrong**: Repsol's own text says the new presentation criteria apply "(mainly
    with respect to the income statement **and statement of cash flows and, to a lesser extent, the balance
    sheet**)", that "operating income" is "the new starting point for preparing the statement of cash
    flows", and that dividends received from investees move within investing cash flows; the Tadawul index
    rendering says the same of the reconciliation's starting point and adds that goodwill becomes a
    separate line. The **measurement limb was right**. All four artifacts are corrected to state: the break
    is **substantive-neutral** (no recognition, no measurement, no change to any reported amount) but
    **presentation-wide** (income statement, statement of cash flows, and to a lesser extent the balance
    sheet, plus the aggregation, disaggregation and management-performance-measure disclosures). **The
    candidate's narrowing survives; its enumerated scope did not.**
13. **The Repair 8 block's own Tadawul claim was index-rendered, not verified.** It quoted the issuer as
    saying the standard "will impact the operating profit subtotal" and that "goodwill moves to a separate
    line with no change in total assets", with no label. The claim is retained but downgraded to
    index-rendered.
14. **Two issuer-identity traps were recorded.** The Euronext document is **Euronext Securities Athens
    S.A.** (formerly ATHECSD), not Euronext Athens Holding S.A., and a similarly titled document at
    `direct.euronext.com/api/PublicAnnouncements/RISDocument/ANN156031.pdf` is a **different (Spanish)
    issuer**. Haleon's results statement has **two divergent renderings**: the RNS-published PDF carries the
    full "Recent accounting developments" text, while the SEC Form 6-K Exhibit 99.2 **omits its first
    sentence**. Standard Life's "UK Endorsement Board" reference covers the IFRS 9/7 amendments and Annual
    Improvements Volume 11, **not** IFRS 18.

**Net effect on the cycle's conclusions.** None. G-01 remains closed as a negative (IDEA-002 rejected,
R-038); G-04 remains closed on the proxy-validity limb with G-28 open and frozen on a structural reason;
G-21 remains null and sharpened; G-30 remains exhausted; G-33 remains closed as a negative with its 2027 Q3
re-check; R-037 remains a bounded negative; the active ranking is unchanged at **IDEA-011 69.0 (rank 1),
IDEA-004 69.0 (rank 2), IDEA-010 68.0 (rank 3), IDEA-009 60.0, IDEA-014 52.0**. The corrections make the
*record* of the cycle exact; they do not move the cycle's result.


### R-039 — CYCLE 59 FAMILY SCREEN VERDICT ENTRY

**Family:** Template (A) — published price of a constraint (repo specialness, securities-lending fee curves, CDS financing spreads, standing repo award rate). Screened state-first with the strict bar (published decision-time state, units/cadence, is the state the candidate conditions on or only a proxy, changes sign/existence not just size per G-12; Cycle-52 third test). Screened against the literature **first**.

**Verdict:** **bounded negative**. See R-039 in `rejected_and_parked.md`, and the known-baseline row the screen wrote.

**Sources consulted:** S-041 (SOFR/BGCR/TGCR), S-042 (repo operations, primary dealer statistics), with the register's existing sources on crowding and funding. **No new `S-` identifier was minted** — the screen's conclusions rest on the *structure* of the available state series, not on a new finding, and no new citation was needed to reach them.

**Reasons:** see R-039. No unclaimed mechanism passed the strict bar; public rates are indicators rather than clean sign-determining decision-time states; securities-lending fee data is fragmented and largely proprietary; G-12's sign-and-existence limb was not met.

**Identifiers and score:** R-039 consumed; **no `S-`, `V-`, `IDEA-` or `G-` identifier consumed or opened**; no score changed; no candidate created; the family was added to the known-baseline table as **row 68** at the Cycle-59 wrap-up.
