"Same Same But Different: The Risk Profile of Corporate Bond ETFs."
FoFI 2026 Conference Paper (Karlsruhe Institute of Technology / Schulich School of Business / Lancaster), December 2025.
- **Type:** Conference working paper; not peer-reviewed at time of entry.
- **Supports (for IDEA-010):** corporate bond ETFs exhibit **lower liquidity risk but higher intermediary risk** than their underlying bond portfolios; exposure differs systematically (ETFs more exposed to intermediation supply shocks, underlying bonds more exposed to demand shocks). Using an AP-capital factor, a **one-standard-deviation deterioration in active AP balance sheets raises ETF–NAV differentials by nearly 10% of a standard deviation**. The arbitrage structure is concentrated: "e corporate bond ETF has roughly 30 registered APs, only about four are active in a given year, and three of these are typically primary broker-dealers... On average, the top three APs handle 95% of the total creation and redemption volume."
- **Why it matters for IDEA-010:** adds a published **intermediary-risk premium** dimension (the candidate's dossier did not carry it as fully specified) and quantifies the AP-capital channel the candidate relies on, with numbers consistent with the mechanism. Also documents extreme concentration (top-3 ~95%, ~4 active of ~30) reinforcing fragility.
- **Caveats:** conference paper/preprint; results author-reported. PDF text-extracted via pypdf from FoFI site; full econometric details not line-quoted beyond the summary above.
- **Verification:** Retrieved directly from http://wp.lancs.ac.uk/fofi2026/files/2026/03/FoFI-2026-108-Marcel-Mueller.pdf (2026-10-20); text-extracted with pypdf; Crossref/DOI not located as of entry time (treat as conference preprint). Verification: **direct fetch + text extraction**.

### S-324 — U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (2026)
"Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) Program: Reallocation of Additional 2025 Small Refinery Exemptions." Proposed
rule. Federal Register doc. 2026-21155, 91 FR 65699–65711 (published 16 October 2026). Docket EPA-HQ-OAR-2024-0505,
RIN 2060-AX09.
- **Type:** Regulator proposed rule; not peer-reviewed research; government document.
- **Supports (for IDEA-014):** the EPA's proposed rule reallocates additional 2025 small-refinery exemptions (SREs)
  under the Renewable Fuel Standard. It confirms the Register-projected 2025 exempted RVO of 990 million RINs against
  actual exempted volume of 1.76 billion RINs (+78% above projection), and proposes reallocating the additional
  ~770 million RINs either equally across 2026–2027 (~1.4 billion each) or entirely to 2027 (~1.81 billion). The
  proposal triggers the automatic compliance-deadline extension mechanism under 40 CFR 80.1451(f)(1)(i)(C): when
  additional exempted RINs are reallocated to a future compliance year, the compliance deadline for that year is
  extended (the 2026 deadline, currently 31 March 2027, may move).
- **Why it matters for IDEA-014:** this is the first post-Cycle-52 source bearing on the RFS compliance-deadline
  obligation and the RIN deadline state. It demonstrates that the agency both projects exempted volumes and then
  reallocates them, with direct consequences for compliance deadlines. However, no published work conditions the
  candidate's effect on a second variable, tests the candidate's sign claim, or changes the baseline. G-20 and
  G-24 conclusions stand; G-15 remains inconclusive.
- **Caveats:** proposed rule, not final; the deadline extension is automatic under the cited regulation but the
  specific new deadline has not been set; market-price impacts (RIN price moves) are reported in secondary sources
  only.

### S-325 — Huang, S., Liu, X., Lou, D. and Polk, C. (2024)
"The Booms and Busts of Beta Arbitrage." *Management Science* **70**(8): 5367–5385.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.4929
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), **peer-reviewed journal article** (INFORMS).
- **Supports (for IDEA-004):** the **nearest published test of the candidate's own prediction 1** — that
  the *direction* of the crowding conditioning on an arbitrage strategy is two-sided rather than monotone.
  The publisher-deposited abstract states, verbatim: "In times of low arbitrage activity, the beta-arbitrage
  strategy exhibits delayed correction, taking up to three years for abnormal returns to be realized. In
  contrast, when arbitrage activity is high, prices overshoot and then revert in the long run." It also
  states a mechanism: "We document a novel positive-feedback channel operating through firm leverage that
  facilitates these boom-and-bust cycles." The crowding state is the arbitrage-activity measure of Lou &
  Polk (S-157 in this ledger) applied to the beta-arbitrage legs — the paper states that it "exploit[s] the
  novel measure of arbitrage activity introduced by Lou and Polk (2022)".
- **Why it matters for IDEA-004:** the candidate's stated differentiator — "the claim is about the
  **direction of the conditioning** (crowding raises expected convergence return in the short run because
  capital is slow, and lowers it while raising tail risk in the exit) — a two-sided relation that a simple
  'avoid crowded trades' rule does not capture" — is **published, in the same asset class (US listed
  equities), for a different but adjacent arbitrage strategy**. The candidate may no longer present the
  two-sided crowding gate as an unclaimed relation, and the Cycle-30 note in the dossier that "the
  non-monotone, sign-flipping gate remains unclaimed" is **corrected by this source**. What remains
  unclaimed is narrower: the *formulation* (pairs, merger-spread and index-convergence relative value),
  the *crowd identity* (the convergence crowd, not a beta-arbitrage crowd), and the *state definition* (a
  position-concentration measure rather than a return-comovement measure).
- **Caveats:** peer-reviewed but author-reported; the trade family is a long-low-beta / short-high-beta
  factor trade, **not** a convergence pair, so the published result is a structural analogue and **not** a
  test of the candidate's rule; the crowding measure is **return-comovement based**, so it is not a
  position-concentration measure of a paired crowd (G-28's structural null is untouched); and there is
  substantial **version drift** — the working-paper lineage carries earlier titles, a different author
  order and a different arXiv/LSE version record (LSE Financial Markets Group Discussion Paper No. 743,
  December 2014; CEPR Discussion Paper No. 11531, 2016; accepted version deposited at LSE Research Online,
  eprint 120807) — so the working-paper versions must not be cited as if they were the published article.
- **Verification:** Crossref REST API (DOI, title, all four authors with affiliations, container
  *Management Science*, volume 70, issue 8, pages 5367–5385, published-print August 2024, is-referenced-by-count
  9, and the **publisher-deposited abstract**) — **direct fetch + Crossref-deposited abstract**; the abstract
  wording quoted above is **line-verified from that deposit**. LSE Research Online eprint 120807 confirmed
  this cycle (accepted-version record). The accepted-version PDF at LSE Research Online was retrieved directly,
  but its text layer could not be extracted in this cycle, so **no body text is quoted** and the working-paper
  passages are recorded as **index-rendered only**.
- **Cycle-85 verification — UPGRADE: the accepted version's body text is now extracted and line-verified
  (47 pages, 104,386 characters); the Cycle-78 "text layer not extractable" note is corrected.** The
  accepted-version PDF was fetched directly again on 20 October 2026 from LSE Research Online
  (`https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/120807/1/bOOM.pdf`) — **HTTP 200, 602,160 bytes, 47 pages** —
  and the text layer **was** extracted this time (the earlier failure was a tooling problem, not a property
  of the file). The passages the register leans on are now confirmed **from the paper's own text**, with the
  extraction artefacts noted in brackets: (i) the crowding measure is the excess-return-comovement measure
  of Lou and Polk — *"we exploit the novel measure of arbitrage activity in troduced by Lou and Polk ( 2022)"*
  [the PDF's spacing artefact], and *"Lou and Polk's innovation is to measure the outcome of the arbitrage
  process, namely, the correlated price impacts that can result in excess return comovement in the spirit of
  Barberis and Shleifer (2003)"*; the paper labels the measure *"the excess return comovement, relative to a
  benchmark asset pricing model, of beta-arbitrage stocks"*; (ii) the measure's behaviour — *"the mean of
  [CCCC] is 0.10 varying from a low of 0.04 to a high of 0.20"*; (iii) the proxies and their limits — *"we
  include the aggregate institutional ownership (Inst Own) of the low-beta decile — i.e., stocks in the long
  leg of the beta strategy — based on 13F filings"*, and *"aggregate institutional ownership …, the assets
  under management (AUM) of long-short equity hedge funds, aggregate liquidity, and the past performance of a
  typical beta-arbitrage strategy together forecast roughly 41% of the time-series variation in [CCCC]"*,
  and *"no one single existing proxy is sufficient for capturing time-series variation in arbitrage
  activity"*; and (iv) the **published corroboration of G-28's objection** — *"we focus on their holdings in
  the low-beta decile as we do not observe their short positions in the high-beta decile"*.
  **Effect on the register.** The verification label for this entry's *body text* moves from "not
  retrievable" to **"line-verified (accepted version, LSE eprint 120807)"**, and the entry's own caveat
  about **version drift** is confirmed rather than relaxed — the extracted text is the **working-paper /
  accepted-version** lineage, so the working-paper passages must still not be cited as if they were the
  published *Management Science* article, and the published article's abstract remains the authority for the
  article's own wording. **The candidate's own relation is still not tested by this source** (the trade
  family is a long-low-beta / short-high-beta factor trade, not a convergence pair) and the crowding measure
  is still **return-comovement based**, so **G-28's structural null is untouched**. This is a **neighbour**
  for IDEA-004 and not a test of its own effect, so **no re-score, no hard-stop change and no new hard-stop
  flag** follow; the finding in (iv) is **published support for the 13F objection already recorded against
  G-28**, and it strengthens the frozen structural null without reopening it.

### S-326 — Dong, X., Kang, N. and Peress, J. (2025)
"Fast and Slow Arbitrage: The Predictive Power of (Persistent) Capital Flows for Factor Returns."
*The Review of Financial Studies* **38**(10): 2936–2987. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhaf036.
Earlier SSRN version: DOI https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3675163 (2020).
- **Type:** Prior empirical and theoretical result (author-reported), **peer-reviewed journal article**.
- **Supports (for IDEA-004):** two distinct hits on this dossier. (i) **The slow-capital mechanism is
  published, with its sign.** The deposited abstract states: "We document that persistent aggregate capital
  flows to hedge and mutual funds predict monthly factor returns with an out-of-sample R2 reaching 6.6%.
  Transient flows display no such power despite being more predictable. We show—both empirically and
  theoretically—that persistent flows' predictive power stems from active fund managers' capital
  constraints. As a result, managers invest persistent, but not transient, capital flows into factor trading
  strategies, leading to factor-return predictability and factor momentum, yet greater price efficiency."
  The candidate's mechanism — arbitrage capital is slow to arrive, and that slowness is what a convergence
  trade harvests — is therefore a **published, quantified baseline**, not a discovery.
  (ii) **The fund-flow state of the strategy complex is a published measure of deployed arbitrage capital.**
  The candidate's own observables list names "the fund-flow state of the strategy complex"; this paper gives
  that state a published construction (persistent versus transient aggregate flows to hedge and mutual
  funds), a published sign (persistent flows predict factor returns; factor momentum follows) and a published
  mechanism (capital-constrained managers). The candidate can therefore no longer present the flow state as
  an unexploited observable.
- **Why it matters for IDEA-004:** the candidate's *residual* is now sharply bounded. What is left of
  SLOWCAP-COND is the **crowd identity** (the convergence crowd in the candidate's own universe), the
  **two-sided gate applied to convergence trades**, and a **position-concentration state** that no published
  source supplies — which is exactly the frozen gap G-28. The paper also bears on the register's crowding
  baseline: it is the fourth independent published route by which *deployed arbitrage capital* has been
  inferred (short interest, comovement, institutional holdings, fund flows), and all four are aggregate and
  security- or strategy-level, none of them pair-level and netted.
- **Caveats:** peer-reviewed but author-reported; the published relation is for **factor** strategies, not
  convergence pairs or merger spreads; aggregate fund-flow data carry a reporting lag and are not a
  security-level position measure; and there is **version drift** — earlier working papers carry different
  titles ("Fast and slow arbitrage: Smart money, dumb money and mispricing in the frequency domain", February
  2019; CEPR Discussion Paper No. 15235, 31 August 2020, "Fast and Slow Arbitrage: Fund Flows and Mispricing
  in the Frequency Domain") and a different author order, so the working-paper versions must not be cited as
  if they were the published article.
- **Verification:** Crossref REST API — the **journal-article** record for DOI 10.1093/rfs/hhaf036 (title, all
  three authors with affiliations, container *The Review of Financial Studies*, volume 38, issue 10, pages
  2936–2987, published 27 May 2025, and the **publisher-deposited abstract**) and the **posted-content**
  record for the earlier SSRN version (DOI 10.2139/ssrn.3675163, 2020, same deposited abstract) —
  **direct fetch + Crossref-deposited abstract**; Oxford Academic article landing page returned HTTP 403
  (blocked), so the article body was not read independently; the journal record plus deposited abstract stand.

### S-327 — Rodríguez Domínguez, A. and Noguer i Alonso, M. (2026)
"Robustness or Crowding: Experimental Design for Trading Strategy Capacity." arXiv:2608.08405
(q-fin.PM; submitted 9 August 2026; 38 pages, 9 tables, 5 figures). DOI: https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2608.08405
- **Type:** Methodological and design paper (author-reported), **arXiv preprint; not peer-reviewed**. The paper
  runs no deployment experiment: "No deployment experiment is run."
- **Supports (for IDEA-004 and for the register's crowding baseline):** (i) a **published statement of the
  crowding-measure inventory and of its non-benchmarked status** — "Deployed arbitrage capital has been
  inferred from the cross-section of short interest (Hanson and Sunderam, 2014), from return comovement
  among the constituents of a strategy (Lou and Polk, 2022), from institutional holdings and their liquidity
  footprint (Brown et al., 2022; Chincarini et al., 2026), and from persistent flows into the funds that run
  these strategies (Dong et al., 2025). These measures rest on different primitives, they are validated by
  their correlation with subsequent returns, and they have rarely been benchmarked against one another."
  (ii) an **identifiability result with direct consequences for the candidate's rule design** —
  Proposition 3.18: under homogeneous overlap, "aggregate crowding is not identified from within-date
  variation by any estimator", with the corollary that "robustness to arbitrary calendar effects and
  identification of aggregate crowding are therefore mutually exclusive in any within-date design"; the paper
  prices the alternative (Remark 3.21: deliberately heterogeneous overlap across disjoint sub-universes,
  borrow pools or liquidity tiers recovers the aggregate estimand at the price of a weaker exposure mapping).
  (iii) a **published borrow-derived crowding state**: the paper's calibration uses "the detrended log
  ninetieth percentile of implied borrow rates" as the crowding state, and (iv) a **published calibration of
  crowding-driven edge decay** — q̂ = 0.280 for the four non-overlapping momentum strategies and 0.269 for all
  thirteen, with 12-month moving-block bootstrap intervals [0.000, 0.995] and [0.000, 0.965] on the 260
  months on which all thirteen strategies and the borrow series overlap.
- **Why it matters for IDEA-004:** (a) it corroborates the register's own bounded negative on crowding-proxy
  cross-validation (G-04's validity limb, closed in the candidate's favour in Cycle 58, and G-18's bounded
  negative) from an **independent, later source** — published crowding measures "have rarely been benchmarked
  against one another"; (b) it adds an **identification constraint** to the candidate's own rule: a crowd-depth
  gate read as a within-date cross-sectional contrast cannot separate aggregate crowding from calendar
  effects, so any future execution of V-002 must pre-register how the aggregate-crowding effect is
  identified (variation across dates, or heterogeneous overlap across sub-universes); and (c) it documents
  that the crowding state in the newest published calibration is **borrow-rate-derived** — i.e. the
  candidate's own cost constraint ("borrow legs in crowded names are most expensive to borrow exactly when
  the trade is most attractive") turned into a published, measurable state — which is still security-level
  and **not** the pair-level netted measure G-28 requires.
- **Caveats:** preprint, not peer-reviewed; the calibration panel is purpose-built for the paper; the
  crowding-decay estimates are the authors' own and their bootstrap intervals are extremely wide — the paper
  itself calls the exercise "essentially uninformative about persistence in this sample"; the paper studies
  the capacity of a *strategy*, not the payoff of a convergence trade, and it offers a **design**, not a
  result about any trading rule.
- **Verification:** **arXiv abstract page and the full HTML rendering fetched directly and read** — title, both
  authors with affiliations, submission date 9 August 2026, subject class q-fin.PM, DOI
  10.48550/arXiv.2608.08405, page/table/figure counts, JEL codes, keywords and the full abstract. The
  passages quoted above (the crowding-measure inventory sentence, Proposition 3.18, the borrow-rate crowding
  state, and the q̂ estimates) were read **in the fetched document body**, not from an index rendering.
  Verification: **direct fetch + text extraction from the arXiv HTML**.

## Cycle 75 sources (2026-10-20)

### S-328 — Wang, Z. (2026)
"Residual Supply and the Price of Risk Absorption." arXiv:2605.30672 (preprint, 29 May 2026).
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30672
- **Type:** Prior theoretical and empirical result (author-reported), arXiv preprint; **not peer-reviewed**.
- **Supports (for IDEA-004 — this is the cycle's trigger source):** the *state-scaled-premium* form of the
  candidate's conditioning, and a **published, constructible capacity state**. The abstract states, verbatim:
  "We develop a market-clearing model of residual supply pricing, where forced-sale pressure predicts actual fund
  selling, contemporaneous price declines, and positive returns over the following one to six months. The premium
  roughly doubles when market-wide absorption capacity is tight, and concentrates in stocks with thin investor
  bases and limited trading capacity — precisely the cross section in which clearing the imbalance should be most
  costly, and a pattern that mechanical return reversal does not generate." The paper's own keyword list includes
  **"slow-moving capital"**, and the state it uses is published and constructible: **13F ownership data to measure
  the thickness of the natural investor base, CRSP liquidity variables and aggregate mutual-fund stress to measure
  absorption capacity**.
- **Why it matters for IDEA-004:** three of the candidate's four published-neighbour legs are now covered in the
  literature the register holds. (i) The **conditional structure** — a premium that varies with the scarcity of
  the capital that absorbs an imbalance, roughly doubling when absorption capacity is tight — is published with a
  **published state**, so the candidate may no longer present "a premium that scales with the capacity of the
  arbitrage capital" as unclaimed. (ii) The **observability** claim is published: a crowding/capacity state that
  is *not* pair-level can be constructed from public data (13F, CRSP, fund-flow stress), which removes the
  candidate's implicit position that its state is unobservable *as such* — what remains unavailable is only the
  *pair-netted* identity. (iii) The **identification** question the candidate must answer is now a published
  methodological problem with a published answer for a neighbouring object, so any future execution of the
  candidate's rule must engage the published identification design rather than assert its own.
- **Caveats:** preprint, not peer-reviewed; the published object is a **cross-sectional flow-pressure premium in
  single stocks**, not a **convergence-pair** trade, so it is a structural analogue and not a test of the
  candidate's rule; the published state is **security-level**, so it is **not** the candidate's pair-level netted
  convergence crowd and **may not be substituted** for it; the reported magnitudes (65 basis points per month
  cross-sectionally, 217 basis points over six months) are large relative to the candidate's cost budget and are
  not comparable to a market-neutral pair's payoff; and the mechanism is a **market-clearing** account of
  *residual supply*, not a claim about *slow arbitrage capital correcting a mispricing*, so it is a **rival
  explanation** for any convergence-return pattern the candidate might observe.
- **Verification:** the arXiv abstract page (`https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30672`) and the full HTML rendering
  (`https://arxiv.org/html/2605.30672v1`) were **fetched directly (HTTP 200)** on 20 October 2026; the title,
  author, date and abstract quoted above are **line-verified from the abstract page**, and the state construction
  (13F investor-base thickness, CRSP liquidity, aggregate mutual-fund stress) and the "slow-moving capital"
  keyword are **line-verified from the HTML rendering**. No arXiv version other than v1 was read, and no body
  claim beyond these passages is quoted.

### S-329 — Sun, J. and Tian, Y. (2026)
"When Banks Retreat: The Demand for Public Safe Assets." SSRN working paper 6913784 (date written 10 May 2026;
posted 3 July 2026; last revised 15 October 2026; 107 pages). Earlier title: "Private Money, Public Debt:
Quarter-End Price Pressure in Treasury Bills."
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), SSRN working paper; **not peer-reviewed**.
- **Supports (for the R-047 screen):** the **sign, the window and the magnitude** of a reporting-date
  balance-sheet flow into Treasury bills are published. The abstract states, verbatim: "This paper shows that
  quarter-end bank window dressing shifts institutional demand from private to public safe assets. Around
  regulatory reporting dates, Non-U.S. banks reduce borrowing from U.S. money market funds; constrained to hold
  short-term, high-quality assets, the funds redeploy the displaced cash into Treasury bills. As a result,
  short-maturity U.S. Treasury yields fall by 3–9 basis points at quarter-ends. Using a network shift-share design
  that exploits predetermined fund–bank relationships and cross-sectional variation in Treasury bill holdings
  across funds, we causally estimate that money market fund demand inflows equal to 1 percent of Treasury bill
  market value lower yield spreads by 4.9 basis points."
- **Why it matters for the register:** it is a **new instance of the register's flow-concession template in a new
  market** (Treasury bills), with a **published sign and a published magnitude**, and it therefore closes the
  family as a baseline rather than opening a candidate — see **R-047**. It also sharpens *why* no candidate can
  be built on the family: the flow that drives the effect is generated by **non-US banks' private reporting-date
  balance-sheet positions**, and the redeployment is observed only through money-market-fund holdings that are
  published with a lag, so the *size* of the effect is not observable at decision time even though its sign and
  window are.
- **Caveats:** working paper, not peer-reviewed; the identification uses a **network shift-share design** whose
  inputs (predetermined fund–bank relationships) are **not public data**, so the design is not reproducible by an
  outside party; the effect is dated to a **quarter-end window of a few days** in the most liquid short-duration
  instrument in the world, where a 3–9 basis point move is small relative to funding, roll and execution costs
  of a market-neutral position; and the paper's own policy framing (stabilising bill yields, informing the ON RRP
  **Cycle 105 provenance:** Crossref REST API `api.crossref.org/works/10.2139/ssrn.6913784`
  (posted-content record) returned HTTP 200 with a deposited abstract (abstract present: yes)
  confirming the 3–9 bps quarter-end bill-yield fall and the network shift-share design. Upgrade
  recorded in place.
  facility) shows the effect is treated as a *policy-relevant market-clearing quantity*, not as an unclaimed
  tradable edge.

### S-330 — Fleming, M. J., Liu, W. and Nguyen, G. (2026)
"Intraday Price Pressure and Order Flow Around U.S. Treasury Auctions." Federal Reserve Bank of New York Staff
Report 1188 (March 2026; revised July 2026). DOI: https://doi.org/10.59576/sr.1188
- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), central-bank staff working paper; **not peer-reviewed**.
- **Supports (for the R-047 screen and for the register's Treasury baseline):** the **auction-window price
  pressure** and its **dealer-intermediation** conditioner are published. The staff-report page states,
  verbatim: "We examine intraday price pressure in the U.S. Treasury market around auctions. We find yields rise
  in the hours before an auction and reverse afterward. This pressure strengthens when dealers face tighter
  risk-bearing constraints, consistent with a model in which dealers' balance sheets absorb inventory risk."
  The page's suggested citation reads: "Fleming, Michael J., Wenqian Liu, and Garphil Nguyen. Intraday Price
  Pressure and Order Flow Around U.S. Treasury Auctions. Federal Reserve Bank of New York Staff Report No. 1188.
  New York, NY: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, March 2026, revised July 2026."
- **Why it matters for the register:** it is a **second, independent published instance** of the same
  institutional mechanism family screened in R-047 — a **dated, non-discretionary, price-insensitive flow
  obligation** in the same market — and it adds a **published conditioner** (dealers' risk-bearing constraints)
  that is not published in real time. Together with S-329 it closes the family twice over: once on
  "the sign and window are published" and once on "the size-determining conditioner is not published at decision
  time".
- **Caveats:** staff report, not peer-reviewed; the auction window is **hours**, and the published pressure is a
  same-day reversal that requires intraday execution in the most liquid government-bond market; the
  risk-bearing-constraint conditioner is **not published in real time** (dealer balance-sheet capacity is
  quarterly and lagged), which is the same decision-time defect that disqualifies a candidate in this family;
  and the pre-auction price pattern is partly the mechanical consequence of **duration-concession conventions**,
  so a large part of the measured effect is an institutional artefact rather than a risk premium.
- **Verification:** the New York Fed staff-report page (`https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/staff_reports/sr1188.html`)
  was **fetched directly (HTTP 200)** on 20 October 2026; the title, the abstract wording quoted above and the

"Same Dollar, Different Impact: Investor Flows are Not Equally Price-Moving." Hong Kong University working

## Cycle 87 sources (2026-10-20)

Five sources were registered by the Cycle-87 screen of the **weather-derivative contract-pricing family**
(HDD/CDD temperature futures, options and seasonal strips on the CME). Three are **line-verified** from
documents fetched directly, one is **bibliographically verified with an unverified body** (an honest
negative), and one is an institutional factsheet used for venue context only.

### S-332 — Weagley, D. (2019)

"Financial Sector Stress and Risk Sharing: Evidence from the Weather Derivatives Market." *The Review of
Financial Studies* **32**(6): 2456–2497. DOI 10.1093/rfs/hhy098. Published online 30 August 2018; print
June 2019. Working-paper lineage: "Financial Sector Stress and Asset Prices: Evidence from the Weather
Derivatives Market", 6 August 2015 (SSRN 2640352, DOI 10.2139/ssrn.2640352).

- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), **peer-reviewed journal article**.
- **Supports:** the **published sign** of the weather-derivative premium and the **published conditioner**;
  the venue's market structure; and the crisis regime. From the working-paper version: "In normal times,
  contracts are priced near their actuarially fair value. During the recent financial crisis, contract
  prices one-month before maturity fall by 2.2%. This discount is equivalent to an annualized weather risk
  premium of 26%. Contract prices decline with increases in the TED spread and the VIX and the declines are
  greatest for high margin and high total risk contracts." On the venue: "The introduction of contracts is
  correlated with proxies for hedging demand, such as a city's population (energy usage) and the region's
  crop production. Although the CME temperature futures market has seen tremendous growth, it is relatively
  illiquid. Bid-ask spreads are large and many deals are conducted off exchange and submitted as block
  trades. Markets typically open in the 1-3 weeks before the contract month (the median market is opened 39
  days before maturity) and participants rarely change their positions. After a market is initially opened,
  open interest does not change on 85% of trading days. Open interest decreases on less than 5% of trading
  days." On the crisis regime: "If hedging demand is driving the decrease in prices, greater quantities of
  risk would be hedged during the crisis. However, this is not the case. The notional value of the weather
  derivatives market decreased by over 50% from $32 billion to $15 billion during the crisis. Similarly,
  open interest in the monthly futures market fell by 40% between the third and fourth quarter of 2008."
- **Why it matters:** this entry is the screen's **reason 1** (the family's sign is already published, with
  its sign-determining state — financial-sector stress — a *published* series) and its **reason 4** (the
  venue's cost floor and structure are published facts, not the register's inference). A candidate in this
  family would be re-presenting a published effect and would have to condition on a state that is already
  in the literature.
- **Caveats:** the **published article's body has still not been read** — the OUP full text is paywalled; the
  direct article route returned HTTP 403 on 20 October 2026, the text-extraction route returned OUP's
  bot-verification page, and **OpenAlex and Unpaywall both report the article as closed with no
  repository copy** — so **every passage quoted above is still the working-paper version's wording**, and
  the working paper's **26 %** annualised crisis figure differs from the dissertation version's **30 %**
  (S-334). **What *is* now verified in the published version** (Cycle 88): the **published abstract**, which
  is quoted from the RePEc record in the entry's verification note and which carries the published version's
  own headline wording; and the article's **Internet Appendix** (S-349), fetched and text-extracted. The
  paper's object is the 1999–2008/09 sample, so the market structure it describes is **historical** and the
  venue's current listing status is now separately verified (S-344 … S-348).
- **Verification:** the **Crossref REST work record for DOI 10.1093/rfs/hhy098** was fetched directly
  (HTTP 200) and confirms the title, the author, the container title, volume **32**, issue **6**, pages
  **2456–2497**, published-print **1 June 2019**, published-online **30 August 2018**, publisher Oxford
  University Press, ISSNs 0893-9454 / 1465-7368. The **working-paper version** was fetched directly
  (HTTP 200, 961,998 bytes, 62 pages) and its text layer extracted (135,050 characters); every passage
  quoted above is **line-verified from that version**. **Cycle-88 upgrade:** the **published abstract** was
  verified verbatim from the **RePEc record** for the published article
  (`https://ideas.repec.org/a/oup/rfinst/v32y2019i6p2456-2497..html`, fetched directly, HTTP 200) — "I
  examine the effect of financial sector stress on risk sharing in a novel setting: the CME's weather
  derivatives market. The structure of the market allows me to disentangle price movements due to
  financial sector stress from price movements due to fundamentals. **Contracts, which are typically priced
  near their actuarially fair value, experience significant price declines during periods of financial
  sector stress. Contracts with greater margin requirements and total risk are the most affected.** The
  results provide causal evidence of the effect of financial sector stress on the pricing of exchange-traded
  financial contracts and risk sharing in the economy. Received July 21, 2017; editorial decision July 22,
  2018 by Editor Philip Strahan." The **Internet Appendix** was fetched from the author's own publication
  page (`danielweagley.com/research` → Google Drive file `108HT_MboCvEw0WW8Wh8sPPJjcvtoZUd4`, HTTP 200,
  316,303 bytes) and is registered as **S-349**. The published article's **body** remains paywalled —
  recorded as a limitation on the entry, not concealed.

### S-333 — Bae, J. W., Jacobs, K., Jeon, Y., Szaura, S. and Zurita, V. (2023; conference version 2024)

"Weather Volatility Risk Premium." SSRN working paper **4572123**, posted 2023, DOI
10.2139/ssrn.4572123. **Conference version:** "Weather Variance Risk Premia", Joon Woo Bae, Yoontae Jeon,
Stephen Szaura and Virgilio Zurita, 29 August 2024 (CAPORIN / CREST copy).

- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), **working paper — not peer-reviewed** in either version.
- **Supports:** the **published option-leg premium**; the contract mechanics; the **published flow
  structure**; and the field's own published liquidity filter. "Implied volatilities of weather derivatives
  are substantially greater than the realized volatilities for all cities in our sample, reflecting the
  positive price associated with the hedging against weather volatility risk. The resulting monthly weather
  variance risk premia is 0.29 on average with standard deviation of 0.22 and ranges from 0.04 (10th
  percentile) to 0.61 (90th percentile)." On the mechanics: "The contract price quotes are in units of $20,
  hence the payoffs of the HDD (CDD) indices are 20×HDD(i,t) (20×CDD(i,t))"; the payoff is the average
  daily temperature at the city's airport weather station, and the index measures the extra amount of
  heating (cooling) needed to keep the temperature above (below) 65 °F. On the flow: "the main purchasers of
  weather derivatives are energy and utility companies whereas the liquidity suppliers are financial
  institutions. Energy and utility companies take a short position in the temperature futures in order to
  hedge their risk exposure to changes in local temperature." On the sample's liquidity filter: "We remove
  option implied volatilities that are either (i) missing, (ii) equal to zero, or (iii) greater than 100%.
  Additionally, we remove futures and options quotes in which open interest is either zero or missing." The
  sample is eight U.S. cities (CME codes for, among others, DFW, LAS, MSP, LGA, SAC); the seasonal-strip
  futures and options data set spans **January 2006 to December 2019**; "the average days to maturity
  (d2mat) of the contracts is very similar across all contracts ranging from 92 to 112 days. The average
  open interest ranges from 706 to 1,153 units"; and "the traded volume of seasonal strips are order of
  magnitude larger than individual monthly derivative contracts for this reason." All option contracts are
  European-style, written on the futures, with implied volatility computed under Black (1976).
- **Why it matters:** the screen's **reason 1** (the option leg's premium is published, with its own
  measure, its own dispersion and its own city cross-section) and its **reason 4** — the field's own
  researchers had to **discard every quote with zero or missing open interest**, which is a *published*
  statement of the venue's liquidity, not the register's inference. It also publishes the **clientele
  structure** the screen's mechanism argument depends on: energy and utility companies short; financial
  institutions supply liquidity.
- **Caveats:** working paper, **not peer-reviewed**; the version read is the **conference version** (four
  authors, 29 August 2024, titled "Weather Variance Risk Premia") while the SSRN posting (five authors
  including Kris Jacobs, posted 2023) is titled "Weather Volatility Risk Premium" — the measure is WVRP in
  both, and the register's quoted wording is the conference version's; the paper's own question is whether
  WVRP predicts local credit spreads and equity variance premia, **not** whether the premium is tradable,
  and its price data come from a third-party replication of Schlenker and Taylor's data; the sample ends
  in 2019, so the venue's post-2019 behaviour is not covered.
- **Verification:** the SSRN record was verified through the **Crossref REST work record for DOI
  10.2139/ssrn.4572123** (HTTP 200), which returns the title "Weather Volatility Risk Premium", the
  five-author list (Joon Woo Bae; Kris Jacobs; Yoontae Jeon; Stephen Szaura; Virgilio Zurita, with ORCIDs
  for Jeon and Szaura), the posting year 2023, and the publisher-deposited abstract; the **SSRN landing
  page itself was index-rendered only**. The **conference version** (CAPORIN / CREST copy) was fetched
  directly (HTTP 200, 471,005 bytes, 51 pages) and its text layer extracted (104,320 characters) — every
  passage quoted above is **line-verified from that version**.

### S-334 — Weagley, D. (2014)

"Essays on the Weather Derivatives Market." PhD dissertation, University of Michigan (Rackham Graduate
School), 2014. Deep Blue handle 2027.42/108993.

- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), **doctoral dissertation — not peer-reviewed as a
  journal article**. Its first essay is the working-paper lineage of S-332; its second essay is an
  unrelated and separately interesting finding.
- **Supports:** the **normal-time null** — "The average risk premium across all contracts over the entire
  period is less than 2% per year and is statistically insignificant. This is consistent with idiosyncratic
  risk not being priced during normal times. During the financial crisis, estimated average risk premiums
  rise to a statistically significant 30% per year." — the market-structure facts in the same terms as
  S-332 ("it is relatively illiquid. Bid-ask spreads are large and many deals are conducted off exchange
  and submitted as block trades. Markets typically open in the 3 weeks before the contract month, the
  median market is opened 39 days before maturity, and participants rarely change their positions. After a
  market is initially opened, open interest does not change on 85% of trading days"), and the crisis
  collapse ("The notional value of the entire weather derivatives market decreased by over 50% from $32
  billion to $15 billion during the crisis. Similarly, open interest in the monthly futures market fell by
  40% between the third and fourth quarter of 2008."). **Essay 2, a separate published finding:** "We argue
  that temperature-based financial markets generate additional scrutiny of the temperature data measured by
  the NWS, which in turn motivates the agency to minimize measurement errors. Consistent with this idea,
  stations with higher economic interests in weather derivatives see greater improvement in measurement
  accuracy."
- **Why it matters:** the register's clearest statement that the family's **normal-time premium is a null**
  (the screen's **reason 3**), which is a stronger ground for the negative than "no published work exists".
  Essay 2 contributes a **published, previously unrecorded** structural fact about this venue: the
  settlement index's own measurement error is a documented, market-induced risk, and the market's own
  presence changes the data quality. Any future candidate in this family must carry it.
- **Caveats:** dissertation, **not peer-reviewed**; essay 1 duplicates S-332's content in an **earlier
  version** (30 % annualised crisis premium against the working paper's 26 %), so a *published* figure must
  be cited from the published article and not from the dissertation; essay 2 is about **data quality**, not
  about returns, and is not evidence about any premium; both essays describe a 1999–2009 sample.
- **Verification:** the **Deep Blue content PDF** was fetched directly (HTTP 200, 2,349,974 bytes, 138
  pages) and its text layer extracted (226,163 characters) — every passage quoted above is
  **line-verified**. A second Deep Blue route (the `/bitstreams/…/download` path) returned **HTTP 403**
  (5,783-byte error body) to this environment on 20 October 2026; the content-API route worked. The failure
  is a **route** failure, not a document defect, and is recorded as an honest negative below.

### S-335 — Chincarini, L. B. (2011)

"No Chills or Burns from Temperature Surprises: An Empirical Analysis of the Weather Derivatives Market."
*Journal of Futures Markets* **31**(1): 1–33. DOI 10.1002/fut.20463. January 2011. (An SSRN version of the
same title exists: DOI 10.2139/ssrn.1340761.)

- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), **peer-reviewed journal article** — **line-verified in
  Cycle 88** (the body is now extracted from the published typeset article; see Verification).
- **Supports:** the register's summary of the **published verdict on this family**: the weather-derivatives
  market is characterised in the published record as **efficient despite its illiquidity**, and the
  temperature-forward premia are reported as **statistically insignificant and sign-flipping** rather than
  as a stable premium. **The published abstract's own wording:** "This article examines the efficiency of the
  weather futures market traded on the CME in both HDD and CDD futures contracts in 18 cities across the
  United States. Efficiency is examined in three ways. First, by comparing the market's implied forecasts
  for the weather against other forecasts. Second, by looking at whether market's overreact or under-react
  to temperature surprises. Third, by looking at weather derivative patterns across cities. **We find that
  generally the market seems very efficient despite its lack of liquidity. We also find risk premia that
  seem to vary across cities and over time.**" **The published premium results (line-verified):** "The
  premium for HDD is 0.47% and insignificant for the most liquid cities from 1999 to 2004. The CDD premium
  is 5.76% and significantly different than zero. … Dallas has an insignificant premium and New York is
  actually significantly negative. … In the latter period (2005–2008), the HDD premia is positive and
  significant and the CDD premia are negative and significant for the top five cities. **Thus, the CDD
  average premia for the top five cities actually changes sign from the 1999–2004 period to the 2005–2008
  period.** … This inconsistency in the realized forward premia might be due to a different mix of hedgers
  across markets and across time. … it is hard to find a consistent value." **The published conclusion:**
  "one fails to reject the hypothesis that this market trades very efficiently."
- **Why it matters:** the screen's **reason 3** — the family's premise is **contested in the published
  literature**, so a future candidate here would have to answer a *published null*, not merely an absence
  of published work. This is a stronger reason against a candidate than "nothing has been published". In
  Cycle 88 this entry moved from a **neighbour with an unverified body** to a **line-verified** basis, which
  **strengthens R-049's reason 3** with the published article's own wording and its own published premia
  table.
- **Caveats:** the document is the **published typeset article** hosted on the author's own site, not the
  publisher's copy of record; the text layer uses **typographic ligatures** (for example "ﬁ" for "fi"), so
  a naive string search for the plain-ASCII form of a phrase will not match — the register's own quoted
  passages above are reproduced with the ligature normalised. The paper's own sample is **1999–2008**, and
  its market-structure description is therefore **historical**; the venue's current listing status, contract
  specifications and settlement basis are verified separately (S-344 … S-348).
- **Verification:** **line-verified (Cycle 88).** Bibliographic metadata verified through the **Crossref REST
  work record for DOI 10.1002/fut.20463** (HTTP 200): title, author "Ludwig Chincarini", *Journal of Futures
  Markets*, volume **31**, issue **1**, pages **1–33**, published **January 2011**; a second Crossref record
  (DOI 10.2139/ssrn.1340761) carries an SSRN version of the same title. The **published typeset article**
  was fetched directly from the author's own site (`https://ludwigbc.com/pubs/pub13.pdf`, HTTP 200, 33
  pages, 216,178 bytes) and its text layer extracted with **PyMuPDF 1.28.5 / pymupdf 2.0**
  (`page.get_text("text")` over every page): **86,239 characters, 33 of 33 pages carrying text**. The
  document's own front matter identifies it as the published article: "The Journal of Futures Markets, Vol.
  31, No. 1, 1–33 (2011) © 2010 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. Published online April 1, 2010 … DOI: 10.1002/
  fut.20463", with "Received August 2009; Accepted February 2010". **Correction to the Cycle-87 record:** the
  Cycle-87 entry stated that "the author-hosted PDF was fetched directly but no text layer could be

"Energy Market and Weather Derivatives." Factsheet in the **#WeatherwiseEnergy** series. FORRS

## Cycle 88 (2026-10-20) — verification-debt closures and one bounded family screen

### S-337 — Cherkes, Sagi & Stanton, "A Liquidity-Based Theory of Closed-End Funds"

- **Type:** Prior theory and empirical result (author-reported), **working-paper version** (the draft is dated
  "May 30, 2007"; the authors are at Columbia University and the Haas School of Business).
- **URL:** `https://faculty.haas.berkeley.edu/stanton/pdf/CEF.pdf`
- **Supports:** the **structural** reason a closed-end fund's traded price can sit away from its net asset
  value at all: "**Unlike other organizational forms, such as open-end funds (OEFs) and exchange-traded funds
  (ETFs), CEFs are not subject to large-scale creation or redemption of shares**, allowing them to better
  manage their trading in illiquid securities"; and the **published rational account of the discount** — "the
  observed behavior of the CEF discount, which results from a **trade-off between the liquidity benefits of
  investing in the CEF and the fees charged by the fund's managers** … the model explains why IPOs occur in
  waves in certain sectors at a time, why funds are issued at a premium to net asset value (NAV), and why
  they later usually trade at a discount", with the empirical finding "which, overall, provides more support
  for a liquidity-based model than for an alternative sentiment-based explanation."
- **Why it matters:** this is the **mechanism-first** statement of the family screened in Cycle 88
  (R-050). It supplies the family two published facts that a candidate could not re-derive: the **absence of
  a creation/redemption mechanism**, and a **published rational explanation** of the discount that does not
  require the discount to be an exploitable mispricing.
- **Caveats:** the retrieved document is the **2007 working-paper version**; no published version was
  verified in this cycle, so any figure taken from it is a working-paper figure. The paper's own claim is
  about the **existence and formation** of the discount, not about its tradability.
- **Verification:** **line-verified.** Fetched directly (HTTP 200; 378,396 bytes; 49 pages); text layer
  extracted with PyMuPDF (`page.get_text("text")` over every page): **107,124 characters**.

### S-338 — Chen & Tour, "The Discount Delusion: The Swedish Closed-End Fund Premium Puzzle"

- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), **student working paper** (dated 2013-05-15; written
  under the guidance of a tutor at the Stockholm School of Economics, Arc/HHS research archive).
- **URL:** `http://arc.hhs.se/download.aspx?MediumId=1926`
- **Supports:** a **published negative result for the family's headline trade** — "we find that **discounts
  are negatively correlated with future abnormal returns. Those who buy high discount CEFs thinking that they
  are bargains will have the numbers against them; the apparent undervaluation of the assets is only a
  delusion**"; and the sample's shape — "**daily observations of 11 Swedish CEF discounts from January 2000-
  December 2012** that has been continually constructed by professionals", contrasted with "the often
  quarterly data that researchers have used in the past."
- **Why it matters:** R-050's **reason 2** — the family's *sign* is published, and the published sign of the
  apparent bargain trade is **negative**. A candidate in this family would be re-presenting a published
  result with a published sign.
- **Caveats:** **not peer-reviewed** — a student working paper, and the register treats it accordingly; the
  venue is **Swedish** CEFs, not the US listing venue, so it is evidence about the *family* and not about
  the US BDC sub-family; 11 funds over 13 years is a **small effective sample**, which is itself part of
  R-050's reason 5.
- **Verification:** **line-verified.** Fetched directly (HTTP 200; 3,143,315 bytes; 83 pages); text layer
  extracted with PyMuPDF: **173,970 characters**.

### S-339 — Davydiuk, Marchuk & Rosen, "Market Discipline in the Direct Lending Space"

- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), **peer-reviewed journal article** — *The Review of
  Financial Studies*, volume **37**, issue **4**, pages **1190–1264** (2024).
- **URL:** `https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10649283` (the **published version**, deposited in the U.S.
  National Science Foundation's public-access repository).
- **Supports:** the **published, dated regime episodes** of the family and the **structural constraint** on
  the listed BDC's ability to act on its own discount — "BDCs often issue equity shares through so-called
  'shelf offerings', even though they operate as closed-end investment companies. **BDCs can access capital
  markets this way without any restrictions only when their shares are traded at a premium to net asset
  value (NAV). For below-NAV issuances, BDCs need to seek an approval from their existing shareholders**";
  and the **episode magnitudes** — "prior to the index exclusion event **BDCs' shares were traded at 5%–10%
  above their NAVs on average**. Absent the SEC decision to exempt BDCs from the AFFE rule, in May 2014 the
  Cliffwater BDC index approaches its NAV level, **subsequently pushing BDCs' shares to be traded at a
  discount for nearly 3 years thereafter**."
- **Why it matters:** R-050's **reasons 2 and 5** — the discount's *size and duration* are published
  episode outcomes with **dated triggers** (the May 2014 index-exclusion decision), and the vehicle's own
  balance sheet cannot act against a discount without a shareholder vote. The family is therefore
  **episodic and rule-bound**, not a standing mispricing.
- **Caveats:** the identification strategy is a **2014 event** on the *funding* side of the balance sheet;
  the paper's object is market discipline and capital structure, not the discount as a tradeable edge, and it
  does not test a buy-the-discount rule. The 5%–10% premium figure is quoted by the authors from the
  Cliffwater report.
- **Verification:** **line-verified.** Fetched directly (HTTP 200; 1,302,909 bytes; 75 pages); text layer
  extracted with PyMuPDF: **231,436 characters**.

### S-340 — Suhonen, "Direct Lending Returns"

- **Type:** Prior empirical result (author-reported), **peer-reviewed journal article** — *Financial Analysts
  Journal*, volume **80**, issue **1**, pages **57–83** (2024); the retrieved document is the **publisher's
  version of record** ("Document Version: Publisher's PDF, also known as Version of record … Licence: CC
  BY"), obtained from the Aalto University research portal (open-access deposit).
- **URL:** `https://aaltodoc.aalto.fi/server/api/core/bitstreams/2039d5fd-46db-4e24-b8f3-5c736070c829/content`
  (record: `https://aaltodoc.aalto.fi/items/81f3a02b-45a3-4465-95e3-1e8444ba06c3`).
- **Supports:** the **published magnitude, direction and decision-time structure** of the listed-BDC discount —
  "BDC industry total returns at market capitalization-weighted index level in December, 2009, to June, 2022,
  were **8.63% per annum based on market values and 9.41% based on NAVs, the difference reflecting mainly the
  deepening discount to NAV in traded BDC prices over the first six months of 2022**"; "the broad BDC market
  to **generally trade close to the NAV, except during times of market stress when the discount can widen
  substantially**—best illustrated by performance during the 2020 pandemic"; the **decision-time
  observability** of the true state — "the NAVs of the BDCs underlying the index are **unknown on such dates
  and will only be published in the financial reporting of the BDC several weeks after the NAV date**"; the
  **cross-sectional sign** — "BDCs with **greater price-to-NAV premium (or smaller discount) outperforming
  those with a smaller premium (larger discount) by all return metrics**"; the **structural constraints** —
  "BDCs that elect to be taxed as regulated investment companies **must distribute at least 90% of investment
  income** to shareholders annually … and BDCs are **not allowed to issue shares to the public below NAV
  without annual shareholder approval**"; and the **sample** — "I construct a sample of **47 listed BDCs over
  the period December, 2009, to June, 2022**, with around $110 billion of aggregate invested assets as of
  year-end 2021."
- **Why it matters:** R-050's **reasons 2, 3 and 5** in one source: the discount's *sign* and *size* are
  published, the *state* that moves it is published (market stress), the **decision-time state is stale by
  weeks**, and the vehicle's own balance sheet is rule-bound.
- **Caveats:** the article's object is **BDC performance**, not the discount as a tradeable edge; the discount
  statements are descriptive and cross-sectional; the NAV-lag passage is the author's own methodological
  convention rather than a claim that the discount is unobservable in principle. No published version of the
  *article's* text on the discount was checked against a second rendering, so quotations are from the
  version of record only.
- **Verification:** **line-verified.** Obtained through the Aalto DSpace REST API (item and ORIGINAL bundle

### S-342 — 15 U.S.C. § 80a-60 (Investment Company Act § 61(a), as amended)

- **Type:** **Primary statutory material** (United States Code), fetched from the Cornell Law School Legal
  Information Institute.
- **URL:** `https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/80a-60`
- **Supports:** the **published, rule-bound partial arbitrage** built into the listed BDC's own structure: a
  BDC that has obtained shareholder approval to issue shares below net asset value must give the approving
  shareholders "the opportunity (which may include a tender offer) to sell the securities held by that
  shareholder as of that applicable approval date, **with 25 percent of those securities to be repurchased in
  each of the 4 calendar quarters following** the calendar quarter in which that applicable approval date
  takes place"; the same section conditions below-NAV issuance on majority shareholder approval, on a
  required majority of the directors, and on a good-faith determination that "the price of the securities to
  be sold is not less than a price which closely approximates the market value of those securities, less any
  distributing commission or discount."
- **Why it matters:** R-050's **reason 3** — the family already contains a **published, statutory,
  quarterly repurchase mechanism at net asset value**, tied to a specific shareholder cohort and a specific
  approval date. A candidate in this family would be re-presenting a published mechanism rather than
  discovering one.
- **Caveats:** the text is the **current consolidated statute** as served by the LII; the section has been
  amended (Pub. L. 115-141, § 802(b)(2), 2018) and the repurchase condition attaches to shareholders who
  approved below-NAV issuance — it is **not** a general, unconditional BDC tender-offer mandate, and this
  entry does not claim that it is. The screen states the mechanism exactly as the statute states it.
- **Verification:** **line-verified.** Fetched directly (HTTP 200; 68,755 bytes of HTML); tag-stripped text
  retained for quotation: **13,528 characters**.

### S-343 — 17 CFR 270.23c-1 ("Repurchase of securities by closed-end companies")

- **Type:** **Primary regulatory material** (Code of Federal Regulations, Investment Company Act of 1940
  rule), fetched from the Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (eCFR) as currently in force.
- **URL:** `https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-270/section-270.23c-1` (retrieved through
  the eCFR content API).
- **Supports:** the **conditions under which a closed-end company may buy its own shares** — "A registered
  closed-end company may purchase for cash a security of which it is the issuer, subject to the following
  conditions: … (2) If the security is a stock not entitled to cumulative dividends, **at least 90 percent
  of the net income of the issuer for the last preceding fiscal year … was distributed to its shareholders
  during such fiscal year or within 60 days after the close of such fiscal year** … (6) **The purchase is
  made at a price not above the market value, if any, or the asset value of such security, whichever is
  lower**, at the time of such purchase."
- **Why it matters:** the **statutory/regulatory floor** under the family: the closed-end vehicle's own
  buyback capacity is bounded by a distribution requirement and by a price rule, so even a discount-closing
  mechanism must operate inside a published rule rather than freely.
- **Caveats:** this rule constrains a closed-end company's repurchases; it is **not** itself a mechanism that
  closes a discount, and the screen does not claim that it is. The eCFR "current" text is as of the fetch
  date.
- **Verification:** **line-verified.** Fetched directly from the eCFR renderer API (HTTP 200; 30,430 bytes of
  HTML); tag-stripped text retained for quotation: **3,982 characters**.

  not through a directional temperature premium.
- **Caveats:** this is the **appendix**, not the article's body; the article's own body remains paywalled
  (see S-332's verification note) and the headline crisis figures quoted in the register still come from the
  working-paper version. The appendix is an author deposit of the article's supplementary material and was
  **not** checked against the publisher's own copy of the appendix.
- **Verification:** **line-verified.** Fetched directly from the author's Google Drive file (HTTP 200;
  316,303 bytes; 21 pages); text layer extracted with PyMuPDF: **44,589 characters**. The author's
  publication page was fetched directly (HTTP 200) to establish the link provenance.

### S-350 — Moutzouris, I. C. and Nomikos, N. (2019), "The formation of forward freight agreement rates in dry bulk shipping: Spot rates, risk premia, and heterogeneous expectations", *Journal of Futures Markets* 39(8): 1008–1031

- **Type:** **Peer-reviewed journal article — the accepted version**, self-archived by the authors in the
  City Research Online institutional repository (City, University of London); the publisher's version of
  record is behind a paywall.
- **URL:** `https://openaccess.city.ac.uk/id/eprint/20713/7/Nomikos%20and%20Moutzouris%20The%20Formation%20of%20FFA%20Rates%20in%20Dry%20Bulk%20Shipping.%20Risk%20Premia%20and%20Heterogeneous%20Expectations.pdf`
  (landing record `https://openaccess.city.ac.uk/id/eprint/20713/`; DOI `10.1002/fut.21980`,
  **Crossref-verified**: title, journal, volume, issue, pages and the 2018-12-14 publication date).
- **Supports:** the **published account of how the FFA forward rate is formed** — "We illustrate that the
  bulk of basis volatility can be attributed to expectations about future physical market conditions rather
  than expectations about future risk premia. However, there exists significant predictability of risk premia
  by both price-based signals and economic variables … we argue that the average investor should hold
  “near-rational” but slightly contrarian beliefs"; the **published decomposition** ("we argue that FFA basis
  moves mainly due to expectations about future changes in the spot prices because the latter can be
  predicted – up to a certain degree – by market agents at time *t* through the shipping supply and demand
  mechanism"); the **published risk-premium stylised facts** ("the 1- and 2-month risk premia are positively
  autocorrelated and their autocorrelation increases with contract maturity which indicates the existence of
  a momentum effect", and "risk premia and spot growth rates are negatively correlated"); the **published
  data construction** ("monthly observations of spot prices, settlement rates, and FFA rates for the BCI 4TC
  and BPI 4TC contracts with 1- and 2-month maturities from **January 2007 to September 2016**, obtained
  from The Baltic Exchange"); the **published liquidity state** ("We have also incorporated trading activity
  variables to examine whether liquidity in the FFA market can forecast either future market conditions
  and/or future risk premia. Our dataset is obtained from the **London Clearing House (LCH)** … trading
  volume is positively correlated with current market conditions"); and the **published candidate
  explanations for the premium** (the "roll yield", the risk premium, and a "liquidity premium" demanded by
  short physical hedgers).
- **Why it matters:** R-052's **reasons 1 and 2** — the freight family's headline (a *published*, structured
  FFA risk premium with a *published* decomposition) and the published conditioner of what survives it
  (price-based signals and economic variables) are **in the literature**, so a candidate in this family
  would re-present published work, and the unclaimed remainder is a *magnitude*, not a sign.
- **Caveats:** this is the **accepted version**, not the publisher's typeset version of record (the
  repository says so on its face: "This version of the publication may differ from the final published
  version"); the sample is **monthly, dry bulk, January 2007 – September 2016**; the paper is an
  **asset-pricing study of the forward rate**, not a trading-cost study, so the premium it reports is a
  modelled pre-cost premium; the "significant predictability of risk premia by both price-based signals and
  economic variables" is the authors' own result and is **not** a claim that the residual is tradeable.
- **Verification:** **line-verified.** Fetched directly from the repository (HTTP 200; 671,628 bytes;
  40 pages); text layer extracted with PyMuPDF: **105,501 characters**. The landing record was fetched
  directly (HTTP 200) to establish provenance, and the bibliographic metadata was verified against
  Crossref. The publisher's own PDF route returns **HTTP 403** (see the honest-negatives table).

### S-353 — Braun, A. and Kousky, C. (2021), "Catastrophe Bonds" (Wharton Impact, the Perry World House)

- **Type:** **Educational/technical primer** from a university impact laboratory — **not peer-reviewed**, and
  used only where a primary or official document was not obtained.
- **URL:** `https://impact.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/Cat-Bond-Primer-July-2021.pdf`
- **Supports:** the **published mechanics of the CAT-bond instrument** — the SPV/collateral structure and
  the premium's economic character: "The SPV invests the investors' principal in highly-rated and liquid
  collateral securities … catastrophe bonds are essentially floating rate notes that exhibit minimal interest
  rate risk. In addition to the floating returns, **catastrophe bonds compensate investors for bearing the
  disaster risk with premium payments from the sponsor**"; the **published model dependence of the premium** —
  "Issuance of a catastrophe bond typically requires engaging a specialized modeling firm to quantify the
  catastrophe risk. The risk modeler will estimate the probability that the conditions for the payout would
  be met over the term of the bond (probability of first loss). The modeling firm also provides an estimate
  of the expected loss for investors … **Such a model-based approach to risk assessment is needed, since
  historical data on the most extreme natural disasters are typically too scarce for a reliable estimation of
  the outer tail of the loss distribution**"; the **four trigger types** (indemnity, industry loss,
  parametric, modelled loss) with their consequences — "**Indemnity triggers typically involve a relatively
  lengthy payout process, since loss reporting and verification must be accomplished before the release of
  funds. Nonetheless, the indemnity trigger is by far the most widely used trigger type in today's catastrophe
  bond market**"; "INDUSTRY LOSS TRIGGERS require aggregate losses experienced by the industry to exceed a
  predetermined value. The determination that the trigger has been met is usually done by an independent
  third-party, such as Property Claims Services (PCS)"; and the **published opacity/moral-hazard point** —
  "For investors, indemnity triggers can be relatively opaque, since they do not have direct access to
  information on the sponsor's insurance portfolio. This raises a moral hazard concern."
- **Why it matters:** R-051's **reasons 2, 3 and 4** — the premium's expected-loss benchmark is a *model
  output*, the sign-determining condition is resolved by third parties over a **lengthy, published** process,
  and the market's most-used trigger type is the slowest and the most opaque.
- **Caveats:** **not peer-reviewed**; the market-size and issuance figures in the primer are attributed by
  the authors to **Artemis.bm** and are **not** independently verified here, so they are not used for any
  reason; the primer is a **2021** document and describes the market as of that date; the trigger taxonomy
  it gives is used as a *structural* description, not as evidence of any current market statistic.
- **Verification:** **line-verified.** Fetched directly (HTTP 200; 1,217,466 bytes; 10 pages); text layer
  extracted with PyMuPDF: **21,989 characters**.

### S-354 — Ando, S., Fu, C., Roch, F. and Wiriadinata, U. (2022), "Sovereign Climate Debt Instruments: An Overview of the Green and Catastrophe Bond Markets", IMF Staff Climate Note 2022/004

- **Type:** **International-organization staff note** (IMF Staff Climate Notes — "aims to quickly disseminate
  succinct IMF analysis on critical economic issues"; **not peer-reviewed**), used for the market's published
  structure and its published premium accounting.
- **URL:** `https://www.imf.org/en/-/media/files/publications/staff-climate-notes/2022/english/clnea2022004.pdf`
- **Supports:** the **published premium as a measured baseline with a published magnitude** — "**Empirically,
  the cedents pay more than they receive in expectation.** According to Artemis, from which only the
  aggregated data of private and public catastrophe bonds is available, **the investors' average return to
  catastrophe bond in coupon is around 2 to 4 times the expected loss**" and "**Whether the positive spread
  is expensive depends on the benchmark to compare**"; the **published spread behaviour at events** —
  "Difiore, Drui, and Ware (2021) note that **risk spreads have widened materially following major
  catastrophes in the past**, such as 2006 following a US hurricane and 2012 following earthquakes in Japan
  and New Zealand"; the **published market shallowness and cost barrier** — "While green and catastrophe
  bonds have gained significant popularity, **their markets remain fairly shallow at the sovereign level**",
  and "the note discusses **significant barriers to the scale up of the catastrophe bond market: high
  transaction costs, the requirement of complicated underlying catastrophe models, and a narrow investor base
  (which could in turn be a consequence of the previous two factors)**"; and the **published model dependence
  and term structure** — "**The typical maturity is three to five years**, so the long-term impact of climate
  change risks may not be fully reflected", with the modeler "calculat[ing] the actual loss after catastrophe
  events".
- **Why it matters:** R-051's **reasons 1, 2 and 5** — the risk premium is a *documented, quantified*
  baseline (coupon ≈ 2–4× expected loss), the spread-widening episodes are **published, dated, retrospective
  events** rather than a decision-time state, and the market's shallowness and transaction costs are the
  documented barrier.
- **Caveats:** an **IMF staff note**, not a peer-reviewed article, and **sovereign-catastrophe-bond**
  focused; its premium statistics are **aggregated private-and-public data reported by Artemis** and are
  used here as the register's *published baseline*, not as a verified measurement; the "2 to 4 times the
  expected loss" figure is the note's own summary of a third-party dataset and is **not** independently
  recomputed here.
- **Verification:** **line-verified.** Fetched directly with a declared browser user-agent and referer
  (HTTP 200; 2,375,165 bytes; 28 pages); text layer extracted with PyMuPDF: **64,551 characters**. The same
  host returned **HTTP 403** for the April-2020 GFSR online box on every route tried (see the
  honest-negatives table).

### S-355 — Supreme Court of Bermuda, Commercial Court, 2020: No. 369, *Aeolus Re Ltd (in respect of its Keystone PF Segregated Account) v CS ILS SICAV-SIF (in respect of Credit Suisse (Lux) Iris Balanced Fund) et al* [2022] SC (Bda) 30 Com, judgment of 6 May 2022

- **Type:** **Primary legal material** — a published judgment of the Supreme Court of Bermuda (Commercial
  Court) on a catastrophe-swap transaction, hosted by the Government of Bermuda.
- **URL:** `https://www.gov.bm/files/media-library/20260514/c6f48cd9-final_judgment_2020_no._369_civ._aeolus_re_ltd_v_cs_ils_sicav_sif_et_al_with_citation.pdf`
- **Supports:** the **published resolution architecture of an industry-loss trigger**, in the court's own
  words — "a **Development Period** applied, namely a further time period in which to monitor whether the
  estimated insured loss developed sufficiently in order to trigger a payment under the Swaps. By clause
  9(f) of the Swap Confirmations, **the Development Period End Date was 18 months after the Risk Period End
  Date** (i.e. 30 June 2020) if the loss estimate for Typhoon Jebi was less than 80 % of the Trigger Amount
  (i.e. less than US$10 billion) by that date"; the **published definition of the sign-determining
  quantity** — "A Trigger Event was defined as a Covered Event where the Reference Amount was equal to or in
  excess of the Trigger Amount … a Reference Amount was defined as the **Estimated Market Loss** for the
  applicable Covered Territory" (aggregated by PCS and PERILS); and the **published "reporting disruption"
  clause** — the loss size "was either **not yet known** or was reported by the agreed report publisher at an
  amount which was not large enough to trigger the payment obligation".
- **Why it matters:** R-051's **reason 3** — the condition that decides whether the instrument pays is
  (i) a third-party **estimate**, not an observable, and (ii) resolved over a **published development period
  of up to 18 months after the risk period**, so the sign-determining state is not a decision-time variable
  at all. This is a primary legal document, not a market commentary.
- **Caveats:** the judgment concerns **one specific 2018-risking swap** and its own documentation; the
  18-month development period is a clause of that transaction, and the judgment is not a market-wide survey
  of trigger design. It is used to document the **architecture** of an industry-loss trigger (a documented
  development period and a third-party loss estimate), not to claim a market-wide average lag. The court
  record also concerns the "Reporting Disruption" provision, whose facts are not the register's concern.

- **Type:** Peer-reviewed empirical.
