### S-358 — Billimoria, F., Mays, J. and Poudineh, R. (2025), "Hedging and tail risk in electricity markets", *Energy Economics* 141, 108132
- **Type:** Peer-reviewed empirical/review.
- **DOI:** https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eneco.2024.108132
- **Supports:** Volatility is a feature; derivatives allow hedging but long-tenor contracts can be scarce (missing markets concerns); literature split between price formation archetypes and empirical analyses with few reconciliations.
- **Verification:** **line-verified (Cycle 96)** — the authors' open working-paper version was fetched directly and text-extracted; see the Cycle-96 upgrade note below. **The entry was previously carried as "line-verified via publisher metadata", and that label is superseded, not erased.** **R-053 is not re-scored**: the upgrade changes the provenance of this entry only, and R-053's verdict, its five reasons and its baseline row 90 stand unchanged.

**S-358 — Cycle-96 upgrade (an in-place upgrade block under the same identifier, not a separate entry; the duplicate `###` heading that used to sit here was demoted in Cycle 126 so that it cannot be counted as a second source):** the body was obtained and text-extracted

The **open working-paper version** of the same study — Billimoria, Mays and Poudineh, "Hedging and Tail Risk in Electricity Markets", **OIES Paper: EL, No. 53** (Oxford Institute for Energy Studies, Oxford, April 2024; ISBN 978-1-78467-240-9) — was located through OpenAlex's open-access location record for the article DOI (`https://www.econstor.eu/bitstream/10419/296660/1/1887037926.pdf`, handle `10419/296660`), **fetched directly** (HTTP 200; 2,437,474 bytes; **40 pages**) and **text-extracted** (**113,195 characters**, pypdf). Every clause of the entry's "Supports" bullet is now confirmed in the document's own words:

- **the volatility feature** — "The volatility of electricity prices is a necessary component in the theory of competitive electricity markets (Boiteux, 1960; Caramanis et al., 1982; Chao, 1983; Harvey & Hogan, 2019). 'Getting the prices right' for an inelastic good, such as electricity, will invariably involve volatility or price spikes during scarcity (Hogan, 2014)." (section 1, "Risk hedging in electricity markets");
- **the hedging function and the scarce long tenor** — "Derivative products (including forwards, swaps, and options) have evolved to allow generators and retailers to exchange volatile spot exposures for more stable cashflows … However, obtaining contract of long tenor has been a concern, with a set of literature arguing there are 'missing markets' for long-term contracts, which are seen as necessary to support capital-intensive generation investment when participants are risk-averse (Abada et al., 2019; Neuhoff & De Vries, 2004; Newbery, 2016; Roques & Finon, 2017; Simshauser, 2019)." (section 1); and in the abstract, "the price required for generators to provide such hedges can be multiples of the expected value of prices", with "when the real-world constraints of credit and financing are considered, the volatility of thermal fuels and their co-dependence under extremes may be a key reason as to why electricity markets have been incomplete in terms of long-term hedging contracts";
- **the split literature with few reconciliations** — "The literature on price formation and hedging in electricity markets is extensive but tends to fall into one of two categories. One set considers price formation in the context of archetypes of electricity market design – these works can be either qualitative or have simulated outcomes … while the second set undertakes empirical and statistical analyses of historical prices. There have been relatively few attempts to reconcile them." (section 1).

**Caveats, stated honestly:** what was fetched and text-extracted is the **authors' working-paper version**, not the Elsevier version of record. The published article's bibliographic identity — title, three authors, *Energy Economics* volume **141**, article **108132**, issued **January 2025** — is **independently confirmed against Crossref** (fetched directly), so the entry's citation is correct; the published typeset text was **not** fetched and no open-access route to it was found. This entry therefore supports **R-053's reasons 1 and 4** (the published, regime-dependent premium; the structural incompleteness of long-tenor hedging) on the same grounds as before, with the provenance strengthened; it adds **no reason** and changes **no verdict**.

## Cycle 93 — new source entries

### S-359 — 17 CFR 270.23c-3 (Investment Company Act of 1940 Rule 23c-3), "Repurchase offers by closed-end companies"
- **Type:** **Primary legal material** — a codified SEC rule under the 1940 Act, read from the current eCFR text.
- **URL:** `https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-270/section-270.23c-3`
- **Supports:** the **published parameter set of the whole mechanism**, in the rule's own words — the
  **repurchase price**, "(b)(1) The company shall repurchase the stock for cash at the net asset value
  determined on the repurchase pricing date … The company may deduct from the repurchase proceeds only a
  repurchase fee, not to exceed two percent of the proceeds"; the **offer amount**, "(a)(3) The repurchase
  offer amount shall not be less than five percent nor more than twenty-five percent of the common stock
  outstanding on a repurchase request deadline. Before each repurchase offer, the repurchase offer amount for
  that repurchase offer shall be determined by the directors of the company"; the **pricing date**,
  "(a)(5) A repurchase pricing date shall occur no later than the fourteenth day after a repurchase request
  deadline … In no event shall an investment company determine the net asset value applicable to the
  repurchase of the stock before the close of business on the repurchase request deadline"; the **payment
  deadline**, "(a)(4) A repurchase payment deadline shall occur seven days after the repurchase pricing date
  applicable to such tender"; the **pre-published fundamental policy**, "(b)(2)(i) The company shall
  repurchase the security pursuant to a fundamental policy, changeable only by a majority vote of the
  outstanding voting securities of the company, stating: (A) That the company will make repurchase offers at
  periodic intervals … (B) The periodic intervals between repurchase request deadlines; (C) The dates of
  repurchase request deadlines or the means of determining the repurchase request deadlines; and (D) The
  maximum number of days between each repurchase request deadline and the next repurchase pricing date"; the
  **notification window and content**, "(b)(4)(i) No less than twenty-one and no more than forty-two days
  before each repurchase request deadline, the company shall send to each holder of record … a notification
  providing the following information: (A) A statement that the company is offering to repurchase its
  securities from security holders at net asset value"; the **rationing**, "(b)(5) If security holders tender
  more than the repurchase offer amount, the company may repurchase an additional amount of stock not to
  exceed two percent of the common stock outstanding on the repurchase request deadline … the company shall
  repurchase the shares tendered on a pro rata basis"; the **suspension grounds**, "(b)(3)(i) The company
  shall not suspend or postpone a repurchase offer except pursuant to a vote of a majority of the directors,
  including a majority of the directors who are not interested persons of the company, and only: (A) If the
  repurchase would cause the company to lose its status as a regulated investment company under Subchapter M
  of the Internal Revenue Code … (D) For any period during which an emergency exists as a result of which
  disposal by the company of securities owned by it is not reasonably practicable, or during which it is not
  reasonably practicable for the company fairly to determine the value of its net assets"; and the
  **asset-disposal requirement**, "(b)(10)(i) … a percentage of the company's assets equal to at least 100
  percent of the repurchase offer amount shall consist of assets that can be sold or disposed of in the
  ordinary course of business, at approximately the price at which the company has valued the investment,
  within a period equal to the period between a repurchase request deadline and the repurchase payment
  deadline".
- **Why it matters:** R-054's **reasons 1, 2 and 4** — the price, the size, the window, the rationing, the
  suspension grounds and the valuation-realisability requirement are all **published law fixed in advance**.
  There is no price-concession object to discover, and the flow is **mandatory and pre-announced by the
  obligor itself**, so there is no third-party concession to harvest.
- **Caveats:** the rule is the **legislative frame**, not evidence about any individual fund's behaviour or
  about realised redemption outcomes; the offer amount and the dates are set by the board within the rule's
  bounds, so the rule alone fixes no individual fund's schedule. Used here as the published legal frame only.
- **Verification:** **line-verified.** Fetched directly from eCFR (HTTP 200; 132,498 bytes); the operative
  paragraphs were read from the returned document and every quotation above is verbatim from that text.

### S-360 — U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, "Interval Fund Modernization; Expansion of Multiple Share Class to Registered Closed-End Management Investment Companies and Business Development Companies", proposed rule, Release No. 33-11444; IC-36351; File No. S7-2026-34, 91 FR 63388 (October 5, 2026)
- **Type:** **Regulator rule-making document** — the SEC's own current analysis of the interval-fund
  framework; a *proposed* rule, so the frame it describes is in motion (comments close 4 December 2026).
- **URL:** `https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/05/2026-20360/interval-fund-modernization-expansion-of-multiple-share-class-to-registered-closed-end-management-investment-companies-and-business-development-companies`
- **Supports:** the **published description of the mechanism** — "interval funds offer the predictability of a
  mandatory, limited, rules-based liquidity framework by requiring interval funds to adopt a fundamental
  policy to make periodic repurchases of their shares at a price based on NAV" (91 FR 63389); the **published
  trade-off** — "We recognize that the interval fund structure offers an inherent tradeoff: the fund offers
  investors the ability to obtain exposure to illiquid or less liquid assets with access to a certain amount
  of liquidity, but investors generally can tender their shares only periodically and in amounts offered by
  the fund" (91 FR 63392); the **published universe** — "The number of interval funds has grown from 58 in
  2020 to 139 in 2025 and the aggregate net assets have increased from $38 billion to $101 billion during that
  same period" and "Credit strategies constitute the largest segment of the interval fund market, representing
  approximately 55 percent of aggregate net assets" (91 FR 63392–63393; the figures are from Form N-CEN as
  of December 2025); the **published 2026 stress episode and where it landed** — "In early 2026, multiple
  non-traded BDCs and registered closed-end funds, including several interval funds, experienced increased
  investor demand to repurchase shares … However, this repurchase pressure has largely affected non-traded
  BDCs … By contrast, interval funds experienced net inflows during the same period, with aggregate net assets
  up 2.2 percent from the prior quarter" (91 FR 63430); the **published direction of the concession** — "an
  interval fund that faces large and persistent repurchase requests that it is unprepared to meet may need to
  borrow (thus increasing fund leverage), sell off less liquid assets at a discount to fair value (thus
  diluting the value of outstanding shares), or both" (91 FR 63438); and the **published contrast with the
  listed class** — "Other investors that prefer more immediate secondary market liquidity and can tolerate
  price volatility may instead buy listed shares representing the same underlying portfolio at a market price.
  Where listed shares trade at a discount to the underlying portfolio's NAV, there may also be opportunities
  for the fund to take actions that benefit all shareholders" (91 FR 63448).
- **Why it matters:** R-054's **reasons 1, 2, 4 and 5** — the mechanism, its trade-off, its size and its 2026
  stress episode are **published by the regulator**, and the SEC's own text locates the **discount-to-NAV
  object in the *listed* class**, which the unlisted interval-fund class does not have.
- **Caveats:** a **proposed** rule, so it describes the current frame and the proposed change, not settled
  law; it says nothing about any individual fund's realised behaviour, and its universe statistics are the
  regulator's Form N-CEN aggregates rather than a measure of realised redemption outcomes.
- **Verification:** **line-verified.** Fetched directly as the Federal Register's full plain-text rendition
  (HTTP 200); the page numbers above are the document's own `[[Page …]]` markers and every quotation is
  verbatim from that text.

### S-361 — Opportunistic Credit Interval Fund, "Notice of Quarterly Repurchase Offer", Form N-23c-3 (Investment Company Act File No. 811-23783), dated 10 December 2025
- **Type:** **Primary fund filing** — the repurchase-offer notification the fund itself files with the SEC

- **URL:** `https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1907437/000139834425022317/fp0096508-2_n23c3a.htm`

### S-363 — Matvos, G., Piskorski, T. and Seru, A. (2026), "Private Credit, Balance Sheets and Financial Stability", NBER Working Paper No. 34991 (March 2026; revised August 2026)
- **Type:** **Working paper** (NBER; not peer-reviewed at the working-paper stage). Used for the published
  account of the private-credit vehicles' redemption mechanics and for the measured scale of the evidence base.
- **URL:** `https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w34991/w34991.pdf`
- **Supports:** the **published distinction between the listed and the unlisted leg** — "Publicly traded BDCs
  face little direct redemption pressure because investors can exit by selling shares in secondary markets
  without requiring the vehicle itself to liquidate assets or return capital. Non-traded BDCs, however, often
  offer investors periodic liquidity through repurchase programs and have therefore been the primary focus of
  recent concerns regarding redemption pressures in private credit"; the **published withdrawal-risk account**
  — "these developments demonstrate that withdrawal pressures can emerge when investors are offered liquidity
  against portfolios of relatively illiquid assets. Such withdrawal pressures are more commonly associated
  with traditional banking and may become increasingly important if liquidity-providing private credit
  vehicles continue to expand"; the **published valuation-information problem** — the paper's own framing of
  "**information frictions and the risk of valuation contagion**" among its four areas of vulnerability; and
  the **published scale and its limits** — a dataset of "approximately 1,300 funds between 2000 and 2024", fund
  lives that "generally span 8–12 years", and the observed episode ("some private credit vehicles have
  experienced redemption pressures despite maintaining relatively conservative balance-sheet structures").
- **Why it matters:** R-054's **reasons 2, 3 and 5** — the **secondary market is the thing that makes an exit
  possible**, which the unlisted interval-fund class does not have; the withdrawal dynamic is **published and
  attributed to the unlisted BDC leg**; and the measured evidence base covers **institutional private credit
  funds (2000–2024)**, not the retail semi-liquid wrapper.
- **Caveats:** a **working paper**, not a peer-reviewed article, and its dataset covers private credit funds
  (institutional partnerships) rather than registered interval funds; it is used for the published account of
  the redemption mechanics and for the limits of the evidence base, not as a measurement of any interval
  fund's outcomes.
- **Verification:** **line-verified.** Fetched directly from nber.org (HTTP 200; PDF; 35 pages); text layer
  extracted with PyMuPDF: **73,866 characters**; every quotation is verbatim.

### S-364 — Alizadeh, A. H., Kappou, K., Tsouknidis, D. and Visvikis, I. (2015), "Liquidity effects and FFA returns in the international shipping derivatives market", *Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review* 76: 58–75, DOI 10.1016/j.tre.2015.02.001
- **Type:** **Peer-reviewed article**, read in the **authors' accepted version** deposited in the University
  of Reading's institutional repository (CentAUR).
- **URL:** `https://centaur.reading.ac.uk/39474/1/Dry%20Bulk%20FFA%20liquidity.pdf` (record: `https://centaur.reading.ac.uk/39474/`)
- **Supports:** the **published liquidity-premium result in the freight-derivative market** — "Results
  indicate that liquidity risk is priced and both liquidity measures have a significant role in determining
  freight derivatives returns. Consistent with expectations, both liquidity measures are found to have positive
  and significant effects on the returns of freight derivatives" (abstract); "the Amihud trading volume-related
  liquidity measure and the bid-ask spread measure are both found to be positive and statistically significant
  in explaining returns on FFA contracts, providing new evidence, for the first time, that market participants
  incorporate transaction costs in their required returns"; and the **published sample and its sources** — "The
  study examines the pricing of liquidity risk in the dry bulk FFA market over the period 2008-2014, using FFA
  (BFA) prices and the Amihud liquidity measure (FFA returns over trading volume) both obtained by the Baltic
  Exchange, and bid-ask spreads obtained from Clarksons Shipbrokers."

  line-verified cost/liquidity ground that **R-052** had to carry on S-351 alone — the published result says
  the liquidity premium is a **priced, measured** component of freight-derivative returns, with a documented
  cost measure and a documented 2008–2014 sample.
- **Caveats:** the **accepted version** (not the publisher's typeset article) is what was fetched; the
  bid-ask spreads are **proprietary Clarksons Shipbrokers data** and are not independently reproducible here;
  the sample ends in 2014, so the result is a **dated baseline** and the register does not assert that the
  premium's magnitude holds today.
- **Verification:** **line-verified.** Fetched directly from the University of Reading's CentAUR repository
  (HTTP 200; PDF; 1,009,954 bytes); text layer extracted with PyMuPDF: **92,459 characters across 40 pages**;
  every quotation is verbatim.

## Cycle 94 source entries (2026-10-21) — the municipal-bond family screen

**Pre-registration.** Before any document was fetched, the Cycle-94 screen frame was fixed as: *does the
tax-exempt municipal securities market (the dealer-intermediated, fragmented, retail-priced secondary market
and the published primary-market underwriting concession) contain an unclaimed, decision-time-state-determined
concession that survives costs, and that is not already published and measured?* The frame names the four
elements carried forward from the Cycle-93 handoff — **the dealer's one-way bid**, **the "Muni Monday" no-bid
window**, **the zero-omission rating disclosure** and **the tax-equivalent arithmetic** — and each was
treated as a *hypothesis to be verified*, not as a premise. The screen stops at five independent reasons;
each reason must be tied to a line-verified passage; a reason that cannot be tied is not a reason.

### S-365 — MSRB Rule G-17, "Conduct of Municipal Securities and Municipal Advisory Activities", with the 2021 Interpretive Notice

- **Type:** primary self-regulatory rule text and Interpretive Notice (MSRB).
- **URL:** https://www.msrb.org/Rules-and-Interpretations/MSRB-Rules/General/Rule-G-17 (HTTP 200; 436,729 bytes; HTML; extracted text 24,795 chars).
- **Supports:** R-055 (reason 5 — the concession is a published, disclosed compensation, and the "no-bid" state is a discretionary risk-management practice rather than a published obligation).
- **Why it matters:** the rule page carries the rule's own summary and history and, in full, the Interpretive Notice of May 2021. Line-verified passages: the rule's own summary, *"Requires dealers and municipal advisors to deal fairly with all persons and not to engage in any deceptive, dishonest or unfair practice"*; the Notice's *"Disclosures Concerning the Underwriter's Role"* item *"(ii) the underwriter's primary role is to purchase securities with a view to distribution in an arm's-length commercial transaction with the issuer"*; the duty item *"(v) the underwriter has a duty to purchase securities from the issuer at a fair and reasonable price, but must balance that duty with its duty to sell municipal securities to investors at prices that are fair and reasonable"*; and, from the Notice's *"Disclosures Concerning the Underwriters' Compensation"*, *"The sole underwriter or syndicate manager must disclose to issuers whether underwriting compensation will be contingent on the closing of a transaction."*
- **Caveats:** the Notice's disclosure regime runs **to the issuer**, not to the investor: it requires the underwriter to make standard and transaction-specific disclosures about its role and its compensation to the issuer at defined points in the engagement, and it is a **conduct** duty ("deal fairly with all persons") rather than a price-publication duty. The rule page therefore **cannot** be read as supplying a published decision-time price, and the register uses it only for the *fair-dealing* and *compensation-disclosure* limbs. (Two phrasings that the Cycle-94 drafting used here — that the dealer's compensation and the offering's expenses "be disclosed in the final official statement to be provided to the investor", and that the rule page states "dealers and advisors are not required to disclose their pricing practices to the public" — were checked against the extracted text of the page in the Cycle-94 verification pass and are **not present in it**; both have been removed, and the passages quoted above are the document's own words.)
- **Verification:** fetched and text-extracted in Cycle 94; the quoted sentences were read in the extracted text layer.

### S-366 — 17 CFR 240.15c2-12, "Municipal securities disclosure" (SEC "disclose everything" rule)

- **Type:** primary regulator rule text (eCFR, current).
- **URL:** https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-240/section-240.15c2-12 (HTTP 200; 186,732 bytes; HTML; extracted text 30,726 chars).
- **Supports:** R-055 (reason 3 — the "zero-omission" reading of the rating disclosure fails, because the permitted omissions are a closed list and the rating's changes are themselves disclosable events).
- **Why it matters:** two line-verified passages carry the reason. First, 15c2-12(b)(1): the Participating Underwriter *"shall obtain and review an official statement that an issuer of such securities deems final as of its date, except for the omission of no more than the following information: The offering price(s), interest rate(s), selling compensation, aggregate principal amount, principal amount per maturity, delivery dates, any other terms or provisions required by an issuer of such securities to be specified in a competitive bid, ratings, other terms of the securities depending on such matters, and the identity of the underwriter(s)."* Second, 15c2-12(b)(5)(i)(C)(11) lists *"Rating changes"* among the events for which the issuer must give notice *"in a timely manner not in excess of ten business days after the occurrence of the event"*.
- **Caveats:** the rule governs the *primary* offering and the *underwriter's* conduct; it does not price the secondary market, and it does not create a disclosure duty for secondary trades. It is used here to test the register's own "zero-omission" framing, and the test is that the framing is **wrong in the direction that helps the candidate**: the rule's own words are *"the omission of no more than the following information"*, a closed list, so there is no unregulated disclosure gap to exploit; and a rating change is a *published, dated* event.
- **Verification:** fetched and text-extracted in Cycle 94; the quoted sentences were read in the extracted text layer.

### S-367 — MSRB, "Data and Research — Academics" and "Data Subscription Services and Products" (the municipal trade-data products)

- **Type:** primary venue publication pages (MSRB) — the market's own statement of what trade data exists, at what price and with what lag.
- **URL:** https://www.msrb.org/Market-Data-and-Research/Academics (HTTP 200; 78,219 bytes; HTML; extracted text) and https://www.msrb.org/Market-Data-and-Research/Data-Subscription-Services-and-Products (HTTP 200; 17,838 bytes; HTML; extracted text).
- **Supports:** R-055 (reason 2 — no published decision-time state).
- **Why it matters:** the Academics page states that the *"Academic Historical Transaction Data Product includes transactions in the current Real-time Transaction Reporting System (RTRS) historical municipal securities transaction data set (report of historical transaction data, including transaction data for inter-dealer and customer trades for a consecutive 12-month period), with the addition of anonymized dealer identifiers. List offering price and takedown transactions (in general, primary market transactions) are excluded. Information is provided with a three-year lag."* — with a price of *"$500 per year, plus a one-time set up fee of $500"*, and the fuller RTRS Historical Data Product at *"$2,500 for each consecutive 12-month period, plus a $2,000 one-time fee"*. The subscriptions page states that EMMA's municipal trade data *"are available at no charge on our EMMA website or on a subscription basis in real-time for a fee"*, and lists the *"MSRB Transaction Subscription Service : All municipal trade data reported to the MSRB by municipal securities dealers."*
- **Caveats:** these pages describe the *access* arrangements; they do not say that no free post-trade summary exists. The register therefore does **not** claim "no free municipal trade data exists"; it claims the narrower, line-verified fact that **real-time** municipal trade data is a paid subscription and that the **historical academic** product carries a **three-year lag** and **anonymised dealer identifiers**, so a dealer-level inventory or bid state is not reconstructable at decision time.
- **Verification:** both pages fetched and text-extracted in Cycle 94; the quoted sentences were read in the extracted text layer.

### S-369 — Simon Z. Wu and Nicholas J. Ostroy, "Transaction Costs for Municipal Securities Odd-Lot Trades" (MSRB Research Paper, April 2026)

- **Type:** primary venue research paper (MSRB) — the market's own measurement of customer transaction costs.
- **URL:** https://www.msrb.org/sites/default/files/2026-04/Transaction-Costs-for-Municipal%20Securities-Odd-Lot-Trades.pdf (HTTP 200; 2,023,905 bytes; PDF; 16 pages; extracted text 38,256 chars).
- **Supports:** R-055 (reasons 1 and 2 — the effect is published and measured by the venue, and the pre-trade quote that would reveal a dealer's one-way bid is not consolidated).
- **Why it matters:** line-verified passages: *"the average effective spread for municipal securities transactions shot up to 63 basis points in May 2022"* and *"As of late 2025, the average effective spread was approximately 50 basis points, still higher than the low of 42 basis points reached in late 2021"*; *"the effective spread for odd-lot customer trades is 2.4 times that for block customer trades"*; *"Both the average and median effective spreads for odd-lot customer trades executed by other dealers are nearly 2.7 times as much as those for odd-lot customer trades executed by institutional dealers."* On structure: *"the municipal securities market and other fixed income markets such as the corporate bond and agency securities markets function as over-the-counter marketplaces where investors place their orders with dealers directly without a centralized facility. Dealers either execute orders by committing dealer capital (principal trades) or by searching for an intermediary in the market to facilitate transactions."* On quotes: *"In fixed-income securities markets, pre-trade quote data are not universally available or nationally consolidated."* On the variable-rate leg: *"Variable-rate municipal securities were excluded from this analysis, as they are typically traded by sophisticated institutional investors at par and with no markup."*
- **Caveats:** the paper's own data are the MSRB's RTRS data, and its effective-spread construction needs a security to have *both* a customer purchase and a customer sale on the same day, which per its own footnote 16 covers *"Only 6,900 of those fixed-rate securities (26%, or about one in four securities traded)"* on an average 2025 day. It is a **descriptive** paper; it does not claim a tradeable edge, and it is used here to establish that the effect is *published and measured*, not that the effect is absent.
- **Verification:** fetched and text-extracted in Cycle 94; the quoted sentences were read in the extracted text layer.

### S-370 — John A. Bagley and Marcelo Vieira, "Convergence of Individual and Institutional Trading Dynamics in Small Size Trades" (MSRB Research Paper, February 2025)

- **Type:** primary venue research paper (MSRB).
- **URL:** https://www.msrb.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/MSRB-Convergence-of-Individual-and-Institutional.pdf (HTTP 200; 1,977,240 bytes; PDF; 7 pages; extracted text 14,546 chars).

In 2024, there were 11 institutional dealers in the top 25 dealers, and they represented about 41% of all customer trades."*; and in the Conclusions, *"these investors saw their market share rise from 10% in 2015 to 44% in 2024"* and *"it is highly likely that at least 50% of odd-lot customer transactions occurred with institutional clients."* The paper also states the mechanism: *"even though these trades are typically on behalf of individual investors, it is financial professionals who are making the final decision of what to buy or sell."*

### S-372 — John M. Griffin, Nicholas Hirschey and Samuel Kruger, "Why Is the Fragmented Municipal Bond Market So Costly to Investors and Issuers?", *Journal of Economic Perspectives* 39(2), Spring 2025, 235–260 (DOI 10.1257/jep.20241411)

- **Type:** peer-reviewed journal article (published version), read in the University of Nebraska–Lincoln institutional-repository copy.
- **URL:** https://run.unl.pt/server/api/core/bitstreams/4ad0d4f6-6e8c-4830-9830-57a738e29a54/content (HTTP 200; 757,990 bytes; PDF; 26 pages; extracted text 86,994 chars). The publisher's article page https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/jep.20241411 (HTTP 200; 31,114 bytes; HTML) was also fetched and text-extracted and confirms the bibliographic record and the abstract.
- **Supports:** R-055 (all five reasons — it is the canonical published synthesis of this family, and each reason is anchored in it where the reason is about prior art).
- **Why it matters:** line-verified passages include: *"Electronic trading platforms exist only in the interdealer market, with no widely used platform for individuals to trade directly with each other. Municipal bond transactions are publicly disclosed after they occur, but individual investors have limited pre-trade information, particularly with respect to quoted prices"*; *"retail investors' trading costs for municipal bonds were 2.3 percent in the early 2000s … they were still 1.1 percent in 2023"*; *"we estimate that 5 percent of small bond transactions have markups over 3.29 percent in 2023"*; *"trading costs are high at least in part because the municipal bond market lacks a trading platform that individuals can access"*; *"A longstanding puzzle in the municipal bond literature is that short-term municipal yields are consistent with the tax rates we would expect for investors in the top income tax brackets, whereas longer-term municipal yields are higher than we would expect"*; *"the tax subsidy to municipal debt increases underwriter competition, which in turn leads to lower underwriting fees"*; *"the ratings upgrades led to an economically large 10 to 33 basis point decrease in credit spreads for the affected bonds"* after *"upgrades of zero to four credit rating notches on $2.2 trillion in municipal debt"*; *"the literature indicates that investors rely heavily on credit ratings, even when changes in ratings convey relatively little new information"*; *"Neither the MSRB's 'best execution' Rule G-18 implemented in 2016, requiring dealers to obtain the most favorable possible price, nor the required disclosure of markups and markdowns in 2018 (MSRB Regulatory Notice 2016-28) had a discernible effect on average or extreme markups"*; and the puzzle list, *"high underwriting costs, conflicting roles by municipal advisors, extreme and widely varying trade markups, investment holdings that are often not tax-efficient, inconsistent implied marginal tax rates, a heavy reliance on credit ratings, little benefit but widespread use of insurance, delayed use of call provisions, and inconsistent treatment of accounting information."*
- **Caveats:** the article is a *review and a set of reform proposals*, not a trading strategy, and it is the venue-neutral published record of what is already known about this family. Its own proposals — *"improvements in the availability of information about prices and competitiveness of price quotes for potential buyers"* — are the *state of the art* of the reform debate, which is precisely why the family is a negative: the identified problem is published, and the proposed fix is published. **Which carrier verified which passage, stated exactly (the register's verification discipline):** the **body-text** passages quoted in this entry — the round-trip trading-cost figures, the "5 percent of small bond transactions have markups over 3.29 percent", the OTC/electronic-platform description and the "publicly disclosed after they occur" sentence, the "longstanding puzzle in the municipal bond literature", the 25-percent median marginal tax rate, the "municipal bond puzzle" framing, the 2010 rating-recalibration natural experiment, the "Rule G-18 / markups-and-markdowns disclosure" finding and the "trading costs are high at least in part because the municipal bond market lacks a trading platform" sentence — were read in the **text layer of the repository copy of the published version** fetched from the University of Nebraska–Lincoln DSpace bitstream-content route. The **puzzle list** quoted in this entry ("Puzzles documented in the academic literature include high underwriting costs, conflicting roles by municipal advisors, extreme and widely varying trade markups, investment holdings that are often not tax-efficient, inconsistent implied marginal tax rates, a heavy reliance on credit ratings, little benefit but widespread use of insurance, delayed use of call provisions, and inconsistent treatment of accounting information") is the **second half of the article's published abstract**, and was read in the text layer of the **publisher's own article page** (the AEA page fetched and text-extracted in the same cycle), **not** in the repository PDF. Both carriers are the same published article and are recorded under this single identifier; the distinction is stated so that no passage is credited to a carrier that does not contain it.
- **Verification:** fetched and text-extracted in Cycle 94 from the institutional-repository copy of the **published version** (the article's own page 1 carries the JEP masthead, volume, issue and page range). The publisher's PDF route returned **HTTP 403** and was not used.

### S-373 — MSRB, "Glossary of Municipal Securities Terms", Third Edition, August 2013

- **Type:** primary venue reference document (MSRB) — the market's own definitions of the tradeable objects.
- **URL:** https://www.msrb.org/sites/default/files/2022-08/MSRB-Glossary-of-Municipal-Securities-Terms-Third_Edition-August-2013.pdf (HTTP 200; 586,104 bytes; PDF; 120 pages; extracted text 324,010 chars).
- **Supports:** R-055 (reason 5 — the concession and the mark-up are *defined, published terms* for the dealer's remuneration, and the "bid wanted" mechanism is a published convention).
- **Why it matters:** line-verified definitions: *"CONCESSION – A price expressed in terms of a net offering price (in basis or dollar price terms) minus a differential (in points or dollars per bond) granted between professionals."*; *"MARK-UP – A form of remuneration received by a municipal securities dealer when selling securities as principal to a customer. Mark-up generally is considered to be the differential between the prevailing market price of the security at the time the municipal securities dealer sells the security to the customer and the higher price paid by the customer to the municipal securities dealer."*; *"BID WANTED – The process by which an investor or municipal securities dealer actively solicits bids on a position of securities from the marketplace."*; *"PRINCIPAL TRADE – A securities transaction in which a municipal securities dealer effects the transaction for its own account."*; and on marketability, *"A municipal security's marketability depends upon many factors, including its coupon, yield, dollar price, security provisions, maturity, credit quality and rating, if any."*
- **Caveats:** the Third Edition dates from **August 2013** and is the most recent edition the MSRB publishes; some defined terms (notably the "Rule G-17" and "Rule G-30" cross-references) have since been renumbered, so the definitions are used for the *market vocabulary* only, and the register does not rely on the document for any rule's current content.
- **Verification:** fetched and text-extracted in Cycle 94; the quoted definitions were read in the extracted text layer.

### S-377 — Simon Wu and John Bagley, "What Drives Trading Volume in the Municipal Securities Market? A Study of Likely Factors", MSRB Research Paper, February 2025

- **Type:** primary venue research paper (MSRB) on secondary-market trading-volume drivers — the market's own regression-based study of why municipal trading volume moves.
- **URL:** https://www.msrb.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/MSRB-What-Drives-Trading-Volume-in-the-MSM.pdf (HTTP 200; PDF; 16 pages; extracted text 35,533 chars). It upgrades R-055's prior-art grounds — it documents that volume drivers are a *published, measured baseline* — but R-055's verdict, its five reasons and its baseline row 92 are unchanged; this is not a re-screen and it adds no sixth reason.
- **Why it matters:** the regression (166 monthly observations, January 2011–December 2024) reports that both 10-year benchmark yields and market volatility are positively and statistically significantly correlated with trading volume even after controlling for primary offering volume. Parameter estimates: Yield 0.4824 (t 6.0603) and 0.4313 (t 4.1879); Volatility 0.0460 (t 3.5037) and 0.1174 (t 6.8862) — all four significant at the 5% level — for Number of Trades and Par Value Traded respectively. Primary offering volume is also positively correlated (0.0801 / 0.0887). Record trade count in 2024 was the third consecutive annual record. Adjusted R-squared 0.44 / 0.50.
- **Caveats:** venue-primary material; describes *drivers* of volume, not a harvestable concession, and makes no claim about an unobservable decision-time state. It confirms the register's prior-art concern rather than opening a new mechanism.
- **Verification:** fetched and text-extracted in Cycle 95 (pypdf); every quoted figure read in the extracted text layer, including Table 5 (regression parameter estimates, t values, statistical significance, number of observations) and Table 6 (impact illustration).

### S-378 — Griffin, J. M., Hirschey, N. and Kruger, S. (2023), "Do Municipal Bond Dealers Give Their Customers 'Fair and Reasonable' Pricing?", *The Journal of Finance* 78(2), 887–934

- **Type:** Peer-reviewed empirical — the market's own trade-level data, obtained by the authors from the market's regulator.
- **DOI:** https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.13214 — **Crossref-verified** (fetched directly): title, three authors, *The Journal of Finance*, volume **78**, issue **2**, pages **887–934**, issued **8 March 2023**, licence CC BY-NC.
- **State-integrity correction (recorded, not erased):** the register's Cycle-94 honest-negative row gave the issue as **78(6)**. The correct issue is **78(2)** (April 2023), as confirmed by Crossref and by the document's own first page. The row is annotated in place below; the wrong issue number is not reused anywhere.
- **Supports:** the **markup object is published, measured and quantified** — "Using MSRB's proprietary data set with dealer IDs for municipal bond trades from July 2011 through December 2017, we find that some dealers consistently charge close to 0% markups over their cost on small trades in both the new issue and the seasoned issue market, but 53% (47%) of dealers charge median markups of more than 1% in the new (seasoned) issue market"; the **same-day dispersion** — "In the new issue market, the difference between the 10% most expensive and 10% least expensive purchase prices for small trades is at least 0.5% on 61% of trading days. Dispersion of at least 1% occurs 44% of the time"; the **dealer-level heterogeneity** — "Dealer fixed effects for transactions of the same bond on the same day differ by as much as 2 percentage points (ppt), even for bonds with extremely active trading"; the **published compensation rules** — "MSRB rules G-18 and G-30 require that transactions traded on the same day should generally receive consistent pricing", "MSRB Rule G-18 … requires that dealers obtain the most favorable possible pricing for customers given current market conditions", "MSRB Rule G-30 requires that commissions and markups for transactions with dealers must be 'fair and reasonable'", and the regulator's gloss — "a 'fair and reasonable' price bears a reasonable relationship to the prevailing market price of the security"; the **quantified size of the retail premium** — "Over the 6.5-year sample, the total value of small trade markups (for purchase transactions) in excess of 2% is $479 million, with $1.83 billion of markups in excess of 1% and $2.83 billion of markups in excess of 0.5%"; the **published null for the regulatory remedy** — "We find no evidence that median or extreme markups decreased following MSRB rule changes requiring best execution in March 2016, even for high-cost dealers. We find some small decreases in seasoned issue markups following regulatory changes that increased markup transparency in May 2018, but no decreases in the new issue market"; the **published, quantified customer cost** — "Practical challenges to accessing pricing information for typical retail investors"; the **published disclosure state** — "Since January 2005, all municipal bond transactions have been publicly posted with a 15-minute lag"; and the **published behavioural mechanism** — "Trading frequently clusters at quarter and odd-eighth percentage-point yield increments, and trades at these yield increments tend to have higher markups, indicating that the practice of rounding is associated with high markups."
- **Why it matters (R-055, by annotation only).** This is the **peer-reviewed, dealer-level study of the municipal retail markup**, and it is the paper the register has been carrying as an **honest negative** since Cycle 94. It **strengthens three of R-055's existing reasons** and adds **no sixth reason**:
  - **reason 1** (the effect is published, measured and quantified) — now quantified by the peer-reviewed literature itself at the dealer level, not only by the regulator (S-369) and the JEP synthesis (S-372);
  - **reason 2** (the decision-time state does not exist) — dealer-level markups are measurable **only** from the regulator's **proprietary** dataset **with dealer identifiers**, for July 2011 – December 2017, through the regulator's own access; there is no public product at that granularity, and even the public post-trade tape is **lagged** (15 minutes) and, per the paper's own account, is of little help to less sophisticated customers;
  - **reason 5** (the tradeable object is a published compensation for a published service) — the compensation is itself a **regulated, defined and published** object under MSRB Rules G-18 and G-30, and its level is published, measured and explained rather than hidden.
  **R-055's verdict, its five reasons and its baseline row 92 are unchanged.** This entry is prior art for the family; it is not a re-screen.
- **It also carries the two closed papers' results inside a line-verified document.** The introduction states that "Harris and Piwowar (2006) and Green, Hollifield, and Schürhoff (2007a) find that small municipal bond trades have substantially higher markups than large trades. Green, Hollifield, and Schürhoff (2007b) use a structural model and find that the high trading costs in municipal bonds likely come from dealer market power", and that "Harris and Piwowar (2006) indicate that the largest reason for high prices is a lack of transparency". The register's claim that those two closed papers' results are available inside its own line-verified corpus therefore now rests on a **fetched, text-extracted document** rather than on a secondary citation.
- **Caveats:** (i) the evidence is the **regulator's proprietary trade-level dataset with dealer identifiers**, used by the authors under access — it is **not** a public product and cannot be re-obtained at a decision date; (ii) the paper measures **realised markups**, not a decision-time state, and its dealer-ID sample ends in **December 2017** (markup panels are described through 2019); (iii) the paper is a **pricing-practice** study, not a study of a tradeable concession, and the register does not claim one; (iv) the markups it measures are, in its own words, the retail customers' cost, which is the register's point about the *existence* of a published cost premium — not a claim that the cost is harvestable.
- **Verification:** **line-verified.** The **published version of record** was fetched as a PDF and its text layer extracted: **48 pages; 147,579 characters** (pypdf). The file's own PDF metadata carry `/Title` "Do Municipal Bond Dealers Give Their Customers 'Fair and Reasonable' Pricing?", `/Subject` "The Journal of Finance 2023.78:887-934" and `/WPS-ARTICLEDOI` "10.1111/jofi.13214"; the first page prints "THE JOURNAL OF FINANCE • VOL. ### S-379 — Green, T. C., Hollifield, R. and Schürhoff, N. (2005), "Financial Intermediation and the Costs of Trading in an Opaque Market", SSRN working paper, DOI 10.2139/ssrn.668847

- **Type:** **Working-paper version** (posted 2005) of the study published as *Review of Financial Studies* **20**(2), 275–314 (DOI `10.1093/rfs/hhl012`).
- **DOI:** https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.668847 — **Crossref-verified** (fetched directly): title, authors Green, Hollifield and Schuerhoff, posted 2005, publisher Elsevier BV (SSRN).
- **Supports:** the **dealer side of the opaque market is a published, estimated market-power outcome** — "Municipal bonds trade in opaque, decentralized broker-dealer markets in which price information is costly to gather. Whether dealers in such a market operate competitively is an empirical issue, but a difficult one to study. Data in such markets is generally not centrally recorded."; "We analyze a comprehensive database of all trades between broker-dealers in municipal bonds and their customers. The data is only released to the public with a substantial lag, and thus the market was relatively opaque to the traders themselves during our sample period."; "We find that dealers earn lower average markups on larger trades, even though larger trades lead the dealers to bear more risk of losses. We formulate and estimate a simple structural bargaining model that allows us to estimate measures of dealer bargaining power and relate it to characteristics of the trades. The results suggest dealers exercise substantial market power. Our measures of market power decrease in trade size and increase in variables that indicate the complexity of the trade for the dealer."
- **Why it matters.** R-055's stated **known limitation** was that the canonical theoretical statement of the "one-way bid" — the opaque-market intermediation model in which a dealer's bid is a put-like claim — sits in a **closed** source. This entry puts the **authors' own deposited abstract** on that statement into the register's corpus for the first time, and S-378 (the fetched published version of the companion study) quotes the same result from the published article: "Green, Hollifield, and Schürhoff (2007b) use a structural model and find that the high trading costs in municipal bonds likely come from dealer market power."
- **Caveats, stated honestly:** **the paper's body is still not obtainable.** What is line-verified here is the **abstract deposited with Crossref for the preprint** (the SSRN record was fetched directly from the Crossref REST API, HTTP 200) — **not** the article and **not** the preprint body. This entry is therefore **abstract-level** evidence, of the same kind as the Cycle-85 upgrades of S-310 and S-312, and it must not be described anywhere as a full-text reading. The published article remains **closed**: Unpaywall reports `oa_status: closed` with no open-access location; OpenAlex lists no open-access location; Semantic Scholar reports no open-access PDF; SSRN's own abstract and delivery routes return **HTTP 403** to this environment. The register therefore continues to carry the published article's result **by citation inside line-verified documents** (S-378 above; S-372 for the early-2000s retail round-trip cost).
- **Verification:** **line-verified at abstract level (Crossref-deposited preprint abstract, fetched directly).** The published article's bibliographic record — *Review of Financial Studies* **20**(2), 275–314 — is independently confirmed against Crossref (fetched directly); the register's existing citation of it as *RFS* 20(2) is correct.

**Cycle-98 corpus-state note (the Cycle-96 sweep re-run; no identifier consumed).** The Cycle-96 sweep
was re-run today over this file, entry by entry, under the **same rule as recorded in the Cycle-96
corpus-state note**: an entry's block ends at the next heading of any level (or the next bold inline
entry); an entry is **index-rendered** if it contains index-render wording (a search-index render, an
index-rendered reading); and it is **index-rendered-only** if it contains **no** positive direct-fetch or
text-extraction assertion anywhere in the entry, with negated forms ("not fetched directly", "not
parsed", "index-rendered, not directly parsed", an HTTP 403 or a failed route) **not** counted as
assertions. **One refinement was made and is disclosed**: a fetch or a read performed *through* a search
index ("the report PDF was fetched through the search index and the quoted passages were read in the
returned document text") is an **index render, not a direct fetch** and therefore does not clear an
entry. The Cycle-96 script was not preserved, so the rule was **re-implemented from its recorded prose
description**; on the corpus as it stood at the start of this cycle the sweep returns **68
index-rendered-only entries** and **74 mixed entries** (plus 228 entries with no index wording), against
Cycle 96's **89 / 51** on the Cycle-96 corpus. The difference is accounted for: **11** entries left the

### S-380 — Ko, B.-W. and Chang, Y.-T. (2024), "Analysis and forecasting of the dry bulk shipping market: structural VAR models using FFA-spot-time charter rates" — the **SSRN record's abstract** (abstract-level evidence only)

- **Type:** **Preprint record, abstract level** — the authors' own deposited abstract on the SSRN
  record for the working-paper version of the article published in *Maritime Policy & Management*
  **51**(5): 717–744 (DOI 10.1080/03088839.2024.2348692). **Not the article and not the preprint body.**
- **URL:** `https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4264797` — **obtained through the
  Internet Archive's replay of that page**:
  `https://web.archive.org/web/20240415180421id_/https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4264797`
  (**HTTP 200; 57,582 bytes; 4,123 characters** of page text). The CDX record for that address lists
  the capture as `text/html`, status **200**, captured **15 April 2024**; the live SSRN route returns
  **HTTP 403** to this environment, so the archive replay is the only working route and is an
  **archive replay of the record itself**, not an index rendering.
- **What it establishes:** the working paper's **title, authorship, affiliations, length and posting
  date** — "Analysis and Forecasting of the Dry Bulk Shipping Market: Structural VAR Models Using
  FFA-Spot-Time Charter Rates by Byoung-Wook Ko, Young-Tae Chang … 44 Pages Posted: 1 Nov 2022 … Byoung-Wook
  Ko, Korea Maritime Institute; Young-Tae Chang, Inha University" — and the **authors' own abstract**:
  "This study investigates dynamic interactive patterns of the dry bulk shipping markets through the
  lens of structural vector autoregression (VAR) models. There are two distinct hypotheses in the extant
  literature. One is that asymmetry between spot and forward freight agreement (FFA) markets causes FFA
  prices to respond more rapidly to new information than spot prices, termed the **Physical-Paper
  Hypothesis** in this paper. The other hypothesis is that there are some diverse shocks with different
  propagation mechanisms, termed the **Shock-Diversity Hypothesis**. This paper combines these two
  seemingly separate hypotheses at one time in two illustrative structural VAR models, based on a
  dataset of weekly spot, FFA, and time charter (TC) rates in the dry bulk shipping markets. The two
  structural VAR models show that spot, FFA, and TC rates have different, particularly dynamic responses
  to identified permanent shocks. Furthermore, they show that the reduced-form tri-variate FFA-Spot-TC VAR
  model produces more accurate forecasts for future spot rates than the bi-variate FFA-Spot and TC-Spot VAR
  models. Therefore, market participants can use VAR models as an information-processing tool for
  understanding of (e.g. data descriptions and structural inferences), and forecasting in, dry bulk
  shipping markets."
- **State-integrity correction (recorded, not erased).** The **Cycle-93 honest-negative row** for this
  paper recorded that the article's text "remains unobtainable", that its abstract "was read through a
  search index and is **not** used as a verification basis", and — correcting the Cycle-91 label — that
  the description of the paper as "the 'Physical-Paper Hypothesis' paper" "is **not corroborated by the
  publisher's bibliographic record** and is no longer relied on by the register". That row is annotated in
  place below. **What changes:** the label is now **corroborated by the authors' own abstract**, which
  is now a fetched, parsed document rather than an index render; the bibliographic-record caveat was
  correct as to the *publisher's record* (a RePEc/Crossref title carries no hypothesis names) and
  stands, but the paper's own text does use both names. **What does not change:** the **body remains
  closed** (the article's and the preprint's full texts were not obtained), the paper is **still not used
  as a verification basis for any reason** in R-052 or R-054, and no reason, verdict, score, row or gap
  moves.
- **Caveats:** abstract-level evidence only, of the same kind as S-379; the abstract is a *summary of
  results*, not the results themselves; the "Physical-Paper Hypothesis" is the authors' own label for
  the **published** asymmetry result, which the register's freight reasoning already treats as
  published prior art carried by S-350, S-351 and S-352.

### Cycle-100 corpus-state note (the provenance sweep, re-measured)

The sweep rule was re-implemented from the prose statement in the Cycle-99 handoff — *an entry counts as
index-rendered if it contains index-render wording and **no** positive direct-fetch or text-extraction
assertion; a negated form is not an assertion; a fetch or read performed **through** a search index is an
index render, not a direct fetch; an entry's block ends at the next heading of any level* — and applied
to the corpus as it stood at the start of the cycle, with the adjudication done **per sentence** (a
positive phrase counts only when the sentence carrying it carries no negation of its own). Measurement:
**62 index-rendered-only entries, 79 mixed entries, 220 entries with no index-render wording**, over the
**361 heading-form entries** in the corpus (the ten bold inline entries S-281 … S-290 are document
records outside the heading form, and the one sub-heading inside S-358 is not a second entry).
**Residual against the inherited figure is disclosed, not smoothed**: the inherited state was 57
index-rendered-only and 85 mixed. The difference is **+5 / −6** and is attributable to the
detector, not to the corpus — the re-implementation had to be written a third time (the Cycle-96 script
was not preserved), and the two cycles' implementations differ in how they treat a positive assertion
that sits in a later, cycle-added annotation of an entry whose original verification bullet is
index-rendered. **Two entries (S-139 and S-141) are Cycle-97 upgrades that a window-based detector
mislabelled** as index-rendered and that the sentence-level detector correctly returns to the mixed class;
the five-entry difference is the mirror image of that effect elsewhere. **No earlier cycle's figures are
restated.** The named targets of this cycle's operation were each **verified by hand**, entry by entry,
against their own verification bullets, before any fetch was attempted: **nineteen** of the
**twenty-one** named targets were genuinely index-rendered at the start of the cycle, and **two (S-136
and S-314) were
not index-rendered entries at all** — S-136 has been line-verified since it was minted (see the
state-integrity table above), and S-314 is a mixed-class entry whose own bullet records a direct fetch
whose text layer did **not** confirm the quoted statistics, so it is "index-confirmed rather than
line-verified" and belongs to the mixed-class pass, not to this operation. **A twenty-second entry was
upgraded on top of that subset: S-202** (40 CFR 80.1405, the Renewable Fuel Standards), which the
Cycle-100 handoff had named as a *Cycle-101* target, was upgraded in this cycle because a working route
for it — the eCFR **renderer** endpoint, which returns the section's full text where the versioner
endpoint and the human-facing page do not — was identified while the next cycle's subset was being
pre-registered. The operation therefore touched **twenty-two entries**: **sixteen line-verified, two
partially upgraded, three honest negatives, and one (S-202) upgraded outside the named subset**. The

### S-381 — U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Division of Corporation Finance (2015)
"No-Action Letter: Abbreviated Tender or Exchange Offers for Non-Convertible Debt Securities" —
Rule 14e-1 staff no-action position, addressed to Cahill Gordon & Reindel LLP, 23 January 2015
(13 pages).
URL: https://www.sec.gov/divisions/corpfin/cf-noaction/2015/abbreviated-offers-debt-securities012315-sec14.pdf
- **Type:** Primary regulator material (staff no-action letter under Exchange Act Rule 14e-1(a)–(b)).
- **Supports:** the **"guaranteed delivery" mechanic** and the **seven-to-ten-calendar-day
  abbreviated-offer period** that S-208 carried but could not source, and the *rule-determined
  offer mechanics* the S-208/S-207/S-209 family screen rests on. Verbatim, the fifth condition: "permit
  tenders prior to the expiration of the offer through a **guaranteed delivery procedure** by means of
  a certification by or on behalf of a holder that such holder is tendering securities beneficially
  owned by it and that the **delivery of such securities will be made no later than the close of
  business on the second business day after the expiration of the offer**". Verbatim, the letter's
  own description of the 1986 relief: "Commencing in 1986, the Staff issued a series of no-action
  letters providing relief from the 20 business day requirement in the context of certain debt
  tender offers. In particular, the Staff granted no-action relief for issuer tender offers for
  non-convertible debt securities (later limited to only non-convertible debt securities with an
  investment grade rating) that are **held open for a period of seven to ten calendar days** and
  meet certain other qualifications." The letter also confirms the Rule 14e-1 framework itself
  ("Rule 14e-1(a) requires a minimum offer period for all tender offers—debt or equity—of 20 business
  days"; "Rule 14e-1(b) requires that a tender offer remain open for at least ten business days after
  any change in the consideration offered"), the five-business-day period the relief is built around
  ("five business day period"), and the announcement mechanics ("at or prior to 10:00 a.m., Eastern
  time, on the first business day of such five business day period"). It records the supersession of
  the 1986 and 1990 letters: "This no-action position supersedes the letters issued to Goldman, Sachs
  & Co. (March 26, 1986); Salomon Brothers Inc (March 12, 1986); Salomon Brothers Inc (October 1,
  1990); and any similar letters relating to abbreviated offering periods in non-convertible debt
  tender offers."
- **Caveats:** a **staff no-action position**, not a rule and not an exemptive order; it binds only
  the Division's staff and is expressly limited to the facts presented. **It was superseded on
  30 June 2026 by S-382**, which continues the five-business-day minimum on materially different and
  wider conditions. The 2015 letter is therefore a **historical** instrument for present practice and
  is the right source only for the period 23 January 2015 – 30 June 2026.
- **Verification:** fetched directly on 21 October 2026 with a compliant User-Agent — **HTTP 200,
  260,761 bytes, application/pdf**; the text layer was extracted with `pypdf` (**13 pages, 39,712
  characters**) and read. The four quoted passages above are present verbatim (the guaranteed-delivery
  condition once in the conditions list and three times elsewhere in the letter, including the
  Credit Roundtable correspondence at the end; "seven to ten calendar days" once; "five business days"
  nine times; "1986" eleven times). The verification label is **line-verified (PDF fetched directly
  and text-extracted)** from the moment of creation — no index-render stage.

### S-382 — U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Division of Corporation Finance (2026)
"Exemptive Order for Tender or Exchange Offers for Non-Convertible Debt Securities", 30 June 2026
(5 pages), signed Tiffany Posil, Chief, Office of Mergers and Acquisitions.
URL: https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/exorders/2026/exemp-order-tender-or-exchange-offers-non-convertible-debt-securities-063026.pdf
- **Type:** Primary regulator material (delegated exemptive order under Exchange Act Sections
  14(d)(5), 14(d)(8)(C) and 36(a), 17 CFR 200.30-1(f)(16)).
- **Supports:** the **current** abbreviated-offer regime, and therefore a **dated supersession** the
  register must carry. Verbatim: "This Exemptive Order **supersedes the 2015 Letter** and any
  similar letters relating to abbreviated offering periods in tender or exchange offers for
  non-convertible debt securities." The order grants an exemption from Rules 14e-1(a) and (b) "to
  permit a tender or exchange offer for any class or series of non-convertible debt securities to
  remain open for a minimum offering period of **five business days**", and the securities need not
  carry a rating ("**regardless of any particular rating** assigned to such securities"). It restates
  the 1986/1990 "Prior Letters" in footnote 2 — "each not recommending enforcement action under
  Exchange Act Rule 14e-1(a) or Rule 14e-1(b) if an issuer conducts a tender offer for non-convertible
  debt securities with a **minimum offering period of seven to ten calendar days** based on customary
  market practice" — and footnote 3 identifies S-381 as "SEC No-Action Letter, **Cahill Gordon &
  Reindel LLP (Jan. 23, 2015)**". Footnote 4 refers to a separate, earlier order in the same month:
  "See SEC Exemptive Order for Tender Offers for Equity Securities (**Apr. 16, 2026**)".
- **Caveats:** a **delegated exemptive order**, revocable at the Division's discretion ("the Division
  may reconsider, modify, or withdraw the relief provided herein"). It applies to non-convertible
  debt securities only; the equity analogue is a different instrument, not registered here. The
  **guaranteed-delivery condition is absent from the order's conditions** — the strings "guaranteed
  delivery" return **zero hits** in the extracted text — and multiple law-firm client alerts
  (Ropes & Gray, Skadden, Nixon Peabody, Sullivan & Cromwell, Debevoise) report that the requirement
  was **eliminated**; this is an *absence plus secondary corroboration*, not a positive sentence in
  the order, and it is recorded as such.
- **Verification:** fetched directly on 21 October 2026 with a compliant User-Agent — **HTTP 200,
  181,960 bytes, application/pdf**; the text layer was extracted with `pypdf` (**5 pages, 15,132
  characters**) and read. The quoted passages are present verbatim ("supersedes the 2015 Letter"

### S-388 — Securities Exchange Act of 1934, Rule 10b-18 (17 CFR 240.10b-18)
"Purchases of certain equity securities by the issuer and others", *Code of Federal Regulations*,
Title 17, Part 240, § 240.10b-18 (as amended at 68 FR 64970, Nov. 17, 2003, and 70 FR 37618, June 29,
2005).
URL: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-240/section-240.10b-18
(renderer endpoint used: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/renderer/v1/content/enhanced/current/title-17?chapter=II&part=240&section=240.10b-18)
- **Type:** Primary law (federal regulation) — the safe-harbour rule that bounds an issuer's repurchase
  purchases, and therefore the intermediary's covering purchases under an ASR.
- **Supports:** the **published, ex ante** constraints on the covering window that S-384's contract
  refers to, quoted verbatim from the fetched text layer: (a)(1) "**ADTV** means the average daily
  trading volume reported for the security during the **four calendar weeks** preceding the week in
  which the Rule 10b-18 purchase is to be effected."; (b)(1) "**One broker or dealer.** Rule 10b-18
  purchases must be effected from or through only one broker or dealer on any single day"; (b)(3)
  "**Price of purchases.** Rule 10b-18 purchases must be effected at a purchase price that: (i) Does
  not exceed the highest independent bid or the last independent transaction price, whichever is
  higher, quoted or reported in the consolidated system at the time the Rule 10b-18 purchase is
  effected"; (b)(4) "**Volume of purchases.** The total volume of Rule 10b-18 purchases effected by or
  for the issuer and any affiliated purchasers effected on any single day must not exceed **25 percent
  of the ADTV** for that security; However, once each week, in lieu of purchasing under the 25 percent
  of ADTV limit for that day, the issuer or an affiliated purchaser of the issuer may effect one block
  purchase if: (i) No other Rule 10b-18 purchases are effected that day, and (ii) The block purchase is
  **not** included when calculating a security's four week ADTV under this section."; and (c) the
  market-wide-suspension alternative, in which "the volume of purchases condition in paragraph (b)(4)
  of this section is modified so that the amount of Rule 10b-18 purchases must not exceed **100 percent
  of the ADTV** for that security."
- **Caveats:** the rule is a **safe harbour**, not a prohibition: (d) "No presumption shall arise that
  an issuer or an affiliated purchaser has violated the anti-manipulation provisions … if the Rule
  10b-18 purchases … do not meet the conditions specified in paragraph (b) or (c) of this section." The
  rule also states that its conditions bind **"Rule 10b-18 purchases"** — purchases made by the issuer or
  an affiliated purchaser — and it does **not** regulate a *third-party* intermediary's own market
  purchases as such; the register uses it here because S-384's contract expressly keys the
  intermediary's daily purchases to "the applicable maximum amount of Shares permitted under Rule
  10b-18(b)(4)". The text is the version current at the date of the fetch (2026).
- **Verification:** fetched directly on 21 October 2026 from `www.ecfr.gov` — the renderer endpoint
  returned **HTTP 200, 91,722 bytes, text/html** and the plain section page **HTTP 200, 10,596

### S-389 — "Funding Rates as a Cross-Sectional Factor in Perpetual Futures" (public practitioner note, GitHub repository `OctopusTakopi/funding-rate-alpha`)
URL: https://github.com/OctopusTakopi/funding-rate-alpha (README fetched at `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OctopusTakopi/funding-rate-alpha/main/README.md`)
- **Type:** Self-published practitioner study (public code repository, **no peer review, no journal venue**), with a disclosed data provenance (public Binance funding, kline, premium-index and open-interest archives, survivorship-free) and a documented method (Newey–West errors, Benjamini–Hochberg multiplicity correction, day-matched placebo cohorts, circular block bootstrap). All results are **author-reported**.
- **Supports:** (i) **the sign of the funding–return relation is regime-dependent.** The raw funding level's next-24-hour Spearman information coefficient is **−3.9 % (2020, t = −2.5), −3.1 % (2021, t = −4.7), +0.0 % (2022), +0.6 % (2023), +1.6 % (2024, t = 3.4), +3.4 % (2025, t = 8.1), +2.0 % (2026, t = 3.6)** — a *reversal* regime over 2020–21 and a *continuation* regime from 2023, the current regime's coefficients being positive and significant. The note's own sentence: "**No unconditional level signal survives this flip.**" (ii) **the candidate's own percentile construction is reported null.** The 90-day rolling z-score, cross-sectionally ranked, "**predicts nothing at any horizon, +0.00 % at one hour**", its 24-hour information coefficient being **−0.0007 (t = −0.3)**; "the preprocessing removes the baseline without creating predictability". (iii) The level predicts "**only at eight hours and shorter, and only by too little to trade**": **+1.89 % at one hour (t = 6.26)**, +1.04 % at eight hours, and **+0.23 % at twenty-four hours (t = 0.79)**; split at 2024, the 2020–23 window shows "**no effect at any horizon except a significantly negative one at a day**" while 2024–26 shows **+4.10 % at one hour** and **+2.39 % at twenty-four hours (t = 8.8)**. (iv) **the crowding reading is contradicted.** "The cross-sectional level of funding measures how retail-oriented a contract is rather than how crowded its current position structure is"; the within-day rank correlation of the rate with 7-day volatility is **−0.013**; and "**open interest builds into and through high-funding settlements**, which refutes a flow reading and leaves the rate as a measurement of the basis" (rank correlation with the open-interest change **+1.73 % (t = 9.90)** over the hour ending at the settlement and **+1.12 % (t = 7.07)** over the hour beginning at it — "positions are opened into the payment, not unwound before it"). (v) **The cost floor.** The one-hour decile spread is **3.66 bps** against an **8 bps** reference round trip; the note's own tradeable residue is a **carry** book (90-day z-score deciles, three-day swing, +8.9 bps/day, Sharpe 1.42) whose *price* leg is the failing component — "raising the liquidity floor removes the return rather than scaling it" (price leg **−0.5 bps/day** at a USD 100M floor) and whose excess over the round trip is "itself indistinguishable from zero (**+2.2 bps, t = 0.68** at a day)". (vi) A **stronger published state** exists in the same venue: the **top-trader long/short account ratio** has an information coefficient of **+0.013 (t = 4.7)** with a **continuation** sign and nets **+4.2 bps/day at Sharpe 0.82** as decile long-shorts, against the funding level's +2.8 (Sharpe 0.51) and the z-score's +1.4 (0.27).
- **Caveats:** **author-reported and not peer-reviewed**; the design is **cross-sectional** (contracts sorted within a timestamp), whereas IDEA-009's rule is **time-series within a single underlying**, so the transfer of the regime-flip finding to the candidate's own form is **suggestive rather than decisive**; the note states that "fees are not what constrains it" (its binding constraints are capacity and drawdown); 2020 and 2026 are partial years. The register does **not** treat this note as authoritative for any sign claim and does not treat it as a replication of anything.
- **Verification:** fetched directly on 21 October 2026 from `raw.githubusercontent.com`; the README text layer was retrieved and read from the abstract through **Section 14** (the retrieval tool truncated the final ~9 KB, which was therefore **not** read).
