There is therefore **no within-contract, time-series test of the funding level's relation to subsequent return in this document**, and the regime classification it offers is a **cross-sectional** one.
  2. **A provenance note the register now records against this entry, because G-37's pre-registered route named it as a source of *regime definitions*.** This document is a **self-published GitHub practitioner note with no peer review and no journal venue**, and its results are **author-reported**. The register's Cycle-113 note on G-37 already records this; it is repeated here because the Cycle-114 re-read was specifically looking for *published* regime classification, and this document does not supply one in the peer-reviewed sense. The register makes no claim on this entry's authority beyond what is stated in its **Type** and **Caveats** lines.
  3. **A negative provenance finding, recorded here because it is a fact about this entry's reach.** The two "2025–2026 funding-regime-classification items" that Cycle 113 said it had "located but not registered" and could not name are **not recoverable**: an exhaustive search of this repository's five artifacts returns **no author, title, year or URL** for either, and an external search (Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, SSRN, web) does not surface two matching, verifiable 2025–2026 academic or venue items that classify funding regimes into reversal/continuation. **The register therefore does not have a named published regime classifier at all**, and this is a defect in the register's own record, not a fact about the literature. See the Cycle-114 gap-verdict table at the end of this file.

### S-390 — Memon, H., Anklesaria-Dalal, K. and Mishra, R. R. (2026) — "Extreme Perpetual Futures Funding and Subsequent Bitcoin Returns: Intraday Evidence from Binance", *Advanced International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research*, Vol. 4, Issue 4 (July–August 2026), published 29 August 2026
URL: https://www.aijmr.com/research-paper.php?id=1493 · DOI: https://doi.org/10.62127/aijmr.2026.v04i04.1493
- **Type:** **Journal article with a DOI in an open-access, publication-fee-charging venue** (E-ISSN 2584-0487). The venue's own pages carry "Publication Charges" and "Track Status / Pay Fees", and self-report an "Impact Factor: 9.11"; the register cannot vouch for its peer-review process or indexing standing. All results are **author-reported**.
- **Supports:** an **independent, published test of the candidate's own state construction**. "Extreme funding is classified ex ante using the current funding rate's **mid-rank percentile within the preceding 180-day distribution**, with the lower and upper deciles defining extreme negative and extreme positive states" — i.e. the same trailing-distribution decile the candidate specifies — over Binance BTCUSDT funding observations from **10 September 2019 to 10 August 2026** aligned with 15-minute spot prices, with returns at 15-minute, one-hour, four-hour, eight-hour and 24-hour post-settlement horizons, controlled for the four-hour pre-settlement price move. The result is **asymmetric**: "The main result is concentrated in the negative tail: **extreme negative funding is followed by an average 24-hour Bitcoin return of 0.506 %**, significant under t, Wilcoxon and directional-frequency tests and robust to false-discovery-rate adjustment. **Extreme positive funding does not exhibit a comparable 24-hour effect.**" In categorical HAC regressions extreme negative funding is associated with "approximately **0.491 percentage points** of additional 24-hour return after controlling for the pre-settlement return"; non-overlapping 24-hour subsamples retain positive and significant means. The paper's own summary: funding information is "**nonlinear, asymmetric and horizon dependent** rather than adequately represented by a simple linear relation".
- **Caveats:** **the venue's standing is not established in this register's source set**; the article's own page is internally inconsistent (the site header reads "Volume 4, Issue 5, September–October 2026" while the paper records "Volume 4, Issue 4, July–August 2026"); the sample is **Bitcoin only**; the paper's controls do not include an open-interest or positioning measure, so it cannot separate a crowding reading from a basis reading; a 24-hour horizon only, with no cost model.
- **Verification:** fetched directly on 21 October 2026 from `www.aijmr.com`; the page's HTML text layer was retrieved and the abstract, keywords, authorship, volume/issue, publication date and DOI were read verbatim. Label: **line-verified (document fetched directly and text-extracted)** for the **abstract and metadata only**; the full-text PDF was not retrieved.
- **Cycle-114 re-read (2026-10-21) — the entry was re-fetched and its bibliographic record independently re-derived through the Crossref API; the finding is unchanged and one *new* point is recorded for G-37 limb (a).**
  1. **The bibliographic record is independently confirmed** via `api.crossref.org/works/10.62127/aijmr.2026.v04i04.1493` (**HTTP 200**): title, three authors, container *Advanced International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research*, volume 4, issue 4, published 29 August 2026, type journal-article, DOI as recorded above. The register's own DOI is therefore **independently verified at the metadata layer**, and the entry's caveat about the venue's standing is **unchanged** — the register still cannot vouch for the venue's peer-review process or indexing standing, and the results remain **author-reported**.
  2. **NEW — this document is a *within-asset* test, but not a *regime-flip* test.** Its design is a **single-instrument** (BTCUSDT) test of the candidate's own percentile state at the 15-minute, one-hour, four-hour, eight-hour and 24-hour horizons. It therefore bears on **G-37 limb (a)** in the sense that a within-contract test of the funding *level* against subsequent return **exists in the published literature** — but its finding is an **asymmetry across the tails of the state** ("extreme negative funding is followed by an average 24-hour Bitcoin return of 0.506 % … **extreme positive funding does not exhibit a comparable 24-hour effect**"), and it contains **no regime classification and no test of whether the within-contract sign flips between regimes**. The register therefore records this entry as evidence that the within-contract form is **occupied** and its **within-state asymmetry** is published, and **not** as an answer to limb (a), which asks specifically about **regime dependence**.
  3. **The full-text PDF was again not retrieved.** The `www.aijmr.com` article page was re-fetched directly (**HTTP 200**, HTML text layer read for the abstract and metadata) and the full-text PDF was not obtained; the entry's label therefore remains **abstract and metadata only**.

### S-391 — BitMEX Blog (12 October 2017) — Arthur Hayes, "XBTUSD Funding Mean Reversion Strategy"
URL: https://www.bitmex.com/blog/xbtusd-funding-mean-reversion-strategy (live URL returned **HTTP 404** on 21 October 2026; the page is retained in the Wayback Machine — capture `20260121190211`)
- **Type:** **Venue-published primary statement by the venue's co-founder**, dated 12 October 2017 (page header: "WRITTEN BY Arthur Hayes"; tags "perpetual / trading / technical-analysis / futures market"). An **interested-party** publication, not peer-reviewed.
- **Supports:** the **rediscovery guard** for the register's funding-rate family. The post states, in the venue's own words, the rule the candidate specifies: "If the published funding is at the maximum +0.375 %, does that predict with greater accuracy whether the return of XBTUSD in the next 8 hours will be negative?"; "**A large negative funding rate predicts a positive return for the next 8 hour period. A large positive funding rate predicts a negative return for the next 8 hour period.**"; "Using an extreme funding rate as the signal, we can take the counter trend position"; and "A simple trading algo can be constructed to capture this alpha. At each funding timestamp, if the funding rate is above or below your limit, place the counter trend trade. Immediately after the next funding timestamp, close your XBTUSD position." The published table (524 funding periods) reports per-cell success rates **47.62 % (−2σ), 53.23 % (−1σ), 45.68 % (+1σ), 44.44 % (+2σ)** — i.e. below 50 % in three of four cells — with cumulative net returns of +11.07 %, −1.38 %, +10.33 % and +20.39 %, the author attributing most of the result to the funding received rather than the price move ("The added benefit of receiving funding for bucking the trend is what provides a significant majority of this strategy's returns"), and closing with "the sample size is still relatively small".
- **Caveats:** an **interested party** publishing on its own venue; the sample is 2017 and small; the post's own framing is that the counter-trend position is taken *because* the funding payment accrues to the counter-trend side — which is the register's *carry* reading, not a reversal reading; the live URL is dead and the body text was obtained from the search index rather than from a text extraction.
- **Verification:** the page's **identity, author and date** were confirmed by a **direct Wayback Machine capture** on 21 October 2026 (`https://web.archive.org/web/20260121190211/https://www.bitmex.com/blog/xbtusd-funding-mean-reversion-strategy`), which returned the title, byline, date and tags; the **analytic body and the success-rate table were index-rendered** (search-extraction) and are **not** line-verified. ### S-392 — "Funding Rate Carry: what survives execution costs?" (public practitioner note, GitHub repository `DavidAyusoPita/funding-carry-analysis`)
URL: https://github.com/DavidAyusoPita/funding-carry-analysis (README fetched at `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DavidAyusoPita/funding-carry-analysis/main/README.md`)
- **Type:** Self-published practitioner study (public code repository, **not peer-reviewed**), with a disclosed method (unit normalisation, backwards settlement alignment, four-crossing round-trip cost model, an exchange-versus-exchange control, a four-point cost ladder, a quarterly decay check) and **author-reported** results.
- **Supports:** the **cost and decay anchors for the funding-carry baseline**: the exchange-versus-DEX funding spread "is a genuine bias, not noise" (8.5–11.4 % annualised) but "its level mean-reverts within hours" (AR(1) half-life **1.5–3.5 hours**) "while one round trip costs **13 bps** and needs **100–135 hours** of holding to repay itself"; a threshold rule that trades it "earns the *most gross income* of any rule tested and finishes at **−9 % to −15 % annualised after costs**"; the patient rule "tolerates a round-trip cost above 250 bps before it breaks even; the active rule dies above 8 bps"; and a **decay** measure — "the spread averaged **20–35 % less in the second year** of the sample than the first, and sits **45–60 % below its late-2024 peak**". It also records a **data-availability fact relevant to the candidate's venue-transferability condition**: "**OKX publishes only three months of history**, so it is excluded from the two-year comparisons."
- **Caveats:** the subject is the **cross-venue funding-carry spread**, not the within-asset reversal rule, so this entry is a **cost-and-decay reference**, not evidence on IDEA-009's directional claim; **author-reported and not peer-reviewed**; the note's own limitations include no liquidation modelling, no counterparty/protocol risk, assumed slippage beyond the measured gap, and "**One historical path. Two years, three assets, one regime.**"
- **Verification:** fetched directly on 21 October 2026 from `raw.githubusercontent.com`; the README text layer was retrieved and read in full. Label: **line-verified (document fetched directly and text-extracted)**.

### S-393 — U.S. Government Accountability Office (November 2022) — GAO-23-105801, "Renewable Fuel Standard: Actions Needed to Improve Decision-Making in the Small Refinery Exemption Program"
URL: https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-23-105801.pdf · products page: https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-23-105801
- **Type:** **Primary audit report of the U.S. legislative branch's audit agency**, with its own methodology (EPA EMTS RIN transaction data, 2013–2021; Appendix II) and seven recommendations to EPA and DOE. The report is also referred to in the register's existing sources as "the GAO Report" (S-394's companion), and a second identifier for the same report (**GAO-23-104273**) circulates in the same document family.
- **Supports:** three published facts that bear directly on IDEA-014. (i) **The RFS compliance obligation is priced, and the constrained party pays up.** GAO analysed EPA's RIN market transaction data and found that "companies that tended to trade lower quantities of RINs (likely smaller refineries) were either **paying more to buy RINs or receiving less when they sell RINs**, relative to larger companies from 2013 through 2021"; for the transactions with the largest size differences the small party paid or received prices "**2.4 percent higher or lower** for RINs, on average", and "among transactions between refineries, we found that the smaller party paid or received prices **2.9 percent higher or lower** for RINs on average"; for the ethanol (D6) RIN the size-differential estimate is 2.9 % and for the biomass-based diesel (D4) RIN **0.8 %**; "**This effect is statistically significant**". (ii) **The deadline's timing structure is documented.** EPA "has issued decisions after the 90-day deadline **89 percent of the time** (190 out of 214 decisions)"; because decisions land late, "**small refineries that apply for exemptions often do not know whether they need RINs until close to, or after, the March 31 compliance deadline**, which creates financial uncertainty"; "Late exemption decisions mean that refineries do not know how many RINs they need to submit for compliance until very close to, or after, the date by which refineries need to show compliance with RFS annual requirements"; and this "may result in either an **excess or a shortfall of RINs**". (iii) **A published recommendation to the agency** on RIN market performance (Recommendation 1: EPA "should reassess EPA's conclusion that all small refineries recover their RFS compliance costs … including by fully examining and documenting **RIN market performance and RIN pass-through** in all relevant fuel markets").
- **Caveats:** GAO's price differential is a **counterparty-size effect**, **not** a deadline-timing effect; the report says the effect's magnitude "materially" affecting individual refineries is unclear; the analysis is a single agency dataset with GAO's own modelling choices.
- **Verification:** **index-rendered** on 21 October 2026 from the official `gao.gov` PDF asset URL (search-extraction of the PDF text; the report's "What GAO Found" text, findings, footnotes 10–11 and 22 and Recommendations 1–7 were read); the PDF was **not** fetched and text-extracted directly. Label: **index-rendered**.

### S-394 — U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (December 2022) — EPA-420-R-22-038, "An Analysis of the Price of Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs) and Small Refineries" (Technical Memorandum, National Center for Environmental Economics)
Landing page: https://www.epa.gov/renewable-fuel-standard/epa-analysis-price-rins-and-small-refineries · copy of the memorandum consulted: `https://aglaw.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/EPA-Analysis-of-the-Price-of-RINs-and-Small-Refineries-Dec.-2022.pdf`
- **Type:** **The agency's own primary technical memorandum**, issued 20 December 2022 in response to GAO's November 2022 recommendation; it is the "final analysis" EPA provided to GAO and is reproduced as Appendix IV of the GAO Report.
- **Supports:** the **published cost anchor and the deadline-timing structure** for IDEA-014, on the agency's own EMTS transaction data (2013–2021; "over 2.2 million RIN transactions for approximately 140 billion RINs", covering separated D6 and D4 RINs). (i) **Price friction around the daily average is measured.** The 24 small refineries that traded on a facility-specific basis "paid on average **1.1 % (1.2 ¢) more per RIN** when buying separated RINs when compared to the average daily price and **0.5 % (0.6 ¢) more per RIN than the largest 20 refiners**"; for D6 RINs, "0.6 % (0.9 ¢) more per RIN than the average daily price"; for D4 RINs, "**2.7 % (2.4 ¢) more per RIN** when compared to the daily average prices and **2.6 % (2.3 ¢) more per RIN than the largest 20 refineries**"; separated by vintage, the same-vintage premium is 1.3 %, the prior-year vintage 0.5 % and the two-years-prior vintage 0.9 % *less*. (ii) **The deadline structure.** "**Compliance dates are generally March 31 of the year following the compliance year**, unless otherwise extended"; obligated parties "can meet compliance obligations using RINs generated in the compliance year and prior year"; and "it is common for companies to transact RINs in the year after they are generated, or even two years after they were generated." (iii) **The memorandum's own sensitivity statement**: under the three alternative modelling assumptions imposed by the GAO Report, "these 24 refineries paid anywhere from **5.3 % less to 7.5 % more** for RINs when compared to the daily average price."
- **Caveats:** the agency's own caveats are binding on the register — "**These estimates should not be interpreted as the actual spot prices** that these 24 refineries paid compared to daily spot market prices. The prices analyzed are self-reported, have limited quality assurance and quality control, in some cases are the result of term contracts unique to the trading parties"; the estimate is **sensitive to modelling assumptions** (−5.3 % to +7.5 %); the price differential is a **counterparty-size** effect, **not** a deadline-timing effect; the memorandum does **not** estimate any pre-/post-deadline price pattern, and it does not estimate a bid-ask spread.
- **Verification:** **index-rendered** on 21 October 2026 from the memorandum's PDF (search-extraction; the "Key Findings", "Purpose", "Data" and "Small Refineries" sections were read) and from the EPA landing page (search-extraction, confirming the 20 December 2022 issue date and the report's status as the response to GAO's Recommendation 1). The PDF was **not** fetched and text-extracted directly. Label: **index-rendered**.
- **Cycle-114 upgrade (21 October 2026) — the memorandum was fetched directly, text-extracted and read, and the label moves to line-verified. Three further passages are added, one of which is a hard constraint on V-012. No earlier content is retracted.**
  1. **Verification.** The copy consulted was fetched directly on 21 October 2026 from the Penn State Ag Law mirror named in this entry's URL line — **HTTP 200, 261,244 bytes** PDF, **13 pages**, text layer extracted to **30,948 characters** and read. Label: **line-verified (fetched directly and text-extracted)**. The EPA landing page named in the URL line was not re-fetched, so the 20 December 2022 issue date remains as previously recorded from the search extraction.
  2. **NEW — the transaction sample, exactly, and the filters applied to it.** The memorandum's Table 1 reads: "**Separated RINs 2,496,671**"; "**Separated RINs; Matching prices for buyer and seller 2,465,581** (−31,090)"; "**Separated RINs; Matching prices; Price Filters; Standard Trades 2,245,685**" (−219,896). And on the buyer/seller control: "**Transactions in EMTS are reported by both the buyer and the seller and so provide a natural check for data consistency. To avoid transactions with potential reporting errors, only transactions where the buyer and seller report the same price are analyzed, as it is unknown whether the buyer or seller's reported price is correct in cases where there is a discrepancy.**" The memorandum also states the data-quality caveat in its own words: "**The self-reporting process raises potential data quality concerns with this data.**"
  3. **NEW — and this is the constraint that decides V-012's data requirement: the trade-type decomposition exists only from 2020.** Verbatim: "**Starting in 2020, EPA made changes to EMTS to split out standard trades into spot, term contract, and consignment trades. Before 2020, details on the type of standard trade are not available. Therefore, trades from 2013 through 2019 may contain consignment trades.**" and "The remaining trades are **standard trades for 2013 through 2019 and either spot or term contract trades for 2020 through 2021**." **This cuts both ways and the register records both directions.** *Favourable:* both moved deadlines — **1 December 2025** for the 2024 compliance year and **1 October 2026** for the 2025 compliance year (S-444) — are **post-2020**, so the spot / term-contract / consignment decomposition **is** available for both, which is what the candidate's forced-flow identification needs. *Adverse:* the *only* published transaction-level price series the agency has analysed is confined to **2013–2021**, so the transaction-level evidence stops **four years before the first moved deadline's pre-window** and the *measurement* of the candidate's effect on the public record is a **weekly volume-weighted average** (S-439, S-440), not a transaction-level series.
  4. **NEW — the register's own count of analysable transactions is now line-verified, and the third limb's detectability bound is computed from it.** The usable transaction count is **2,245,685** standard trades over 2013–2021 (9 years), which is the denominator for the transaction-level minimum-detectable-effect calculation recorded in IDEA-014's Cycle-114 block. The memorandum's own sensitivity band — the 24 small refineries paid "**anywhere from 5.3 % less to 7.5 % more**" for RINs than the daily average price — is the register's **published dispersion proxy** at the transaction level, and the memorandum states that its price differentials "**should not be interpreted as the actual spot prices**".

### S-395 — Chen, Y.-C. and Gwati, R. (2013; updated December 2014) — "FX Options and Excess Returns" / "Understanding Exchange Rate Dynamics: What Does The Term Structure of FX Options Tell Us?"
URL: https://faculty.washington.edu/yuchin/Papers/FXOv3.pdf · update: https://faculty.washington.edu/yuchin/Papers/FXOupdate.pdf
- **Type:** **Faculty working papers** (University of Washington), author-reported, not shown here to be peer-reviewed in the version consulted.
- **Supports:** that the **currency-option implied distribution is a published return-predictor family**, which is what defeats the Cycle-112 FX-options screen. "Using daily options data for six major currency pairs, we show that the options-implied FX risk measures — **standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis** — consistently explain subsequent currency excess returns for horizons between **one week to twelve months**"; the construction uses "a cross section of option contracts (at-the-money, risk reversals and vega-weighted butterflies at 10- and 25 deltas)"; the measures "can predict the full distribution of subsequent excess returns" by quantile regression; "the term structure and cross-correlation of the options-implied moments add further predictive power"; adjusted R² "range from 13 % (USDJPY) to 28 % at 1 month tenor and from 20 % (USDJPY) to 42 % (EURJPY) at the 3M tenor", and 58–84 % for quarterly movements with the term structure; and the authors note "significant breaks in the relationship … around late 2008 and early 2009".
- **Caveats:** working-paper versions consulted; the sample ends in the 2010s and the register does not rely on the magnitudes; the *predictor* is the option-implied distribution of the **exchange rate**, and the dependent variable is **excess returns**, not a market-structure trade.
- **Verification:** **index-rendered** on 21 October 2026 from the two `faculty.washington.edu` PDFs (search-extraction of the abstract, the introduction, the data description and the results tables). Label: **index-rendered**.

## Cycle-109 gap verdicts (2026-10-21) — three bounded state-availability audits (P-4, P-5, P-6) and the P-3 screen

Cycle 109 executed **four pre-registered, bounded screens** (P-3 … P-6, pre-registered in
`cycle_notes.md` before the first fetch). **P-3** was the IDEA-011 first-adopter/repeat-adopter
state-availability question and is logged as **R-057** in `rejected_and_parked.md`; its evidence is the
S-254 and S-267/S-270 entries above. The three audits below are recorded here because they **confirm
existing positions and consume no identifier** — no candidate, family or gap is rejected, re-screened or
re-scored, and no `S-`, `V-`, `R-`, `P-` or `G-` identifier is consumed by any of them. Each verdict is
also written into the candidate's own dossier, in the register's standard form.

**P-4 — IDEA-004 (SLOWCAP-COND): is the correlation-inferred crowding state decision-time and free?
BOUNDED NEGATIVE on the candidate's state as specified, with the binding constraint named correctly.**
- **Limb A (architecture observable): NEGATIVE for the candidate's state.** The candidate's state is the
  **pair-level, netted** convergence crowd, and no published source represents it (G-28, structural null).
  The **correlation-inferred** route does not repair this: S-157 (Lou & Polk) is a **security-level**
  measure of arbitrage activity inferred from return correlations, and the register's own crowding
  inventory is now **eight** published routes (S-026, S-157, S-222, S-242, S-291, S-296, S-325, S-326),
  all of them **aggregate and security- or strategy-level**, none of them pair-level or netted, with
  S-327 reviewing the inventory rather than adding a route.
- **Limb B (decision-time): POSITIVE for the proxy — and this is the finding that sharpens the record.**
  A correlation-based crowding measure is computed from **past returns**, so it is available at the
  candidate's own decision time; S-157's line-verified, Crossref-deposited abstract states that
  crowding/arbitrage-activity intensity is inferred from return correlations — "a measure computable from
  public price data alone". **Timing is therefore not the binding constraint on
  IDEA-004**, contrary to how the register has sometimes framed the crowding problem: the missing thing is
  **identity**, not speed. The published inventory's own point is that these measures "rest on different
  primitives, they are validated by their correlation with subsequent returns, and they have **rarely been
  benchmarked against one another**" (S-327) — so substituting a faster measure would not produce a
  *pair-level* quantity.
- **Limb C (free): NEGATIVE.** The state is not unclaimed: crowding is a published first-order
  conditioning variable, the candidate's own hard-stop flag forbids presenting it as one, and the
  published inventory already contains the candidate's *mechanism* ("persistent aggregate capital flows …
  predict monthly factor returns", S-326) and a published *identification* constraint on any aggregate
  crowding measure — S-327's Proposition 3.18: under homogeneous overlap, "**aggregate crowding is not
  identified from within-date variation by any estimator**", with the corollary that "robustness to
  arbitrary calendar effects and identification of aggregate crowding are therefore **mutually exclusive**
  in any within-date design", and Remark 3.21's priced alternative (deliberately heterogeneous overlap
  across disjoint sub-universes, borrow pools or liquidity tiers).
- **Consequence.** G-28's frozen gap is **confirmed and its unfreezing condition is sharpened in one
  respect**: a re-freezing attempt must supply not merely a *published* crowding measure but a
  **pair-level, netted** one **and** an identification design that survives the within-date exclusion
  result. No score, rank, flag, gap or specification changed; the candidate is unchanged at 63.0.

**P-5 — IDEA-009 (PERP-FUND): is the funding state published, decision-time and free? POSITIVE on the
state; the candidate's binding constraint is elsewhere, and it is not state availability.**
- **Limb A (architecture observable): POSITIVE.** The venue publishes the state itself, its **cap** and
  its **components**: S-321 (the dYdX funding rulebook) publishes the premium component (impact bid and
  impact ask against the index price, impact notional set as 500 USDC divided by the initial-margin
  fraction, the premium a time-weighted average of 60 one-minute premiums over the preceding hour), the
  funding rate (the premium component divided by eight plus a fixed interest-rate component), the
  **hourly** settlement, the **cap** ("The 8-hour rate cap is calculated by 600 % * (Initial Margin -
  Maintenance Margin)", with the tier table, so the BTC-USD eight-hour rate is capped at 600 % × (5 % −
  3 %) = 12 %), and the fact that **governance can adjust** the funding parameters. The register's Cycle-66
  qualifications — the state is **clamped** and **path-dependent** — are therefore **published
  quantities**, not hidden ones.
- **Limb B (decision-time): POSITIVE, with the construction separated out.** The rate for the coming
  settlement is computed from a **preceding** window of published premium data and is therefore fixed
  before the trade; the clamp is a published function of the margin tier; the *percentile* the candidate
  uses is computable at decision time from the venue's published history — but it is a **transformation**,
  not a published series, and the register's own rule treats a constructed state as failing the "published
  state" test. The audit's added precision: **the state is decision-time; the candidate's *conditioning
  variable* is a construction of a decision-time state.**
- **Limb C (free): PARTIAL — the state is free, the *claim* is not unclaimed.** The funding rate is
  published at no cost, but the **unconditional** funding-level reversal the candidate asserts is
  **published prior art**: S-320 (the closest published test of the candidate's own prediction 1: slope
  −0.668, R² = 0.00109, F = 0.388 on 357 degrees of freedom — a near-null for the general form, with
  reversals only at the extremes) and S-310 (the nearest published test, on 274 funding-rate extreme events
  across BTC, ETH and SOL: up-day events revert +1.88 % over the next 24 hours while down-day events
  continue −1.74 %, a +3.62 pp gap reported significant, i.e. the reversal is **conditional on market
  direction**).
- **Consequence.** The audit **confirms that state availability is not what binds IDEA-009** and narrows
  the register's own framing: the candidate's residual is the **unconditional** sign claim against a
  published conditional result, plus the already-recorded venue-transferability and momentum-confound
  qualifications — not a missing state. No score, rank, flag, gap or specification changed; the candidate
  is unchanged at 53.0.

**P-6 — IDEA-014 (RIN-DEADLINE): is the sign-determining net position published before the deadline?
BOUNDED NEGATIVE on the state as specified, with the architecture and the sign-determining quantity
separated.**
- **Limb A (architecture observable): POSITIVE.** The obligation, the deadline and the generation data
  are published instruments: the annual RFS standard and its compliance date (40 CFR 80.1405, 80.1451(f),
  S-128, S-129), the agency's own volume tables and set-aside and waiver mechanics (S-130, S-131), the
  RIN price and generation series (S-132, S-136) and the final rule (S-201).
- **Limb B (decision-time): NEGATIVE for the sign-determining quantity.** The *projected* net obligated
  position is near zero **by construction** — the RVO is calibrated to the agency's own supply projection
  (S-201: the "Analyzed Volumes" are the agency's projected supply, and the rule states the projected
  supply "are very similar to the quantities we projected would be supplied to meet the proposed volume
  requirements") — so the one signed component carried a **+78 % error** (990 million RINs projected for
  2025 against 1,760 million actual), and where a shortfall arose the agency **waived** the volume
  (1.21 billion cellulosic RINs projected against 1.38 billion needed, "a shortfall of approximately 13
  percent") rather than letting a binding obligation form. The **realised** net position publishes only
  after the deadline, and the weekly generation data are lagged.
- **Limb C (free): NEGATIVE.** The only inputs that can determine the sign are **projections** — the
  agency's own supply forecast, the lagged three-year average of exempted volumes (7.55 billion gallons for
  2025), and the small-refinery-exemption reallocations (0.99 billion RINs for 2026, 1.04 billion for
  2027) — so the state is a **forecast with a published error**, not a published measurement.
- **Consequence.** G-20's closure is **confirmed in the three-limb language this cycle used (R-056's
  form)**: the architecture is public and the *sign-determining* quantity is not published before the deadline. The register's other limb — the
  **RFS-deadline price-effect existence limb** — is **not re-run** (it is inconclusive, and no new source
  bearing on it was sought); and the audit states plainly that an R-056-form audit **cannot** settle it,
  because that limb needs a **price** observation, not a state. No score, rank, flag, gap or
  specification changed; the candidate is unchanged at 52.0.

## Cycle 113 sources (2026-10-21) — the Priority-1 position-limits and Commitments-of-Traders screens, the Priority-2 IFRS-18 re-read, and the G-38 RIN cost anchor

### S-398 — 17 CFR Part 150 (Federal speculative position limits; exchange-set limits; position accountability)
*Code of Federal Regulations*, Title 17, Part 150 (Position Limits), as amended by the CFTC's 2020 "Position Limits for Derivatives" final rule (see S-400); the part's own amendment notes read "[86 FR 3463, Jan. 14, 2021]" and "[86 FR 3475, Jan. 14, 2021]".
- **Type:** Primary law (federal regulation).
- **Supports:** the four load-bearing facts of the position-limit screen, quoted verbatim from the fetched text layer.
  1. **The accountability mechanism is a request, not a forced reduction.** § 150.1: "Position accountability means any bylaw, rule, regulation, or resolution that: (1) Is submitted to the Commission pursuant to part 40 of this chapter in lieu of, or along with, a speculative position limit, and (2) Requires an entity whose position exceeds the accountability level to consent to: (i) Provide information about its position to the designated contract market or swap execution facility; and (ii) Halt increasing further its position or reduce its position in an orderly manner, **in each case as requested by** the designated contract market or swap execution facility."
  2. **The spot-month number is a ceiling on an unpublished estimate.** § 150.5(b)(1)(i): a trading facility "shall establish speculative position limits for the spot month **no greater than 25 percent of the estimated spot month deliverable supply**, calculated separately for each month to be listed"; and § 150.3(f): "Each designated contract market listing a core referenced futures contract shall supply to the Commission an estimated spot month deliverable supply **upon request** by the Commission, and may supply such estimates to the Commission at any other time."
  3. **Outside the spot month the obligation is limits *or* accountability.** § 150.5(b)(2)(i): a trading facility "shall adopt **either** speculative position limits **or** position accountability outside of the spot month at a level that is **necessary and appropriate** to reduce the potential threat of market manipulation or price distortion of the contract's or the underlying commodity's price or index."
  4. **The non-spot-month level is anchored to a lagged annual input.** Appendix F(a)(1), an "acceptable practice" for § 150.5(b)(2)(i), lists (i) "The average of historical position sizes held by speculative traders in the contract as a percentage of the average combined futures and delta-adjusted option month-end open interest for that contract for the most recent calendar year" and (iv) "**10 percent of the average combined futures and delta-adjusted option month-end open interest in the contract for the most recent calendar year up to 50,000 contracts, with a marginal increase of 2.5 percent of open interest thereafter.**"
  5. **The reduction horizon is administrative and negotiated.** § 150.3(b)(3)(ii)(B): "the person must bring its position within the Federal speculative position limits **within a commercially reasonable time, as determined by the Commission in consultation with the applicant and the applicable designated contract market or swap execution facility**"; § 150.3(b)(3)(ii)(C): the Commission "will not pursue an enforcement action for a position limits violation" for the review period if the application was submitted in good faith and the position is brought within the limits; and § 150.5(a)(2)(ii)(D) lets an exchange require a position "to exit any referenced contract positions in excess of position limits during the lesser of the last five days of trading or the time period for the spot month".
  6. § 150.3(i) is the **anti-evasion** provision; § 150.2(d) enumerates the core referenced futures contracts; Appendix A is the list of **enumerated bona fide hedges**, positions in which "may exceed Federal speculative position limits for such positions without requesting prior approval"; § 150.5(b)(1) applies the spot-month rule to physical-delivery and, separately, cash-settled referenced contracts.
- **Caveats:** the rule constrains **positions held by a person**; it does not publish any participant's position, so the *headroom* series a candidate would need is absent by construction. The 25 % figure is a **ceiling on the exchange's chosen limit**, not the limit itself. Appendix F is expressly "guidance and acceptable practices", not a mandate, and its own preamble says it "does not state the exclusive means". The enumerated-hedge and spread exemptions mean the constrained population is a strict subset of open interest whose membership is not published. The part as fetched is the text as of the eCFR's 2026-10-01 snapshot.
- **Verification:** fetched directly on 21 October 2026 from `www.ecfr.gov` using the **versioner XML API** (`/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-10-01/title-17.xml?chapter=I&subchapter=B&part=150` — HTTP 200, 25,205 bytes), the tags stripped and the text layer extracted to **115,759 characters** and read. The same endpoint was fetched for 2025-01-01, 2026-01-01, 2026-03-01, 2026-06-01 and 2026-09-01 and returned the identical byte length, so the part is unchanged across that window; the 2026-10-20 request returned HTTP 404 (no such snapshot). The plain HTML page `www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/part-150` returned only 3,191 bytes of navigation chrome and was **not** used. Label: **line-verified (document fetched directly and text-extracted)**.

### S-399 — U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, "Position Limits for Derivatives" (the Commission's own statement of the limits in force)
URL: https://www.cftc.gov/IndustryOversight/MarketSurveillance/SpeculativeLimits/index.htm
- **Type:** The regulator's own primary web statement of the current regime, with the per-contract limit tables and seventeen footnotes.
- **Supports:** the **publication mechanics** of the regime, which is the screen's first question. The 2020 Final Rulemaking "established new and/or amended federal speculative position limits for **25 physically-settled commodity derivative contracts**"; the 25 core referenced futures contracts were "expanded from the **nine** contracts that were previously subject to federal position limits (the 'Legacy Contracts')". The non-spot-month federal limits "are generally set at **10 percent of open interest for the first 50,000 contracts, with an incremental increase of 2.5 percent of open interest thereafter**, and apply on a futures-equivalent basis based on the size of the unit of trading of the relevant CRFC". The **step-downs are published in advance**: for Light Sweet Crude Oil, "6,000 contracts at the close of trading three business days prior to the last trading day of the contract; 5,000 contracts at the close of trading two business days prior to the last trading day of the contract; 4,000 contracts at the close of trading one business day prior to the last trading day of the contract"; for Live Cattle, "600 contracts at the close of trading on the first business day following the first Friday of the contract month; 300 contracts at the close of trading on the business day prior to the last five trading days of the spot month; and 200 contracts at the close of trading on the business day prior to the last two trading days of the spot month". The exchanges file a **monthly report** under § 150.5 and the Commission "will instead leverage cash-market information submitted directly to the exchanges by market participants" under new § 150.5. The general compliance date was **1 January 2022**, with a separate 1 January 2023 date for certain pre-existing positions and the pre-enactment and transition-period swaps.
- **Caveats:** a web statement, not the rule text (S-398 is the rule text and S-400 is the rulemaking document). The page carries no revision date, so "in force" means as read on 21 October 2026. The 10 %/2.5 % construction is stated as a *general* rule ("generally set at"), with the per-contract table governing. The page publishes **no participant's position**, so the headroom state a candidate would need does not exist here either.
- **Verification:** fetched directly on 21 October 2026 from `www.cftc.gov` (HTTP 200, 18,253 bytes of HTML); the text layer was extracted to 25,149 characters and read, including the contract-limit tables and footnotes 1–17. Label: **line-verified (document fetched directly and text-extracted)**.

Document number 2020-25332 · URL: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2021/01/14/2020-25332/position-limits-for-derivatives
- **Type:** Primary rulemaking document (Federal Register), action "Final rule", 86 FR 3236, pages 3236–3493.
- **Supports:** the identity, date and scope of the regime that S-398 codifies, which is what makes the *historical* test (S-401) a test of a superseded regime rather than of the law in force. The abstract records: "The Commission is adopting: **New and amended Federal spot-month limits for 25 physical commodity derivatives**; amended single month and all-months-combined limits for most of the agricultural contracts currently subject to Federal position limits; new and amended definitions for use throughout the position limits regulations, including a revised definition of 'bona fide hedging transaction or position' and a new definition of 'economically equivalent swaps'; amended rules governing exchange-set limit levels and grants of exemptions therefrom; a new streamlined process for bona fide hedging recognitions for purposes of Federal position limits; new enumerated bona fide hedges; and amendments to certain regulatory provisions that would eliminate Form 204 while also enabling the Commission to leverage and receive cash-market reporting submitted directly to the exchanges by market participants."
- **Caveats:** the register relies on the **abstract** and on the codified text in S-398; the 258-page rule text was **not** fetched and text-extracted, so no claim is made about the rule's own economic analysis beyond what its abstract states.

Label: **line-verified (metadata and abstract fetched directly and text-extracted)**.

### S-401 — Till, H. (2013), "An Update on the Debate over Commodity Futures Position Limits", EDHEC-Risk Institute working paper (also SSRN 2641327)
URL: https://www.premiacap.com/publications/EDHEC_Working_Paper_Update_Debate_Commodity_Futures_Position_Limits.pdf · SSRN: https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.2641327 · EDHEC landing page: https://climateinstitute.edhec.edu/publications/update-debate-over-commodity-futures-position-limits
- **Type:** Working paper published on the author's/host's own site and deposited on SSRN ("5 Pages", posted 8 August 2015; the DOI record shows **0 citations**). **The author is a declared opponent of federal position limits**; the register records the advocacy and does not rely on the paper's policy conclusions.
- **Supports:** the closest published test of the position-limit → price relation the screen located, and **its result is a null**. Quoting a CFTC economist memorandum of 21 August 2009: "In our analysis of the impact of position limits, we find **little evidence to suggest that changes from a position limit regime to an accountability level regime or changes in the levels of position limits impact price volatility in either energy or agricultural markets.** Our results are consistent with those found in the existing literature on position limits." The paper also records the surrounding published contest: Jacks (Simon Fraser) on commodity volatility before and after specific contracts were prohibited, and before and after futures markets were established (data "from 1854 through 1990"), and Irwin and Sanders (2011), who found "index positions have led to lower volatility in a statistical sense" across 12 agricultural markets and 2 energy futures markets, June 2006 – December 2009.
- **Caveats:** the memorandum it quotes is from **August 2009** and therefore speaks to the **pre-2020 regime**, whose federal limits were vacated in September 2012 and replaced by the 2020 rule (S-400) — so the paper tests a **superseded regime** and cannot be read as a test of the law in force. The paper is not peer-reviewed, and its "no evidence of an effect" finding is a claim about *volatility*, not about any candidate's sign, and a null on volatility is not a null on every price relation.
- **Verification:** **index-rendered** on 21 October 2026 — the paper's text was read through the search index's rendering of the author's own PDF copy; the document's identity, date (January 2013), author and abstract were corroborated against the SSRN record and the EDHEC Climate Institute landing page as rendered. The PDF was **not** fetched and text-extracted. Label: **index-rendered**.

### S-403 — U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, "Commitments of Traders" (programme page, including the Division of Market Oversight's FAQs)
URL: https://www.cftc.gov/MarketReports/CommitmentsofTraders/index.htm
- **Type:** The regulator's own primary programme page, including the Division of Market Oversight's FAQ responses.
- **Supports:** the COT's **publication mechanics and its structural limits**, verbatim. "Generally, the data in the COT reports is from **Tuesday and released Friday**. The CFTC receives the data from the reporting firms on **Wednesday morning** and then corrects and verifies the data for release by Friday afternoon." "The COT Report is generally published each **Friday at 3:30 pm Eastern Time (US)**, using the data from the immediately preceding Tuesday of that week." "The COT Reports are typically based upon data calculated as of the close of business of **Tuesday** of a given week. It takes **three days** to process the data, and therefore the COT Reports are generally released Friday at 3:30 p.m. Eastern Time (US) of the same week." "Because of resource constraints, we are currently only able to release this report **once a week**." The **coverage rule**: "when the number of reportable Large Traders drops below **20** for a commodity or contract market, it no longer appears in the COT report." The **classification and revision rules**: classifications are "based on the predominant business purpose **self-reported** by traders on the CFTC Form 40"; "CFTC staff does not know specific reasons for traders' positions"; "Due to legal restraints (CEA Section 8 data and confidential business practices), the CFTC **does not publish** information on how individual traders are classified"; "**No**, historical data is not updated once published"; and week-to-week changes arise in three ways — a re-filed Form 40 changing a trader's classification, a new trader's positions altering the previous week's numbers, or an existing trader's exit. Four report types are published: Legacy (data from 15 January 1986), Supplemental (13 agricultural contracts, three classifications including index traders), Disaggregated (four classifications: producer/merchant/processor/user, swap dealers, managed money, other reportables; from 13 June 2006) and Traders in Financial Futures.
- **Caveats:** the FAQ "reflect only the views of DMO staff, and not necessarily those of the Commission"; the release schedule moves with holidays; and the report is a **coarse aggregate of reportable positions only** — traders below the reporting thresholds are absent, so the state is not a census of positioning.
- **Verification:** fetched directly on 21 October 2026 from `www.cftc.gov/MarketReports/CommitmentsofTraders/index.htm` (HTTP 200); the page text was extracted and read, including the DMO FAQs and the report-type descriptions. ### S-404 — NERA Economic Consulting, "Ethanol RIN Market Analysis and Potential Reforms" (18 October 2018), filed in EPA docket EPA-HQ-OAR-2018-0775
- **Type:** Consultancy white paper prepared for Valero Services and filed with the Environmental Protection Agency as an attachment to an industry submitter's comment (grey literature; no peer review; prepared for a party with a commercial interest in the outcome).
- **Supports:** the **published cost anchor for the RIN market that G-38 asks for**. Using the **Roll (1984)** model of the effective bid-ask spread, the paper estimates that RIN spreads reach **up to five times** those of comparable energy markets, that transaction costs are of the order of **five times** those of comparable energy markets, that RIN market **liquidity is of the order of one-tenth** of the comparable energy markets, and that RIN **price volatility is five to ten times** that of the comparable energy markets. It also reports that RIN transaction volume as a percentage of outstanding RINs declines as the compliance expiry approaches over 2015–2018.
- **Caveats:** **index-rendered** — the docket document was read through the search index's rendering and was not fetched and text-extracted. The estimates are **modelled** (Roll), not measured from transaction data, and the paper is advocacy-adjacent; the register therefore relies on the **order of magnitude** and not on the precise multiples. The volume-decay finding bears on the *deadline window*, not on a price effect.
- **Verification:** **index-rendered** on 21 October 2026 (search extraction of the docket document in EPA docket EPA-HQ-OAR-2018-0775; the PDF was not fetched and text-extracted directly). Label: **index-rendered**.
- **Cycle-114 upgrade and wording correction (21 October 2026) — the document was fetched directly, text-extracted, and the register's paraphrase is corrected. No earlier content is retracted, but the wording below replaces the paraphrase it corrects.**
  1. **The entry's label moves from index-rendered to line-verified.** The document was fetched directly on 21 October 2026 from a publicly posted copy of the filed paper — **HTTP 200, 2,309,768 bytes** PDF, 48 pages, text layer extracted to **120,004 characters** and read. The paper's own title page confirms it: "**Ethanol RIN Market Analysis and Potential Reforms**", "**Prepared for Valero Services, Inc.**", "**18 October 2018**", "**NERA Economic Consulting**", "© NERA Economic Consulting". The docket copy the register originally consulted remains at EPA-HQ-OAR-2018-0775; the copy fetched here is a public posting of the same filed paper, and the register records the copy it actually read.
  2. **CORRECTION — the register's paraphrase of the cost anchor was imprecise, and the document's own sentence is different in a way that matters.** The register wrote that "RIN spreads reach **up to five times** those of comparable energy markets, that transaction costs are of the order of **five times** those of comparable energy markets". The paper's own words are: RINs "**(1) are generally five to ten times more volatile than similar energy commodities like oil, ethanol, and natural gas futures, (2) are generally only about one tenth as liquid as comparable commodity futures, (3) have estimated economic transaction costs that peak five times higher than oil, ethanol, and natural gas futures, and (4) frequently transact at prices that defy rational pricing expectations.**" The differences that matter: the transaction-cost claim is a **peak** multiple, not a general one; the paper attributes the **one-tenth** liquidity figure (not "liquidity of the order of one-tenth" as a separate finding — it is the same sentence); and the paper states the **spread** multiple separately in the abstract as effective spreads rising "**up to five times higher**" under the Roll model. **The register's "five times" is therefore right in order of magnitude and wrong as a general statement**: the correct formulation is "**estimated economic transaction costs that *peak* five times higher** than comparable energy futures, with liquidity **generally only about one tenth** as great and volatility **five to ten times** as great." **No published cents-per-RIN round-trip magnitude exists anywhere in the document** — the cost estimates are figure-only — and the register records that limit explicitly, because the third limb's cost floor is then anchored on the *published* same-day traded ranges (S-443) rather than on a modelled number.
  3. **NEW — the volume-decay finding is line-verified and is adverse to the candidate's mechanism.** The paper's own words: "**Figures 5, 6, and 7 below show that transaction volume as a percentage of outstanding RINs declines as compliance expiry approaches for that vintage. This trend is observed for all RIN vintages between 2015 and 2018.**"; "it is clear that for RINs, transaction volume does not increase proportionate to RIN generation or spike as expiry approaches whereas for the energy commodity futures, both transaction volumes and open interest increase significantly as expiry approaches"; and the conclusion: "**The absence of an upward trend in transaction volume relative to available supply as compliance dates approach, particularly when coupled with the paucity of RIN transaction volume, suggests that illiquidity may impede efficient price discovery in the RIN market when it is most needed.**" The candidate's mechanism requires **forced buying** into the deadline; the published evidence is that **liquidity falls into the deadline and price discovery deteriorates precisely there**.
  4. **NEW — the negative-time-value finding is line-verified and it is a second, independent complication.** The paper: "**All three major price sources in the RIN market (EPA, Argus, and OPIS) show that RIN markets violated a fundamental economic expectation over dozens of weeks by pricing RINs closer to expiration above RINs with longer useful lives. This outcome is an inefficient result (referred to as negative time value)**". The candidate's identification is a **within-vintage** comparison across a moved deadline; the published expiry structure is of the *same order of magnitude* as the whole cost floor (S-443: the 2024-vintage D6 traded 1.375¢ below the 2025 vintage on 25 March 2025), so an unidentified vintage effect is **indistinguishable from the effect being tested**.

### S-406 — Cui, L., Lin, S. and Yang, Y.-w. (2026), "Does Classifying Earnings into Operating, Investing, and Financing Categories Enhance Earnings Informativeness? Evidence from Applying IFRS 18 to U.S. Data", *Accounting Horizons*, pp. 1–21
DOI: https://doi.org/10.2308/horizons-2025-080 · published online 6 August 2026, print 1 August 2026 · publisher: American Accounting Association
- **Type:** **Peer-reviewed journal article** with a DOI, indexed by Crossref, with a publisher-supplied abstract.
- **Supports:** the nearest published, post-2010 test of the *accounting-information* content of an IFRS 18-style reclassification, and its verdict is **modest in kind and adverse in magnitude**. The abstract: the study "examines whether classifying earnings into operating, investing, and financing categories, based on the IFRS 18 framework, improves earnings informativeness for U.S. firms"; using "Compustat data from 2003 to 2023", the authors "reclassify GAAP-based earnings components into IFRS 18 categories and construct mandated subtotals—operating profit and profit before financing and income taxes—while holding recognition and measurement constant"; "We find that this classification yields **modest improvements** in out-of-sample forecasts of future performance and returns. It also produces **statistically significant, although economically small**, improvements in explanatory power for stock returns, analyst forecast accuracy and dispersion, as well as higher cross-firm comparability. Overall, the results are consistent with the idea that organizing earnings into economically meaningful categories is associated with modest improvements in the informativeness and comparability of U.S. financial reporting."
- **Caveats:** the design is a **reclassification of historical GAAP data**, not an observation of IFRS 18's implementation — so it is **not** post-implementation market-effect evidence; the sample is US firms, not IFRS adopters; the object is the informativeness of the *subtotals*, not a post-adoption *price drift*; and the register does not treat it as a test of IDEA-011's conditional claim. Under the register's own ordering (G-12), "economically small" is a **magnitude** finding, not a null and not a sign reversal.

### S-407 — De Melo Gaspar Neto, A. (2025), "IFRS 18 and the Global Standardization of Result Subtotals: A Multijurisdictional Econometric Analysis in the Light of Institutional Theory", Harvard Dataverse, DOI 10.7910/DVN/DRXI9F (published 16 December 2025)
- **Type:** **Author-deposited dataset with a description** in an institutional repository — grey literature, single file, no citation record, **not peer reviewed**.
- **Supports:** a multi-jurisdiction econometric study of IFRS 18's cross-country effect on the comparability of operating profit. The description: "This study investigates the impact of IFRS 18 on the standardization of performance subtotals through the lens of institutional theory, critically addressing methodological limitations inherent to the short post-implementation period. Using a hybrid sample of **425 companies (85 per country)** and aggregated data from regulators in the **United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, South Korea, and Brazil** over the period **2015–2024**, we implement a multilevel econometric strategy combining triple fixed-effects panel models with difference-in-differences approaches, instrumental variables, and mediation analysis. Our results, robust to extensive sensitivity tests including statistical power analysis (1−β = 0.89), indicate that the adoption of IFRS 18 is associated with a **42.3% reduction in cross-country dispersion of operating profit** (p < 0.01), an effect mediated by **65%** through the quality of institutional enforcement. Heterogeneity analyses reveal that the effects are **73% larger** in jurisdictions with high-quality enforcement, corroborating institutional theory assumptions. Additionally, we document a **58.7% contraction** in heterogeneous Management Performance Measures (MPMs) intensity (p < 0.01) and a **34.5% increase** in the value relevance of standardized operating profit."
- **Caveats:** grey literature, single author, single file, no peer review and no citation record. The sample spans 2015–2024 — **before** IFRS 18's 1 January 2027 effective date — so the "adoption" studied is a proxied or modelled one rather than an observed implementation, and the author's own description concedes "methodological limitations inherent to the short post-implementation period". The register treats the entry as **mechanism-level and as a competing-conditioner record**, not as a test of IDEA-011's conditional claim.

### S-418 — USDA, Economic Research Service, "Sugar and Sweeteners Outlook: March 2021", SSS-M-391 (15 March 2021)
URL: https://www.ers.usda.gov/sites/default/files/_laserfiche/media/16435/SSS-M-391.pdf
- **Type:** Primary government outlook report (USDA ERS), the agency's published account of **how the US sugar price is formed** in its own model. This is the single most decision-relevant document in the Cycle-114 screen.
- **Supports:** the **mechanism test of the construction** — the state of the world *before* the exhaustion event, and the agency's own price-formation statement. Verbatim: "**In the model, U.S. tariff-rate quota (TRQ) imports are not responsive to price movements, but only change in the event that Mexico would not have sufficient surplus sugar to supply U.S. import requirements. However, the level of high-tier imports is responsive whenever the margin between the U.S. and world prices exceeds the high duty and freight costs.** In the high world price scenario, high-tier imports fall as a result of the narrowing spread between U.S. and world prices. On the flip side, high-tier imports are elevated in the low world price scenario as the wider spread between U.S. and world prices provides a greater incentive to pay the tariff to import." And on the *measured* spread: "**The spread between the U.S. refined beet sugar and world refined sugar prices was around 28 cents per pound from July through September, then fell sharply to less than 20 cents per pound** as the U.S. beet sugar price declined based on projections of a much-improved 2020/21 beet crop." And on the step: "for raw sugar, the tariff is set at **33.87 cents per kilogram or 15.4 cents per pound**; for refined sugar, it is set at **35.74 cents per kilogram or 16.21 cents per pound**", with "the usual cost of freight and associated logistics can be as low as **2-4 cents per pound for raw sugar and 5-6 cents per pound for refined sugar**."
- **Supports (second, decisive for Route 4):** the *identity of the price series*. The report's own table carries three price rows — "**World raw sugar price (U.S. cents per pound)**", "**Raw sugar price, 3q No. 16 (U.S. cents per pound)**" and "**Refined beet sugar price, 3q Midwest (U.S. cents per pound)**" — i.e. the **US domestic price is a published cash/spot series**. **Cycle-114 CORRECTION (21 October 2026):** this entry originally added the clause "and both listed futures references (No. 11, No. 16) are **world** raw-sugar contracts". **That clause was wrong and is withdrawn.** The direct read of the exchange's own specification at **S-427** establishes that **ICE Futures U.S. Sugar No. 16 is a US domestic contract** — it "prices the physical delivery of US-grown (or foreign origin with duty paid by deliverer) raw cane sugar at one of five U.S. refinery ports as selected by the receiver" (contract symbol **SF**). The correct statement is that **the world leg is listed (No. 11, FOB country of origin, S-419) and the domestic leg is also listed (No. 16, five US refinery ports, S-427)**, and that the *refined beet* leg, which is the price the register's own construction and the ERS report both use for the measured US–world spread, is **not** a listed contract at all — it is the published "Refined beet sugar price, 3q Midwest" cash series. The withdrawal matters because the "the domestic leg is not tradable" reading would have been a *false* kill, and this cycle's screen was required to record it as a correction rather than let it stand.
- **Caveats:** the 2021 vintage describes the 2020/21 crop year and its own price environment; the *structural* statements (TRQ volume price-insensitive, high-tier volume spread-responsive) are statements about ERS's **model** and are the agency's characterisation, not a law; the 94,000-STRV "usual shortfall" and the FTA quota volumes have since changed.
- **Verification:** fetched directly on 21 October 2026 — **HTTP 200, 634,078 bytes** PDF, text layer extracted and read. Label: **line-verified (fetched directly and text-extracted)**.

URLs: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1858985/000185898526000018/onholdingag-20260630_d2.htm (On Holding AG) · https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/887028/000162828026050377/R12.htm (Rio Tinto Ltd) · https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1429937/000142993726000010/exhibit991-63026.htm (B2Gold Corp) · https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1453015/000162828026051245/bldp063026-ex991fs.htm (Ballard Power Systems Inc.) · https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1756607/000175660726000004/eqx-20260630financialstate.htm (Equinox Gold Corp) · https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1846715/000184671526087513/ea030083701ex99-1.htm (Eco Wave Power Global AB) · https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1364125/000106299326004092/exhibit99-1.htm (Western Copper & Gold Corp) · https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1567529/000121390026088030/ea029970701ex99-3.htm (Kamada Ltd) · https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1894693/000121390026090274/ea030200001ex99-2.htm (SaverOne 2014 Ltd)
- **Type:** Primary issuer interim disclosures, filed with the US SEC as Form 6-K exhibits by foreign private issuers (IFRS filers, several outside the EU and therefore **outside ESMA's supervisory perimeter**). The sample was selected by the EDGAR full-text search API (`efts.sec.gov`) on the phrase "IFRS 18" restricted to Form 6-K filings dated 1 July – 15 September 2026, and the first nine hits in filing-date-descending order were read in full.
- **Supports:** the **Cycle-114 Priority-2 observation** that the ESMA-mandated pre-adoption disclosure is being delivered in the 2026 interim season in **sign-bearing but unquantified** form, and that the **encouraged** quantified limb is not being exercised. Verbatim, per issuer:
  - **On Holding AG** (6-K, 11 Aug 2026): "The Company's current assessment of IFRS 18 impacts indicates that certain income and expense amounts are expected to be reclassified within the consolidated statements of income … **These expected presentation changes will not affect reported net income** … **On is currently finalizing its assessment of the impact of adopting IFRS 18, which will be effective January 1, 2027.**"
  - **Rio Tinto Ltd** (6-K): "**Based on analysis to date, we expect that the adoption of IFRS 18 will change the current structure of the consolidated income statement, and how the operating profit is calculated.** Under IFRS 18, net interest related to pension and healthcare benefits currently included within operating profit will be reclassified to the financing category … **Finance income and foreign exchange gains or losses on bank balances currently included within financing items will move to the investing category.**"
  - **B2Gold Corp** (6-K, 7 Aug 2026): "**The Company is still continuing to assess and quantify the effect of IFRS 18 on our consolidated financial statements.**"
  - **Ballard Power Systems Inc.** (6-K, 31 Jul 2026): "**The impact of adoption of IFRS 18 is currently being assessed by the Corporation. Based on a preliminary assessment, the Corporation expects that the adoption of IFRS 18 will change the presentation of the statement of loss and comprehensive loss** …"
  - **Equinox Gold Corp** (6-K, 5 Aug 2026): "**The Company is in the process of assessing the impact of IFRS 18 on its consolidated financial statements. Based on its preliminary assessment, the Company has identified the following possible impacts of initial application of IFRS 18** …" followed by the reclassification directions.
  - **Eco Wave Power Global AB** (6-K, 11 Aug 2026): "**The Company is currently assessing the new requirements of IFRS 18.**"
  - **Western Copper & Gold Corp** (6-K, 7 Aug 2026): "**Management is currently assessing the effect of this new standard on our financial statements.**"
  - **Kamada Ltd** (6-K, 12 Aug 2026): "**The Company is currently assessing the impact of the Standard on its financial statements. As of June 30, 2026, the Company is currently evaluating the impact of this new standard.**"
  - **SaverOne 2014 Ltd** (6-K, 14 Aug 2026): Note E "New Standards not yet effective", describing the three new categories, the two new subtotals, the MPM guidance, the aggregation/disaggregation guidance and the IAS 7 amendments.
  - **Across all nine: no issuer discloses a quantified expected effect on operating profit or on any other subtotal.** In **five of the nine** (B2Gold, Ballard, Equinox, Eco Wave, Western Copper) the assessment is explicitly **not concluded**; in a sixth (On Holding) it is "currently finalizing"; in two (Rio Tinto, SaverOne) the disclosure is the standard's own structure with a preliminary or unstated assessment.
- **Caveats:** the sample is a **first-nine-by-filing-date** convenience sample from a single search route, not a random or exhaustive census of the 2026 interim season, and the register makes **no claim about the season's overall quantification rate** beyond these nine documents; several of these issuers are **not** ESMA-supervised, so the *mandated* limb (IAS 8 paragraph 30) rather than ESMA's *expectation* is the binding instrument for them; the EDGAR full-text search is a **US** filing route and therefore structurally misses EU-only issuers, which is why the register separately holds four EU-side first observations (S-409 Bayer, S-410 Novartis, S-411 Nestlé Capital Corporation, S-412 HSBC).
- **Verification:** each of the nine documents was **fetched directly** from `www.sec.gov` on 21 October 2026 with a declared User-Agent — all nine returned **HTTP 200** — and in each case the HTML tags were stripped and the IFRS 18 note read in the document's own text. Label: **line-verified (all nine fetched directly and text-extracted)**. The issuer's identity for the two non-6-K-indexed filers was confirmed through the SEC submissions API (`data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK0000887028.json` → "RIO TINTO LTD"; and the EDGAR full-text search result metadata for the others).

### S-438 — Xuan, H. (2026), "Funding Rates and the Conditional Informativeness of Order Flow: Evidence from the Binance XAUUSDT Gold Perpetual", SSRN working paper, DOI 10.2139/ssrn.6872638
URL: https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6872638
- **Type:** Preprint working paper (SSRN / Elsevier SSRN), posted content.
- **Supports:** **G-37 limb (a)** — the existence of a **within-contract** (single-instrument, XAUUSDT perpetual) study of the funding rate, published in 2026. The register records it as evidence that the *within-contract time-series* form of the funding–return question **is being worked on in the current literature**, which is the context in which the gap is stated. The retrieved abstract (index-rendered, below) reports a **positive funding-rate → return relation** at five-, fifteen- and thirty-minute horizons (t = 2.22, 2.95, 3.71) together with a **negative funding-by-order-flow interaction** at all three horizons (t = −2.64, −2.28, −2.26), which the paper characterises as a funding-based positioning-and-reversal channel rather than a classical informed-trading channel. Effects are small and not profitable after trading costs. This is the nearest citable instance of the within-contract funding–return sign question G-37 addresses.
- **Caveats:** the **bibliographic record** was line-verified from Crossref (title, author Hezhen Xuan, The University of Sydney – Discipline of Economics, year 2026, publisher Elsevier BV, type posted-content, DOI). The **abstract was not retrieved from the paper itself** — `papers.ssrn.com` returns HTTP 403, SSRN abstract page returns HTTP 403, Semantic Scholar returns HTTP 404 — but the abstract text below was obtained from the SSRN search-index rendering via web search, so it is **index-rendered and not line-verified**; no quotation from it may be treated as extracted from the document body. The Crossref record carries no abstract; OpenAlex's `abstract_inverted_index` is empty.
- **Retrieved abstract content (index-rendered, SSRN search-index rendering; not line-verified):** "One of the key institutions in a perpetual futures contract is the funding-rate mechanism, yet its role in information processing remains largely unexplored. This paper examines the question using the Binance XAUUSDT gold perpetual, a commodity-linked cryptocurrency perpetual introduced in January 2026, and 203,037 one-minute observations from its early trading period. In this benchmark-anchored instrument, whose reference value is discovered off-exchange, the order-flow proxies used in the paper have no unconditional predictive ability: trade-based order-flow imbalance is insignificant in-sample, produces negative out-of-sample predictive R-squared, and fails to survive multiple-testing corrections. The active channel is instead the funding mechanism. The funding rate positively predicts returns at five-, fifteen-, and thirty-minute horizons (t = 2.22, 2.95, 3.71), while the funding-by-orderflow interaction is negative and significant at all three horizons (t =-2.64,-2.28,-2.26). The positive funding coefficient captures the persistence and directional component of leveraged-driven demand, whereas the negative interaction captures the marginal reversal effect of additional buying pressure when positioning is already crowded. Session-level patterns around the European window are stable in sign but do not survive multiple-testing correction, alternative window definitions, alternative normalisations, or non-overlapping sampling schemes; event-study and placebo evidence do not isolate the London afternoon fix as the source of the pattern. The effects are small and not profitable once trading costs are considered. The evidence points to a funding-based positioning-and-reversal channel rather than a classical informed-trading channel in commodity-linked perpetuals." Posted: 22 Jun 2026 (date written June 03, 2026). 19 pages.
- **Verification:** bibliographic record fetched directly on 21 October 2026 from Crossref — **HTTP 200**; OpenAlex — **HTTP 200**; Semantic Scholar — **HTTP 404**; `papers.ssrn.com` — **HTTP 403**. Abstract retrieved on 21 October 2026 via web search of the SSRN search-index rendering — **index-rendered, not line-verified**. Label: **bibliographic record line-verified (Crossref, fetched directly); abstract index-rendered (search-index rendering), body not verified**.

### S-449 — Ambrose, B. W., Cai, K. N. & Helwege, J. (2012), "Fallen Angels and Price Pressure", *The Journal of Fixed Income* 21(3), pp. 74–86
URL: https://doi.org/10.3905/jfi.2012.21.3.074

### S-454 — Mesfin, M. (2026), "A Validated Volatility-Volume-Gap Classifier for Regime Identification in MNQ Intraday Data", arXiv:2605.11423 [q-fin.TR] (v1 12 May 2026, v3 16 September 2026)
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11423 · DOI: https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.11423 · **additional carriers located in Cycle 126:** https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6750442 (the same paper on SSRN, a preprint server) and the author-hosted copy https://mathias-mesfin.netlify.app/mesfin_2026_vvg_classifier_mnq_final.pdf
- **Type:** **arXiv preprint**, single author, **not peer-reviewed**. The paper's own subject classification is q-fin.TR / q-fin.CP / q-fin.ST; 13 pages, 4 figures; the page records "Comments: … literature organized around central claim" and a v3 revision on 16 September 2026.
- **Supports (for IDEA-009 and gap G-37):** the **first named, citable, published instance of the general proposition G-37's open limb asks about** — a **within-contract** reversal-versus-continuation **sign flip** — and, at the same time, the first **published null on tradability** of such a rule. Read from the abstract page's own text: the **Volatility-Volume-Gap (VVG)** classifier uses "three simultaneously elevated pre-market conditions: absolute overnight gap, absolute first-30-minute return, and first-bar volume relative to a 20-day rolling baseline"; it is "evaluated on 947 trading days of five-minute data from 2021-2025, with all thresholds computed on an expanding window to prevent lookahead bias"; it "activates on roughly 4.4% of sessions (40 days)"; classifier days "exhibit measurably distinct behavior: 77.6% reverse from their intraday peak before the close, mean peak-to-close giveback of 11.73 points, and a 25.6 basis point next-day return spread versus non-classifier days". The **sign flip** is explicit: "Year-by-year analysis reveals substantial path heterogeneity — **2024 classifier days closed at mean +40.74 points while 2025 crashed to −42.48** — which is the core obstacle for any directional strategy". The **null** is equally explicit: "**Eight directional configurations were tested. None passed.** Best result: T = 1.46, mean net +7.80 points, 127 OOS trades, reversal entry with OLS regression filter. 2024 broke year stability. Binding constraints are the 40-day sample (roughly 10 per year) and regime-dependent intraday behavior that no fixed rule survives across all test years. The classifier is preserved as a research asset: it identifies a real behavioral phenomenon but cannot generate a deployable directional signal under current constraints."
- **Why it matters for the register:** it is **not** a peer-reviewed source and **not** a funding–return relation, so it **cannot** close G-37's remaining limb, and the register records it as a **qualifying** entry rather than as an answer. It does three things. (i) It shows the limb's **substance** — a within-contract reversal↔continuation sign flip that flips between years — is **already in the literature in named, citable form**, so the limb's premise is not in doubt; what is in doubt is whether the flip can be *traded*, and this source's own authors answer **no**. (ii) It supplies the **nearest published analogue of IDEA-009's third hard-stop** (the regime gate) and that analogue carries an explicit **null on tradability after costs**, which raises the register's prior against a regime gate as a *rescue* for a within-contract sign flip. (iii) It **sharpens G-37's re-screen condition**, which now reads: *a peer-reviewed source establishing a within-contract trailing-sign flip in the funding–return relation, or a peer-reviewed version of the S-454 classifier work applied to a funding state.*
- **Caveats:** **not peer-reviewed** (an arXiv preprint; the register's G-37 condition requires peer review, and the condition is therefore **still unmet**); the relation is an **intraday price-path** relation, **not** a funding–return relation; the flipping variable is the day's regime, **not** the within-contract trailing sign of the funding–return relation, which is what the limb asks about; the instrument is **Micro E-mini Nasdaq-100 futures**, not a perpetual; the sample is 40 classifier-positive sessions over five years (≈10 per year); the results are the author's own and are not reproduced here; and the register uses it for **the existence and character of the phenomenon and of its null only**, not for any parameter.
- **Verification:** the **arXiv abstract page was fetched directly on 21 October 2026 — HTTP 200** — and the passages above are read in the page's own text, including the submission history ("v1 … Tue, 12 May 2026", "v3 … Wed, 16 Sep 2026"), the DOI ("https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.11423") and the subject classification.
